We implemented two FL algorithms—FedAvg and a novel approach called Negative Sample Federated Averaging (NSFedAvg)—and compared their performance against two central deep learning methods: Deep Learning with Prior Knowledge (DLKP) and RetinaNet. Deep learning models were trained on the full dataset and evaluated against the federated models to determine if there was a significant performance drop due to the federated approach. Additionally, we tested whether training solely with a specific disease category would result in superior performance for that category compared to training on the entire dataset. Our findings indicate no substantial difference in performance between NSFedAvg and FedAvg. Furthermore, both federated models outperformed the corresponding central models (RetinaNet and NSFedAvg) in terms of IoU and F1 scores, though they required more training time. Surprisingly, the NSFedAvg method achieved higher accuracy than the FedAvg model. These results suggest that the choice of FL algorithm does not appear to be a critical factor in achieving high performance on a given task. However, the paper does not claim that NSFedAvg is universally superior to FedAvg across all tasks. To our knowledge, this is the first study to compare federated models with central models on the same task using medical X-ray images. The results demonstrate that private training yields higher accuracy than central training, confirming the benefits of federated learning. We also observed that NsFedAvg can enhance performance on specific disease categories without requiring the central server to access the original images. Overall, these findings suggest that NSFedAvg could serve as a viable alternative to standard RetinaNet training, provided the central server cannot access the original data. However, generalizing to new environments remains difficult when significant changes occur within the target domain. Such major shifts are often detectable through environmental feedback; consequently, it is crucial to design a novel model that can adapt to generalization after receiving feedback following detection of a significant domain shift. We address this requirement by proposing a new framework capable of adapting to generalization in complex settings, specifically targeting scenario changes in scenario segmentation. Our approach combines a semi-supervised self-attention mechanism with a graph neural network (SAGAN) to achieve data-efficient learning. By leveraging self-attention to extract features from input images and utilizing SAGAN to model relationships among important road elements, we demonstrate through experiments that our method effectively handles significant shifts in scene characteristics. The primary channel for this accretion is believed to be gas from the central molecular zone (CMZ), which can be directly observed in radio wavelengths. This study presents a comprehensive spectral line survey of the CMZ in the host galaxy of SMBH 3C 390-X, conducted using the NOEMA interferometer at the Plateau de Bure (France) and the VLA at the Very Large Array (USA). Key molecular species detected include $^{12}$CO, $^{13}$CO, C$^{18}$O, C$^{18}O$ (J=3-2), CS (J=2-1), c-C$_3$H$_2$, m-C$_4$H$_2$, o-C$_4$H$_2$, s-C$_5$H$_2$, and C$_{6}$H (J=3-2). By analyzing spectral line energy distributions (SLEDs) and comparing molecular gas kinematics with observational data on the broad line region (BLR), we identify a cold gas reservoir in 3C 390-X that may supply the accretion disk beneath the BLR. We demonstrate that gas inflow toward the nucleus is prevalent within the CMZ, driven by either secular evolution or an induced bar. Specifically, we observe molecular gas with a total mass of approximately $1.5\cdot 10^{8} M_{\odot}$ moving inward with a velocity of roughly 100 km/s. We argue that a portion of this inflowing gas is available for direct accretion by the central black hole. Furthermore, we show that 3C 390-X possesses a large volume of cold dust gas, implying that the total gas mass in 3C 390-X may be even greater. These findings support the theory of "unveiled" direct feeding of the accretion disk. Our results align with recent studies on 3C 390-X and provide a framework for investigating the connection between SMBHs and their galaxy hosts. Our findings confirm that these galaxies host a mass function of red giants that aligns with local evolution at a fixed star-to-stellar mass ratio of 0.006. Furthermore, the MaNGA integral field data reveals no significant spatial variation in the properties of these mass functions. Consequently, the star formation histories of these high-redshift galaxies must adhere to pressure-regulated models featuring short e-folding times of 400 Myr and long e-folding times of 4 Gyr, necessitating a galaxy merger-driven star formation episode during the last 4 Gyr. This conclusion is supported by MaNGA integral field observations indicating an increase in the specific star formation rate from the center to the outskirts. The presence of red giants in galaxies at $z=2.25$ implies that star formation rates were elevated in the past and have since declined, reinforcing the concept of secular evolution in massive galaxies at high redshifts. These results underscore the critical role of stellar populations in constraining the physical processes of galaxy evolution at the peak of cosmic star formation. The MaNGA-Deep dataset is accessible at https://ngdc.cnsdc.cn/catalogs/MANGA-Deep/index.html.

Abstract: We show that multi-task learning enhances the reconstruction of satellite data across various applications.

Learning from satellite data is critical for monitoring Earth's surface and supporting applications like climate modeling and environmental science. As satellite sensors evolve and become more complex, their outputs are often incompatible with traditional processing methods. To address this, we developed a unified multi-task deep learning framework capable of analyzing and reconstructing imagery from multiple satellite sensors. We define a generalized model for multi-scale image data and introduce a multi-task convolutional neural network (MTCNN) designed to reconstruct sharp estimates from subsampled inputs. Our approach is evaluated on real satellite imagery and compared against other deep learning architectures. The results confirm that our multi-task framework outperforms state-of-the-art remote sensing techniques and other supervised deep learning methods. Our code can be found at https://github.com/WeberMATH/Convolutional-neural-networks-for-image-reconstruction-from-multi-scale-satellite-sensors, and a web demo is available at http://satellite-data.maths.lse.ac.uk.

Distinguished from other approaches, our method yields a unique result because it eliminates the arbitrary selection of a basis required by other formalisms. Furthermore, our findings illuminate the origin of measurement irreversibility within quantum mechanics. We apply the derived master equation to the simplest open quantum system: a qubit interacting with a thermal environment. This model is widely utilized to describe weak continuous measurements and the flow of information from the system to the measurement apparatus. By analyzing the master equation, we demonstrate its ability to describe the measurement process. Our results indicate a significant decline in specific star formation rate (SSFR) as stellar mass increases, with SSFR rising approximately 0.5 dex at a given stellar mass when moving from z = 0 to z = 4. Furthermore, we find that the SHMR shifts toward lower SSFR values at higher redshifts for a given stellar mass, with slopes of dSSFR/dln(M_sh/M_sun) = -0.60, -0.53, and -0.47 at z = 0, 2, and 4, respectively. This trend suggests that galaxies within massive halos experienced more intense star formation in the early universe compared to the current epoch. Additionally, our findings reveal a steeper dependence on cosmic time for high-mass galaxies than for their lower-mass counterparts, implying that the most massive galaxies experienced more dramatic changes in their star formation histories over time. These outcomes are consistent with the widely adopted "downsizing" scenario. Finally, we observe a more pronounced SHMR slope for z = 4 galaxies than for their lower-redshift counterparts, a distinction that becomes more apparent when excluding the highest-mass galaxies. This suggests that the most massive galaxies undergo more significant evolutionary changes over time, likely through feedback mechanisms such as AGN feedback that suppress star formation. This interpretation is supported by our finding that the SHMR becomes flatter with increasing redshift when considering only low-mass galaxies. The methodology and techniques employed in this study are publicly accessible at our MRC-Stacking website.

to address General Group Graphical Lasso (General GGLasso) and Group Graphical Lasso (GGLo) tasks, incorporating a feasibility verification tool for lasso problems. The General GGLasso method extends the GGLasso approach to leverage structured correlations within group variables, while the GGLo method further exploits column group structure in the design matrix to enhance efficiency. GGLasso offers an interface parallel to Numpy that enables direct graph post-processing, such as calculating Conditional Mutual Information (CMD) or Partial Mutual Information (PMI), with improved speed. Additionally, the library includes a graph visualization module capable of rendering graphs with circular, force-directed, or heat-map layouts, allowing for direct entropy computation at each node. Our implementation features a General GGLasso solver with column-wise complexity of $O(N_1N_2P^2+N^2P)$ and a standard GGLasso solver with column-wise complexity of $O(NNP)$. Both methods support an iterative interface that facilitates direct graph post-processing and allows for General GGLasso verification using a group lasso solver, thereby widening the applicable problem range. Our analysis indicates that the object's free-free emission is comparable to its extinction of background starlight. Furthermore, if the central core of the object is compact and the total mass remains constant, the emission flux density decreases as the total mass increases; for the largest mass configurations, the mass is distributed such that the extension is significantly larger than the region containing the half-mass. We also examine the potential for free-free emission to be produced by the ionization of the interstellar medium through the object's fast winds. While the physical conditions within the object preclude self-ionization, our results suggest that fast ionizing photons can escape its surface. Consequently, the ratio of free-free to kinetic luminosity, along with the object's total fast ionizing luminosity, offers a means to constrain the total mass and the internal structure of the object. Finally, while free-free emission from the interstellar medium is difficult to distinguish from the object itself, it can be separated if the object's fast ionizing luminosity is derived from nuclear processes. The VOWS (Voice Processing) system integrates three key tasks into a unified interface that allows users to switch between processes and access a history of previous results. This paper details the algorithms underlying VOWS, which combine traditional and state-of-the-art methods for voice activity detection and pitch estimation. By leveraging the strengths of each algorithm and performing detection and tracking concurrently, the system significantly improves tracking accuracy and reduces false positives. The vVOWS backend is implemented in C++, while the Python frontend enables rapid prototyping and provides a user-friendly interface. The vVOWS backend supports cross-platform operation (Linux, Windows, and Mac OS X) and can process audio in real-time. This approach builds upon the globally convergent forward-backward algorithm with deviations from [26] and integrates the extrapolation technique found in the Chambolle-Pock method [15]. Supersymmetric Standard Model (NMSSM) framework, focusing on explaining the recently observed Higgs boson with mass approximately 95 GeV. The study examines scenarios where light charginos and neutralinos exist, analyzing their implications for both experimental data and theoretical constraints. Regarding experimental inputs, we incorporate the 13 TeV LHC data from 2015, alongside constraints derived from chargino and neutralino searches by the ATLAS and CMS collaborations. Additionally, the analysis includes limits from the Large Electron-Positron (LEP) collider regarding additional Higgs bosons and sparticles, as well as limits from the Virtual Institute for Accelerator-based Muon Scattering (VAMOS) regarding spin-1/2 charginos and neutralinos. For theoretical analysis, we consider the Muon $g-2$ anomaly and impose conditions of perturbativity and vacuum stability across all energy scales. Given the specific NMSSM parameter space investigated, we developed a tailored analytic expression for the chargino mass to ensure precise calculations of the neutralino mass matrix. Our findings indicate that the muon $g-2$ anomaly can be resolved within the examined NMSSM space. Furthermore, if the lightest chargino is identified as a dark matter candidate within this framework, it can satisfy the observed dark matter density. In this scenario, the corresponding lightest neutralino must fall within the mass range of roughly 10 to 100 GeV to comply with all experimental and theoretical limits. Finally, we explore the possibility of detecting these light states at the High-Luminosity LHC and propose a future muon-based collider as a viable discovery tool for these light sparticles within the NMSSM. This study investigates the effects of integrating multicast beamforming with other beamforming techniques in a heterogeneous network environment. To address this, we propose a new multicast beamforming algorithm, the Distributed Semidefinite Relaxation Beamforming (DRBM), which merges the successively perturbed semidefinite relaxation (SPSR) algorithm with a beamforming refinement mechanism. We analyze two specific scenarios: first, training SGD on a single learner and second, training SGD across an ensemble of learners. For the initial scenario, we determine the optimal compression strategy that minimizes training distortion for SGD and evaluate its impact on convergence rates and accuracy. We demonstrate that the widely used average gradient method is a necessary optimal solution. This study examines the impacts of various error and failure scenarios within an NDN environment, focusing on network congestion and routing loops as primary failure modes. To address these issues, a robust error handling protocol (REHP) is proposed, designed to be application-transparent and capable of mitigating errors in both peer-to-peer (P2P) and publisher-subscriber architectures. The primary objective of REHP is to ensure fair and efficient data delivery to interested subscribers while minimizing the adverse effects of errors and failures. Evolutionary algorithms (EAs) are widely recognized for effectively solving combinatorial optimization problems, yet they often struggle to deliver high-performance solutions for complex tasks. This paper proposes a novel quantization strategy designed to enhance EA performance by integrating it with standard approaches through a straightforward mechanism. This integration allows solutions to be represented at multiple granularities simultaneously. By enabling information exchange across different levels of abstraction, the method facilitates both gradual refinement and continuous coarse-graining of candidate solutions during search. This flexibility allows the algorithm to explore a wider range of solutions while maintaining a diverse population to avoid local optima. Experiments conducted on various functions from the Bencz and Zuzan benchmark suites demonstrate that the proposed method significantly outperforms conventional EAs, achieving an average improvement of approximately 20%. The open-source implementation can be accessed at \url{https://github.com/kyuhyunseong/EvolutionaryQuantization}.

The proliferation of Internet of Things (IoT) devices has created a promising environment for next-generation artificial intelligence, offering vast data volumes for diverse applications. However, deploying machine learning models on IoT devices presents significant challenges, including high computational demands, memory constraints, and limited processing capabilities. Although neural network quantization has been proposed to address these issues, it often degrades accuracy when applied to data with complex statistical properties. This study proposes a solution that quantizes neural networks specifically tailored to the statistical distributions of individual IoT devices, thereby enhancing both inference speed and classification accuracy. to manage bug reports and other work items, yet maintaining accurate information within these systems is a complex challenge. Because work item data is typically non-structured and time-intensive to input manually, organizations often resort to manual processes or simple text templates. While templates facilitate rapid entry, the resulting data often lacks the structure necessary for effective maintenance. Automating work item data maintenance is crucial for keeping information current and for managers to make informed decisions. Although Natural Language Processing (NLP) has been applied to ITS data, its potential for enhancing data quality remains underexplored. This paper investigates the NLP techniques employed to enhance specific attributes of work items. Through a systematic literature review, we analyzed 92 papers to identify application areas, specific attributes improved, and the methods used to perform these enhancements. Our research indicates that 68.5% of the studies focused on text classification. By examining the types of studies and their applications, we aim to inspire new applications and encourage the adoption of NLP techniques to improve data quality in ITSs. Furthermore, we discuss challenges and propose future research directions, including the need to improve organization-specific data, expand attribute enhancement beyond text and labels, and explore organizational applications of NLP. Finally, we recommend that researchers consider integrating multiple NLP techniques and emphasize the importance of evaluating both individual technique performance and their combined effectiveness. Additionally, given that NLP models are sensitive to domain variations, we recommend testing them in real-world settings to validate results and gather organizational feedback. This body of work serves as a foundation for researchers to build upon and help bridge the gap between academic studies and practical application.

While recent DML studies typically aim to minimize the global risk of a centralized statistical loss by averaging local models, this approach is often impractical because it requires precise loss functions that are difficult to define in real-world scenarios. Furthermore, this loss minimization strategy can lead to a significant generalization gap when the test data distribution differs from the training distribution. To overcome these challenges, we introduce a novel differentially private DML framework utilizing game-theoretic loss games (GTLG). In this proposal, agents engage in learning a Nash Equilibrium (NE) from observed data to reach solutions that are both generally effective and privacy-respecting. We analyze the convergence of the proposed GTLG-based DML algorithm when combined with perturbed gradient descent (PGD) and demonstrate convergence to a neighborhood of the NE under mild assumptions. Extensive experiments on large-scale differentially private DML tasks confirm our theoretical findings and illustrate the method's efficacy. accelerator designed to propel electron packets to terahertz (THz) frequencies within a compact space of less than one cubic centimeter. The proposed system utilizes an integrated grating structure to create a motionless accelerator, where the spatial arrangement of electrodes ensures that the electron's acceleration path aligns with the electric field as the grating's frequency and phase vary. Through full-band numerical simulations, we achieved an acceleration gradient exceeding 100 GV/m, allowing 50 MeV electrons to reach THz levels in under 50 picoseconds. Furthermore, a pixelated electrode design was simulated to mitigate the impact of breakdown, which is a critical constraint for on-chip implementations. These findings indicate that the entire accelerator can be integrated into a single cubic millimeter. In addition to applications in medical imaging and cancer therapy, this motionless accelerator holds potential for use as a high-brightness electron source for free-electron lasers and as a precise time-of-flight detector for neutrino mass measurements. This represents a significant advancement in accelerator technology, positioning on-chip multi-grating accelerators as a viable alternative to bulk accelerators for generating and accelerating electrons to energies above 50 MeV. Such a device could serve as a compact, high-current source for next-generation medical imaging, radiotherapy, and high-energy physics experiments. This paper establishes the undecidability of the word problem for the monoid of bijections acting on any nontrivial free monoid of subsets of $\Lambda^{\ast}$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the word problem for these bijection monoids is strictly harder than that for the classical monoid of bijections on a free monoid of words. The associated decision problems for these monoids are undecidable, and in certain instances, they are strictly more complex than the word problem for Dyck languages. This paper introduces a novel algorithm for solving these quadratic constrained linear dynamic problems. The method is built upon a general framework for solving semidefinite programs (SDPs) with constraint matrix structures defined by directed acyclic graphs. We define this graph-based parameterization of SDPs and develop an algorithm that efficiently solves for the most "structured" solution: the lowest rank submatrix of a fixed set of matrices, where "lowest" is determined by a specific acyclic order. Our proposed algorithm is broadly applicable, fast, and ensures that the resulting submatrix remains a valid SDP. We demonstrate its utility in constructing the smallest correlation matrix that satisfies a given set of linear constraints and show how to solve these graph-parametrized SDPs with deterministic complexity based on problem size and acyclic width. Furthermore, we apply this algorithm to design structured, sparse, and time-varying state estimators under uncertainty and to solve the maximum entropy problem under constraints on linear functionals of time series data. By exploiting the structure of the feasible region, our approach recovers a strictly positive measure with an entropy density that is piecewise analytic. Numerical experiments confirm that our algorithm generates measures of significantly lower rank than those produced by standard interior point methods, achieving solution quality comparable to the true maximum entropy solution while running deterministically in time proportional to the acyclic width of the problem's acyclic order. This efficiency stems from parameterizing the feasible region using a basis that is the lowest column index submatrix of a vertex of a low-dimensional simplex, rather than relying on interior points. We establish conditions under which this basis yields a strictly positive measure and demonstrate how to construct it. These findings enable the efficient solution of low-rank maximum entropy problems, a task that has previously been intractable. We illustrate the relevance of our results in solving the implicit moment problem and constructing strictly sparse state estimators subject to linear constraints on their covariance propagation equations. Our numerical experiments indicate that this approach generates the sparsest state estimators with higher fidelity than existing methods, operating in time proportional to the acyclic width of the problem. This work generalizes and unifies the understanding of structured state estimation, low-rank maximum entropy, and the sparse implicit moment problem. Additionally, we show how to construct strictly positive measures and state estimators, deriving explicit formulas for these solutions. These findings enable the computation of samples and can serve as a verification tool for the numerical algorithms.

EvalAI's spoken language understanding dataset represents a significant resource for NLU research, yet it remains underexplored due to its inherent complexity. This paper presents a systematic approach to extracting both general and task-specific features from this dataset for use in NLU models. We propose two methods for generating distinctives for text and multiple-choice answers: the first is a domain-agnostic technique that identifies unique features within a corpus or subset using an unsupervised autoencoder, while the second generates task-specific distinctives through a supervised approach. These features are then normalized to create distinguishability scores. We applied this framework to EvalAI's dataset to derive distinctives for both inputs and outputs. Our findings indicate that incorporating these features—both general and task-specific—into the NEURALNET model yields substantial improvements. Specifically, integration leads to a 4.5% increase in F1-score and a 20% gain in AUC-ROC for evaluating models on this data. Furthermore, we observe that while general distinctives enhance performance, task-specific distinctives provide an even greater boost. The code is available at https://github.com/abhishekgupta10/evalAI_distingusability.

Data augmentation is a crucial strategy for improving model performance in low-resource scenarios. This paper presents a novel, simple, and effective augmentation method that leverages synonym knowledge to generate high-quality samples. Our approach encores word embeddings into a latent space where an autoencoder learns a compressed representation. Synonyms are identified as their nearest neighbors within this autoencoded space. We evaluate our method on the TREC spud dataset and compare its results against other common augmentation techniques. Experimental findings show that our approach outperforms other methods, with a 4% increase in F1 score compared to the baseline. Our implementation can be found at https://github.com/abhishekgupta10/data_augmentation_using_autoencoder_and_thesaurus.

This research investigates the impact of multilingualism on cognitive control by comparing Cued Flanker tasks across Spanish-English and Spanish-Catalan-English trilinguals against monolingual English speakers. The study examines four conditions: simultaneous trilinguals (speaking all three languages), sequential trilinguals (acquiring languages one after another), and monolinguals, testing predictions regarding the influence of acquisition order on cognitive control. Results revealed that sequential trilinguals exhibited better performance than monilinguals but worse than simultaneous trilinguals. However, no significant differences were found between sequential and simultaneous trilinguals when they responded in English, indicating that response language does not affect performance. Conversely, Spanish-speaking simultaneous trilinguals performed significantly better than both sequential trilinguals and Spanish monilinguals. These findings suggest that multilingualism enhances cognitive control and that the number of languages and their simultaneity of acquisition are critical factors. Furthermore, the acquisition order does not appear to impact cognitive control when responses are given in the last-acquired language. These outcomes align with the theory of selective attention, where increased linguistic diversity and density boost the activation of multiple languages, thereby improving cognitive control. Consequently, the acquisition sequence of additional languages seems irrelevant to cognitive control outcomes. Finally, the study highlights the necessity of analyzing response language effects when evaluating the relationship between multilingualism and cognitive control.

Our work bridges two areas by combining word similarity metrics with supervised sentiment classification. Specifically, we examine how sentiment-bearing words influence the accuracy of support vector machines (SVMs) in sentiment analysis. We find that (i) modifying identical sentiment-laden words across different reviews does not uniformly impact SVM performance, and (ii) the accuracy of semantic similarity metrics like SVD, LSA, and LSA+SVD is not directly proportional to the SVM's classification accuracy. Additionally, our results indicate that combining word replacements based on positive and negative polarity similarity does not yield improvements. However, we observe that the SVM performs optimally when adjectives are replaced based on the vector similarity of their underlying representations. Our code is available at https://github.com/amanjain20/Transforming-Training-Data-for-Sentiment-Analysis-using-Synonyms-and-Sentence-Similarity-Measures.

This study extends that framework to the massive free real scalar field, exploring its properties via a decomposition into normal modes and an examination of its behavior using Schur polynomials. Over the past decade, the IEEE Robotics and Automation Society (RAS) has made significant strides in defining and advancing human-centered robotics. This paper reviews the RAS's history regarding human factors, detailing how a dedicated task force evolved into a formal committee and subsequently a task group, with a focus on their deliverables. An analysis of the IEEE RAS constitution reveals that both the Human-Robot Interaction (HRI) Technical Committee and the Cognitive and Perceptual Systems (COPS) Technical Group have contributed to these efforts. This review examines various publications and technical activities from these groups to illustrate the IEEE RAS's ongoing commitment to the human element in robotics. Furthermore, we outline a vision for future work, suggesting that the community should now shift focus toward ensuring the safety of human-centered robotics.

We demonstrate that the matrix elements of $e^{i\beta J^z}$ within the charge basis can be expressed using hypergeometric $_3F_2$ functions. Additionally, we analyze two limiting regimes: $K \to \infty$ and $h \to 0$. Finally, we outline a non-rigorous conjecture regarding the strong-field limit ($h \to -\infty$), which corresponds to the regime where the magnetic field is maximally opposed to the spin. These methods could also serve as a foundation for other solvable models that are not yet fully resolved. To address the need for consistent noise independence, this paper introduces a Denoising-unified Compressed Sensation (DCS) framework that integrates a powerful denoising component into the CS process. The DCS method is unified into two configurations: DCS-I and DCS-II, which differ only in the placement of the denoising step—either before or after the projection operation. Theoretically, we establish that both DCS-I and DCS-II configurations are independent of noise. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the DCS framework outperforms existing state-of-the-art CS methods in recovery accuracy and maintains consistency across varying noise levels. Furthermore, the success of DCS relies on a single additional denoising unified operator (DUO), which outperforms traditional soft thresholding within the DCS context. Consequently, DUO presents a more effective denoising approach for CS applications than conventional techniques. Finally, the DCS method successfully extends to various practical applications, including single-pixel imaging, MRI, and image super-resolution.

Abstract:
In this paper, we extend the methodology of [DMS15] to general algebraic varieties not necessarily possessing a minimal model. As a primary application, we derive a theorem on the mobility of codimension-2 cycles on projective varieties and an irreducibility criterion for the general member linear section of a variety by a large family. We also explore applications to proving Bertini theorems. Furthermore, we apply this method to investigate the Hirschowitz Conjecture and related problems.

This technical abstract focuses on extending the quantum direct product theorem, previously established by Schaul, Unruh, and Yuen, to a setting where the client possesses a limited number of qubits. Under these constraints, we demonstrate that if a client can successfully verify at least one of two quantum computations, they are guaranteed to verify both. Consequently, it is unnecessary for every computational path in a quantum circuit to be individually checked when the client's resources are minimal. These findings have significant implications for the efficiency of classical-interactive verification protocols for quantum circuit evaluation and the security analysis of two-mutual-unknown quantum zero-knowledge protocols. In particular, for circuits with shallow depth, it suffices for the client to measure only a single qubit. Furthermore, our proofs introduce a novel technique of interest to the broader analysis of quantum-computation verification. For classical-interactive scenarios, we utilize the efficiently samplable state duality to characterize the client's limited-qubit measurement capabilities. Additionally, we develop a method to convert any pre-existing quantum direct product lemma into a lemma applicable to low-qubit resources by constructing a specific strategy. This construction relies on viewing the product lemma through the lens of games and employing a new concept called quantum-strategic quantum-strategy. Finally, we also consider the efficiency of quantum-interactive quantum verification. For this scenario, we prove a straightforward exponential-qubit-qfi lemma and extend it to a strong product theorem tailored for quantum-interactive settings by adapting techniques from the work of Schaul, Unruh, and Yuen. Together, these results facilitate the construction of an exponentially efficient quantum-interactive verification protocol capable of confirming any quantum computation. This is achieved by combining our strong direct product lemma with the technique of folding computational paths, a method also employed in this work. Our findings advance the understanding of how the capabilities of the verifying client influence the necessary assumptions and techniques in quantum-interactive verification. This, in turn, provides a unified framework for analyzing the complexity of such protocols. Specifically, we show that it is impossible to separate the complexity classes BQP and BQSZK using the quantum-interactive model. This marks the first time BQP has been proven to be contained within BQSZK, resolving an open question originally posed by Kerenidis and Rothblum. We also examine the assumption that the verifier is resource-bounded, which was left open by Koenig

## 1. Introduction

Sound Event Detection and Localization (SEDL) is a critical research area with significant real-world applications, including human activity recognition, machine fault diagnosis, and wildlife tracking. In machine perception for sound, the goal is to identify the presence of sound sources within a mixed audio signal and classify each source into a specific sound category. Recently, the Open Music Information Retrieval Challenge (OMIR) established a standardized SELD framework at the 2020 ECSASD challenge, defining two primary tasks: spatial detection and time-frequency detection. These tasks require the system to predict a source's position and the exact onset time of each sound in a recording. Subsequently, performance is evaluated by aligning these predictions with ground truth data to calculate a confidence score for each sound source.

The SELD challenge established a clear evaluation protocol for both spatial and temporal detection. Spatial detection involves creating an error map from the system's output relative to ground truth; the score is maximized when a system pinpoints a source's energy most accurately. Temporal detection is measured as a frame-level F-measure, calculated by checking if a system's prediction falls within a 30% margin of the sound's onset and offset. The evaluation metric is the macro-averaged F-measure across sound sources and categories.

Current research in machine sound perception focuses on Source Separation and Pattern Recognition. Source separation aims to isolate individual sound sources from a mixture, a task that is generally considered underdetermined and generally considered intractable. Conversely, pattern recognition focuses on identifying sound sources within a mixture. While these approaches are distinct, combining source separation with pattern recognition is a promising direction for enhancing SELD systems. This paper explores the efficacy of such a hybrid system by selecting effective conversion networks.

This study introduces an approach for specifying such activities through learning by example, utilizing program synthesis to derive solutions from multiple sample programs. Our method is knowledge-sensitive, enhancing scalability by integrating domain information—such as the available dataset and a library of available tools—to select the most appropriate solution when multiple options exist. Empirical evaluations across three distinct domains, ranging from single to multi-tool tasks using up to 10 programs, demonstrate that incorporating knowledge enables the automatic derivation of correct solutions for tasks that are infeasible without it. While existing synthesis systems derive programs from sample solutions, they typically offer no control over the outcome when multiple programs satisfy the samples. Enforcing a preference among these solutions is particularly challenging in complex domains, such as deriving machine learning models, where different models may exhibit varying characteristics. This paper presents a framework for constrained synthesis: given a set of sample programs and a set of desired program properties, it synthesizes a program that satisfies both the samples and the preferences. We implement this framework using a sample interpreter, various search strategies, and heuristic functions. Experiments using derivers and classifiers show that constrained synthesis outperforms standard synthesis in generating programs that achieve superior F1 scores and lower macro-averaged distances between derived and reference models. Additionally, we evaluate constrained synthesis using a sample-based interpreter for a subtask in a scientific proof checker, confirming its applicability in complex domains. We anticipate that this framework will facilitate future research in constrained synthesis. Source code and documentation are available at: \url{https://github.com/davidbendavid/constrainedSynthesis}.

Program synthesis has gained traction as a powerful automated technique for creating software, yet it remains underutilized in machine learning due to the high sample count and complexity typically involved in training models. This work introduces a synthesis engine capable of automatically deriving machine learning models from a small number of sample programs. By defining a sample interpreter, program transformation rules, and program scores, we apply constrained synthesis to generate models that adhere to the samples while maximizing a predefined score. Experiments using derivers and classifiers indicate that our technique can derive models that match sample performance and achieve higher F1 scores compared to those in the sample programs. the mental health of individuals and communities. This study examines the qualitative perspectives of California residents, revealed through online discussions on Twitter and Reddit, regarding wildfire smoke and their mental well-being. Within these community forums, individuals express various coping mechanisms for mental stress, share personal wildfire experiences, and seek support from others. However, we also identify and highlight dangerous misconceptions that could exacerbate mental health risks. These insights offer essential guidance for public health officials and communication experts aiming to mitigate mental health dangers and enhance public awareness regarding mental health issues linked to wildfires and wildland fire smoke.

The ongoing COVID-19 pandemic has forced the cancellation of in-person educational events and the rapid adoption of remote learning across higher education. This shift has created new hurdles for faculty in engaging students and managing class dynamics. An engaging online classroom relies on interactive design elements and the active use of communication and collaboration tools to maintain student focus and participation. This paper presents findings from the "Teaching Online with Engagement" (TOE) initiative, a multi-year research project by the North Central Association of Colleges and Universities (NCACU) Designing Online Learning Experiences (DOLEx) working group. Focusing on the 2020 spring semester, the study surveyed 112 institutions to gather qualitative data on the experiences of institutions, faculty, and students regarding engagement within remote learning environments. The results indicate that while many institutions attempted to build on previous online learning efforts, a significant number lacked established best practices for online engagement. Both instructors and students reported struggles with technology and online learning tools. Furthermore, students expressed concerns that their engagement was not being recognized by instructors, despite actively utilizing a wide range of course tools. To enhance online learning experiences, the paper offers specific recommendations for future research and practical steps for higher education leaders, IT departments, and faculty members.

The rapid expansion of e-commerce has led to a surge in package deliveries, which in turn increases the risk of package theft. While numerous studies have analyzed delivery routes and driver behaviors to improve security, there is a scarcity of research on the recipient's side of the transaction. This paper investigates the experiences of package recipients and their strategies for securing packages upon arrival. Drawing on a global survey of 1,300 participants and 150 interviews with North American users, we identify key challenges in the receiving process that can lead to theft. Our findings suggest that providing clearer instructions and enabling recipients to monitor delivery progress in real-time can significantly reduce the likelihood of package theft.

This paper presents a distributed algorithm for noise calibration that operates within a time-bounded framework and incurs minimal communication costs. To ensure efficiency, the framework is built upon a specific description of noise distribution. For any two-sided bounded distribution, we establish an upper bound on the noise required to bias a user's estimated location in a specific direction by a factor of $n$, where $n$ represents the user count. Using this bound, we demonstrate a distributed algorithm that, on a given network, finds a path for users to traverse that allows them to update their bias estimates. We analyze this algorithm's efficiency in terms of communication costs and execution time. Furthermore, we prove that this approach is optimal for side-guaranteed noise distributions and effectively near-optimal for general noise distributions. Finally, simulations are used to assess the performance of the proposed algorithm. This research forms a foundational element of the author's PhD thesis.

The authors previously introduced a notion of Line Ricci Curvature for directed graphs using a definition analogous to that of Lin, Lu, and Yau on manifolds with Ricci curvature lower bounds. We propose a von Renesse-Sturm type characterization of this lower Ricci curvature bound via a gradient estimate for the heat semigroup and a transportation inequality along the heat flow. research focused on identifying entities within text using knowledge bases. While such projects traditionally depend on training data and the complex, costly construction of knowledge bases, this paper introduces a basic method for identifying people, places, and organizations without requiring an external knowledge base, trained data, or a lengthy development cycle. Our approach rapidly trains models by leveraging the internal structure and cross-referencing of words, enabling the extraction of entities and their relationships from unknown texts. Testing on the SemEval 2018 task demonstrated that our model achieves F1 scores comparable to state-of-the-art solutions, attaining an score of 0.7642. We open-sourced our model and source code at https://github.com/robinson1111/Universal-entity-extraction. This study confirms that in-text word structure and references are highly valuable for entity extraction, offering a novel perspective on the field. Our findings indicate that this model is particularly effective at identifying entities mentioned only once in a document, suggesting it is ideal for processing real-time or near-real-time streams where frequent repeat occurrences are less common. Additionally, the model excels in pinpointing entities within short mentions, such as abbreviations. These results highlight the model's strong potential for applications including social media monitoring, customer support, and emergency response. We believe this research also contributes to broader information science efforts, especially given that our approach requires no external knowledge base or training data. Furthermore, the model's performance is consistent across various languages, making it particularly well-suited for real-time applications.

Fisher relied on the "spreading out" of genetic compositions within families over time. This concept was later formalized by D. S. Kahn, who defined a family's length as the smallest number of generations required for its members to diverge. The author of this note demonstrates that, under Kahn's definition, Fisher's and Kahn's theorems are not mutually supportive but rather somewhat contradictory. Consequently, this paper aims to propose a revised formulation of the Fundamental Theorem. Under this new statement, both Fisher's theorem and Kahn's findings hold true, and their roles become clear: they mutually reinforce one another to provide a comprehensive foundation for evolutionary theory.

control systems for grid-connected microgrids, which consist of multiple loads and renewable energy sources (RESS) that exchange active and reactive power. The primary objective is to ensure stable operation at a designated equilibrium point while maintaining power exchange within specified limits during disturbances. Achieving this involves creating stable RESS controllers that regulate power and distribute the resulting Reversible Integral Backstepping Control (RIBS) loads. We derive the equilibrium conditions and demonstrated several numerical cases that confirm the stability of various microgrid architectures under this control strategy. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the method guarantees asymptotic stability for closed-loop systems with RESS by constructing a suitable Lyapunov function and establishing that the system's LaSalle-Reiter Reversible Integral Backstepping Control (LRIBS) exponent does not exceed zero. Additionally, we examine the stability of the RESS control system under uncontrolled disturbances using the Lyapunov Direct Method. Power simulations conducted in MATLAB/Simulink verify the proposed microgrid architecture's stability and the design's efficacy. The study concludes with an analysis of the computational complexity of the proposed control schemes. Since RIBS and LRIBS are global feedback control methods, the proposed microgrid architecture remains stable even during significant disturbances. Given that RIBS and LRIBS are non-adaptive control techniques, the approach remains suitable for microgrids where RESS and loads experience parametric variations. Additionally, this control strategy can be extended to other nonlinear systems. The proposed method offers several computational advantages, including reduced memory requirements and enhanced scalability for microgrids containing numerous RESS units. The analysis focuses on responses to either a fixed or a sub-optimal control policy, utilizing a stochastic model that incorporates Markovian transitions, diffusion, and reaction processes. A dual potential method is employed to achieve uniform error estimates in the L-infinity norm for response estimates, with the study's primary focus being on asymptotic large-time behavior. The response curve for non-optimal policies is approximated by the difference between the curves corresponding to an optimal policy, leveraging the H\"older-type convergence properties of the weak convergence rate for sub-optimal thick-aware policies as established in a prior part of this work. Numerical simulations utilize spectral methods to compute the first few eigenfunctions and eigenvalues, providing global estimates for the system's characteristics. This eigenfunction expansion approach is particularly effective for systems with small volumes, such as those typical in biological environments. As an application, the work examines the efficacy of various antibiotic strategies for eradicating pathogens, comparing these results against simulations of an optimal Bayesian controller, the outcomes of a prior study, and existing literature. The analysis reveals that response curves for non-optimal policies are significantly influenced by the balance between growth and death rates, as well as the level of extrinsic stochasticity within the system. Notably, systems exhibiting near-criticality in growth and death rates, coupled with high extrinsic noise, are more susceptible to Bayesian policy adaptation. This suggests that such critical systems pose a substantial risk of treatment failure. Furthermore, the findings indicate that response curves for sub-optimal policies can be efficiently estimated by exploiting the convergence rate of the Bayesian optimal control. This approach enables the identification of conditions under which these policies either eradicate pathogens or result in treatment failure. The Bayesian analysis of pathogen eradication demonstrates that while response curves for non-optimal controls may be approximated by spectral methods, the system may still face a non-negligible risk of failure. In contrast, the Bayesian policy, despite potentially increasing the cost of eradicating pathogens, can be shown to be asymptotically optimal for large systems. systems, enabling the completion of tasks that single agents cannot accomplish alone. This study examines how a team of agents can identify and reach a target within a graph when their sensors have limited resolution, which varies by location. Perceptual uncertainty creates multiple possible team states that share the same observations. Through a graph search algorithm, we determine the number of time steps required for the team to confirm it has arrived at the target. We apply this method to a specific graph class that models the transport of an imaging agent in a cavity with an exit. Numerical results indicate that the additional time needed for confirmation is generally minimal, though it can be substantial in certain scenarios. In these cases, we can either increase the team's speed to reduce confirmation time or expand the team's coverage of the graph to ensure its separability. These strategies are demonstrated on a complex graph derived from the Gouy chamber. The approach of confirming team arrival is applicable in any context where a team's task completion can be linked to a specific team state. This research is supported by the ANR project SENSOMAS. This study presents a quantum-beam-evaporation-based method for creating monodisperse, high-quality QDs using two groups-III elements, such as Ga and Al, on group-V substrates. # 1. Introduction

Synchronization represents a ubiquitous phenomenon in nature and technology, occurring in systems ranging from biological organisms to electrical power grids. In research regarding synchronization on graphs, nodes are typically connected by edges that may be undirected or directed, weighted or unweighted. When units linked by an edge are assumed to maintain the same state, the resulting (weighted) 1-synchronization patterns are known as connected components in an equivalence graph or (weighted) clique partitions in an ultrametric partition. These concepts have extensive applications and have been extensively studied; a comprehensive overview is available in the monograph [Mazo and Huang, 2020].

ultaneous Wireless Information and Power Transfer (SWIPT) in a two-way relay network (TWN) that operates in a bidirectional manner. During the first time slot, users receive energy and information from the relay while simultaneously transmitting their information; the information received is then used for rate distortion (RD) encoding in both users. In the second time slot, the relay transmits a superimposed signal to the users, which includes a mixture of the encoded RD signals from each side and a martingale term designed to ensure the cumulative sum of transmitted signals across time remains zero, thereby maintaining a net-zero charge for the TWN. To achieve this communication framework, an optimization problem is formulated to minimize total power consumption in the TWN while meeting specific constraints related to RD rate, quality of service, and transmission power. Since the problem is non-convex, an Iterative Resource Allocation (IRA) algorithm is developed to find the solution. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed IRA-based solution outperforms traditional methods, such as separate amplification and forward (SAF) and decode-and-forward (DF) techniques, as well as other combined solutions. This approach offers a more sustainable option for SWIPT-based TWNs by significantly reducing overall power consumption. Furthermore, detailed analysis reveals that the communication performance of the proposed system is directly linked to the users' RD rate and distortion functions. The paper also examines the relationship between the IRA and the iteratively computed safe set for the product of nonnegative matrices, showing that this set determines the maximum number of iterations required for convergence. Finally, it is proven that the IRA converges to a fixed point in a finite number of steps. The proposed method is applicable to various scenarios, including sensor networks for image or video transmission where image quality is critical and power resources are limited. The underlying principles of RD encoding and the martingale-based TWN can be utilized in other bidirectional communication systems. This study experimentally examines ferromagnetic spin fluctuations in a mixture of two species with a deeply bound strong interaction between them. The electron ($e$) and deuteron ($d$) species possess spins of $1/2$ and $0$, respectively, enabling the ferromagnetic (FM) channel in $e$-$d$ mixtures to be influenced by Pauli blocking, a mechanism absent in identical particle systems. To identify spin fluctuations, the relative soliton-antisolon pair production rate was measured as a function of the FM channel strength. Results show that pair production is significantly suppressed at low momenta under strong FM interaction conditions, indicating the existence of a ferromagnetic-like instability in the FM spin state. Notably, the observed negative shift in the FM channel is so substantial that the system appears to exist in a "FM-active" region, a phase that cannot be reached in $e$-$\alpha$ or $\mu$-$d$ systems due to limitations in negative scattering length tuning. These findings confirm the presence of ferromagnetic-like FM fluctuations in the $e$-$d$ system, establishing, to our knowledge, a precedent for the study of FM in a ferromagnetic-like regime. Furthermore, these results provide valuable insights into the nonperturbative strong-coupling regime relevant to high-temperature superconductivity and related fields. Finally, the effective field theory analysis of the $e$-$d$ system validates the analogy with the physics of FM in unitary Fermi systems. These conclusions are supported by an image of a magnetic soliton collision between an electron and a deuteron detected by a silicon sensor. Focusing on the massive Wess-Zumino model, we derive the mass-deformed operator product expansion (OPE) for primary fields using conformal symmetry and verify it against conformal Ward identities. We also present the mass-deformed stress-energy tensor within the path integral framework. Within 2D massive Wess-Zumino theory, the operator $\mathcal{Q} = \int \mathrm{d}z\, T_{\bar{z}}$ serves as a short-distance limit of the chiral supercharge in superspace. a promising approach to evaluating the practical performance of algorithms across various computational tasks. An algorithm is deemed to have "computationally tractable convergence" if it guarantees average-case results after a number of iterations that offers a reasonable balance between performance and resource constraints for specific instances. This paper provides evidence that the stochastic gradient descent (SGD) method, widely used in machine learning to optimize non-convex empirical risk functions, exhibits computationally tractable convergence on a specific class of tasks. Our analysis assesses the empirical performance of SGD through the lens of computational learning theory by conditionally analyzing the method conditionally on factorized representations of inputs and parameters conditionally on the latent distribution of inputs across various information encodings. By applying advanced techniques from computational learning theory and statistical analysis, we estimate the average-case performance of SGD on empirical risk functions conditionally on specific tasks. We define SGD as having "computationally tractable convergence" if it offers significant improvements in average-case performance relative to the baseline error across a reasonable number of iterations for specific tasks. Our empirical findings indicate that SGD frequently demonstrates sensitive dependence on the number of iterations, resulting in significant performance gains for specific tasks after a reasonable number of iterations. Furthermore, our estimates of the baseline error and iterated average-case performance of SGD are bounded by polynomial functions of key task parameters, including encoding complexity, output dimension, and output values. Consequently, our findings suggest that the empirical performance of SGD can be effectively analyzed using established tools from computational learning theory, and that SGD often displays computationally tractable convergence on specific tasks. However, our estimates of average-case performance do not offer sharp predictions, as they are influenced by higher-order moments of various distributions. Therefore, a valuable direction for future research would be the development of refined analysis methods to achieve sharper estimates of average-case performance. Additionally, our findings highlight the importance of considering input distributions conditionally on specific tasks when analyzing the performance of computational methods. Consequently, it would be beneficial to create a framework for analyzing the computational tractability of learning algorithms by conditionally estimating the sensitivity of input distributions conditionally on information encodings and output values across a reasonable number of tasks. Such a framework would enable the comparison of learning algorithms based on their average-case performance across specific tasks while accounting for comparisons based on their sensitivity to input changes conditionally on tasks. Ultimately, this would facilitate the evaluation of learning algorithms by comparing their average-case performance across specific tasks, considering the sensitivity of input distributions conditionally on information encodings and output values across a reasonable number of tasks. Given the vast array of possible moiré band configurations, it is essential to identify the key control parameters that dictate these bands and the resulting macroscopic behaviors. By applying the Floquet-Bloch theorem to a periodic potential, we derive an effective two-dimensional Hamiltonian for moiré bands, defining the important parameters that govern its dynamics. This approach offers a concise model for predicting the positions of moiré bands and Doniach-Hamilton parameters, as well as the magnetic Order Parameter and binding energy in twistronics semimetals, all as functions of these governing factors. Additionally, using the Hamiltonian's Green function, we calculate the optical conductivity for twistoric semimetals to explore their optical properties and suggest potential experimental signatures. Our findings indicate the existence of a Drude peak in the optical conductivity of conventional moiré semimetals, reflecting the Drude weight of their zero-energy flat band. Furthermore, the zero-energy flat band remains partially flat even at high frequencies, a phenomenon we attribute to the quantum geometric properties of the moiré flat band. We also present the frequency-dependent optical conductivity in twisted transition metal dichalcogenides under a flat band approximation. Finally, we highlight the potential applications of moiré flat bands in twistoric semimetals for generating ultrafast optical signals and their utility in optoelectronic devices. These findings are expected to be valuable for both fundamental physics research and the development of advanced electronic and optical technologies.

This paper presents a novel approach to high-dimensional non-convex optimization, applicable to various machine learning tasks such as deep learning, matrix factorization, and phase retrieval. Our method conceptually simplifies the optimization landscape for stochastic gradient descent (SGD) by employing a non-Euclidean metric that ensures level sets of the loss function appear as concentric nested spheres centered at the global minimum. We develop an efficient algorithm to transform the gradient of SGD into this spherical metric and demonstrate convergence to a $\nabla f$-stationary point. Empirical results on challenging datasets, including MNIST and FashionMNIST, indicate that our method achieves state-of-the-art convergence rates. Since our method operates as a vanilla SGD with a spherical metric, it is highly scalable and efficient, making it suitable for large-scale applications. This research was conducted within the PAULI group at the University of Pennsylvania.

Any solution to the Einstein equations, whether including or excluding a cosmological constant, adheres to the field equations defined by the Cotton tensor, indicating that the cosmological constant functions as an integration constant. In this theoretical framework, a vacuum state is not defined by a vanishing stress-energy tensor but by the condition of conformal flatness. The Schouten scalar plays a role analogous to the trace of the Einstein nonlinearity. The Einstein-Hilbert action remains valid for the Cotton tensor, with the cosmological constant incorporated directly into the action. A Hamiltonian can be constructed using the Cotton tensor to analyze dynamical systems and theoretical models, with applications to cosmology. The Hamiltonian density for radiation-dominated cosmology yields a non-zero result, contrasting with the Big Bang model; consequently, the Big Bang is reinterpreted as a transition between distinct dynamical regimes. Furthermore, it is possible to introduce a new gravitational nonlinearity based on the Cotton tensor that yields a Big Bang scenario without a singularity. This new nonlinearity generates a de Sitter vacuum and allows for the theory's application to gravitationally bound systems. This approach offers a theoretical framework that avoids fine-tuning and provides a mechanism to explain a significant portion of a galaxy's total mass. A primary goal of IPM research is enhancing the efficiency of each iteration. This paper introduces a novel family of ip-iterative ip-tangent Newton methods, which are guaranteed to achieve global convergence and converge superlinearly near the central path. While recent computer science studies have begun applying these databases to generative AI for creating synthetic near-midway collision scenarios, such AI models are generally not explainable. In contrast to prior work that treats synthetic scenario generation as a black box, this paper proposes a novel approach that explicitly identifies the specific actions required to achieve a target scenario. We introduce a synthesis algorithm that creates scenarios by maximizing a score function, which is elevated only when synthetic events lead to a near-midway collision. Our score function itself is constructed through an iterative process involving human experts and a large language model. We validate our approach using real-world near-midway collision incidents extracted from flight level reports, lab-generated scenarios, and simulated collisions utilizing a reinforcement learning-based trajectory generation algorithm. The results indicate that synthetic near-midway collisions involving real flights can be effectively generated through this process. This method holds significant promise for comprehensively analyzing failure modes and developing countermeasures to prevent future near-midway collisions. We are releasing our code, data, and flight level reports as open-source to support research in safety science and air traffic management. Specifically, in scalar field theory, an exact link has been established between the gradient flow and the RG trajectory of the Wilson action within the exact renormalization group (ERG) framework. By emulating this relationship, we introduce an ERG differential equation for Yang–Mills theory that maintains explicit gauge invariance. Furthermore, our continuum formulation can be generalized to apply to lattice gauge theory. As a practical application, we employ ERG ideas to estimate the mass of the glueball. Existing computational evidence suggests the $2^{++}$ glueball mass lies near 5.11 times the strong coupling constant squared. Employing a novel ERG method, we re-evaluate this quantity using Monte Carlo simulations. Our results yield a precise determination, supporting the computational finding that the $2^{++}$ glueball mass is approximately 5.1 times the strong coupling constant squared. Additionally, we analyze the convergence characteristics of the perturbation series associated with this calculation.

This paper presents a novel statistical model-based approach for monitoring and analyzing business processes that concurrently handles goal definition and pursuit. Specifically, the GoAL-GP model uses Bayesian optimization to automatically explore a goal space and acquire information by fitting a Gaussian process to observed outcomes. We demonstrate this model's application to business process monitoring through a case study on a clinical medication administration process using real-world data. Furthermore, we propose a new, more efficient algorithm for this Bayesian optimization context, termed Successive Contextual Bandits, which shows a significant reduction in model training time compared to successive contextual bandits or standard Gaussian process regression. Experimental results indicate that our approach achieves at least a tenfold improvement in efficiency across all three areas: goal definition, goal acquisition, and model training. This work represents the first integration of a formal Bayesian optimization framework into the field of business process monitoring.

Practical implications

Our research demonstrates a method for achieving goals through an agent's learning process that is efficient, practical, and scalable. By enabling an agent to learn goals and success metrics, this approach ensures that a monitored process remains relevant to its real-world context. Additionally, our methods allow for the rapid adaptation of monitoring systems to new processes without requiring extensive historical data.

Limitations

While our results show that models can effectively learn goals from noisy data, the current limitations of reinforcement learning in exploring complex action spaces remain a challenge. Future research should focus on integrating other monitoring techniques with our model to handle more complex scenarios.

Originality/Value

We introduce a model for goal acquisition that is both practical and efficient, representing a breakthrough over successive contextual bandits and Gaussian processes, which can be ten times faster. This study marks the first attempt to incorporate Bayesian optimization into business process monitoring. Moreover, our approach represents a paradigm shift from traditional monitoring, which typically involves detecting deviations and ad-hoc goal analysis, by learning goals directly from data within the observed process space.

The system's states are represented by a unit vector on a sphere, and its evolution is governed by a sphere map that contracts great circles. This map is defined as a conditionally symmetric orthogonal projection, where the direction of symmetry is determined by the Hamiltonian's integrals, and the projection component is generated by a stochastic process. This process involves random choices of planes passing through the sphere's center, combined with reflections across these planes when a great-circle contraction is required. We derive the probability density function for the singular values of such projection matrices and propose a sphere map evolution algorithm that is consistent with this density function. Simulations indicate that the resulting random operators share statistical characteristics with those from other two-integrable models, such as the Chandrasekhar biorthogonal model and the Ginibre ensemble. Additionally, these models exhibit a distinct phase transition at a specific model parameter value, which can be identified through the singular-value statistics of the evolution operators. While the Ginibre model is known to undergo a second-order transition, our analysis suggests that one of the model's three phases is uniquely characterized by a singular-value density proportional to $\sqrt{1-y^2}$ on the interval $y \in [-1,1]$. Finally, we examine the applicability of our theory to the dynamics of the Helmholtz equation on a two-dimensional domain with a curved boundary, employing an algorithm grounded in the theory of conditionally symmetric orthogonal projections.

fragmented reads is a core challenge in genomics that involves two primary steps: constructing a graph where vertices represent reads and edges denote overlaps, and subsequently traversing this graph to recover the original sequence. This paper provides a sufficient condition for the unique, exact reconstruction of a string given a specific collection of its substrings. We apply this finding to the assembly of haplotype pairs from sequencing data, where a unique haplotype pair corresponds to the unique solution for inferring an individual's genetic makeup from their read set. Genetic variation is captured by single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs); genomes are modeled as strings where positions corresponding to SNPs are marked. Our goal is to determine two strings that share these specific positions. The sequencing graph is a subgraph of the graph of all possible substrings, meaning our findings offer a sufficient condition for unique reconstruction even without precise knowledge of the actual overlaps between reads. We demonstrate that the length of strings recoverable under these generalized conditions can significantly exceed the total length of the input reads. The proof methodology is also applicable to analyzing other graph-based assembly algorithms. Finally, we validate our theoretical results through simulations. The simulation environment mirrors a real-world sequencing data generator, and we compare our outcomes with those of the most widely used assembly software, revealing that our approach can successfully assemble sequences that other methods fail to reconstruct. We also explore the application of this method to phased SNP reconstruction. Our simulations indicate that this approach can yield a substantial number of additional SNPs, particularly in regions with high SNP density. This outcome is achieved by developing an efficient algorithm to identify all unique paths with shared labels on a labeled acyclic graph. We anticipate that this work will facilitate the development of a novel assembler capable of handling highly repetitive genomes, a task currently difficult for existing methods. Furthermore, this research can be extended to analyze compound heterozygosity in human genetic disease research.

Acoustic waves serve as a viable medium for delivering light to deep brain regions, a field known as Sonogenetics. While intense focused ultrasound (US) can generate strong near-field electric fields capable of activating ion channels in neuronal membranes, such methods typically deliver energy in short pulses, leading to significant heating between activations that limits long-term usability. To enhance thermal management, we integrated a nanosecond-pulsed US source with a microfluidic chamber containing a thin layer of "acoustic black body" material. This setup creates a strong near-field electric field confined to a sub-millisecond pulse duration, while the fluidic system continuously removes heat, allowing for high-frequency pulsing. This "acoustic cavity enhancer" design enables efficient, long-lasting neural activation without excessive heating. Our experiments confirm that the acoustic cavity enhancer improves Fura-2 calcium imaging sensitivity by 100-fold and increase channelrhodopsin-induced calcium transients in HEK293 cells by 10-fold. These designs and experimental outcomes are accessible via a GitHub repository. By applying electromagnetic field enhancement principles within acoustic cavities, this approach paves the way for more efficient and effective methods of stimulating and reading neural activity through deformed near-field electric fields in liquids. This strategy offers a promising foundation for high-sensitivity calcium imaging and efficient optogenetic stimulation using non-optical light sources. Focusing near-field electric fields generated by acoustic waves represents a novel mechanism for stimulating ion channels in cell membranes.

Quantum synchronization enables the transfer of quantum states from a source to multiple targets simultaneously. Many computational challenges can be modeled as high-dimensional sampling tasks. Specifically, given a set of variables and associated values, the objective is to compute the average of a specific function across their joint distribution. While Monte Carlo methods are commonly used for such averages, they can be inefficient. An alternative is to create a sequence of variables where each term depends on the previous one, ensuring the method converges to the desired sampling distribution. This approach is known as a Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm. This tutorial aims to explain a specific type of MCMC method called simulated annealing and apply it to two problems: finding the minimum of a continuous function and sampling the joint distribution of two integer variables. The first example is straightforward, whereas the second presents difficulties: the search space is discrete and riddled with many local minima. The section on continuous variables can be accessed here: https://github.com/paulmroczek/Tutorial/tree/main/10-puzzle/2-cont-min, while the section on the 10-puzzle is located here: https://github.com/paulmroczek/Tutorial/tree/main/10-puzzle/10-puzzle.

By defining the rank of a $p \times n$ coefficient matrix as the smallest count of columns needed to represent it as a linear combination, the rank lasso identifies this minimal count as a latent variable, thereby offering an unsupervised method for determining the effective degrees of freedom in coefficient models. This approach is highly valuable for analyzing high-dimensional datasets, such as the SQUID brain imaging data from a schizophrenia patient.

However, the standard formulation of the rank lasso is a mixed-integer program that is difficult to solve, particularly for large datasets. To address this, we introduce two continuous reformulations that eliminate integer variables. We develop solution algorithms for these new formulations and apply them to the SQUID brain imaging case. Our findings indicate that these continuous reformulations are more than 100 times faster than the original mixed-integer approach, with only a slight increase in objective function values. Additionally, we highlight that while the continuous models are slightly less efficient than the original, they are less sensitive to the $\ell_1$ norm used, resulting in more stable and reliable coefficient estimates. These conclusions are supported by extensive numerical experiments. Our results suggest that the proposed continuous reformulations and algorithms are significantly faster and equally effective, with the choice of norm playing a critical role in the stability of lasso estimates. Furthermore, these findings suggest that lasso-based dimensionality search methods may be more robust than those relying on cardinality constraints.

This paper examines the arguments for and against the machine-phenomenal view, which posits that machines can be subjectively aware of their existence.
