However, CPs argue that such payments are unjustified, asserting that ISPs should not profit from the growing value chains of content creation and distribution. This circular argument stalls negotiations, as neither party yields. Consequently, we propose a formal game-theoretic analysis of the Content Distribution Over Internet Service Provider (CDIS) architecture. Our study examines how ISPs and CPs allocate costs and revenues when supplying content to subscribers through ISP infrastructure. We demonstrate that Nash equilibrium is generally unattainable in this domain. Furthermore, we identify a critical constraint on subscribers: they are only willing to access online content if the resulting Quality of Experience (QoE) exceeds specific thresholds. Incorporating this subscriber constraint into our model reveals that stable solutions exist only under certain conditions. Through numerical simulations, we show that these stable outcomes are feasible even without subscriber constraints, provided that cost and revenue parameters are configured appropriately.

This paper introduces a novel distributed routing algorithm tailored for Vehicular Ad Hoc Networks (VANETs). We define a new metric called the stability factor (SF), which measures the fluctuation of road traffic density over time at specific locations to determine routing feasibility. Vanish Road, characterized by its linearity and sparsity of intersections, is employed as the simulation environment due to its constant topology. Subscriber movements are modeled using a combination of Poisson and Uniform distributions. Simulation results indicate that while most routing protocols struggle with high link breakage rates and significant packet loss under varying traffic conditions, the proposed algorithm successfully delivers the majority of packets. Performance evaluations across different scenarios reveal that the algorithm outperforms existing routing methods in terms of delivery ratio, average delay, and link breakage rate.

In recent years, the rapid expansion of wireless networks has intensified the need for efficient and effective routing protocols. However, the high dynamic nature of these networks poses significant challenges to routing mechanisms. Stability factors are crucial in VANETs because vehicle-to-vehicle communication reliability depends on the density fluctuations of roads. We introduce a new metric, the Stability Factor (SF), which quantifies these fluctuations to assess the feasibility of vehicle-to-vehicle communications on specific roads within VANETs. By integrating SF with other vanishing road metrics, we develop a distributed routing protocol that adapts to local conditions, thereby enhancing overall VANET performance. Simulations using OMNET++ and OMNET++/OMNET++/OMNET++ show that our protocol achieves superior performance compared to existing routing methods.

We demonstrate how irreducibility within the C*-algebra representation translates to the irreducibility of the affine transformation representation. Furthermore, we show that the C*-algebra and its dynamics can be recovered (up to a unique irreducible *-isomorphism) from the associated affine model. Finally, we provide a negative answer to a question posed by Tomita and extend findings by Choda and Kustermans regarding the smoothness of the modular flow and the structure of invariant subcontents in the non-abelian case.

The paper begins by reviewing the definition and fundamental properties of time-translation invariant quantum statistical systems, meaning quantum statistical systems where the state and dynamics are mutually invariant. We establish the equivalence between two perspectives on countable non-abelian quantum group content invariants: first, as established in [17], as subcontents invariant under the co-regular representation of the quantum group content, and second, as defined in [11] and [10], as subcontents of the dual quantum group keeping the state invariant. First, we generalize the definition of the content spectrum to the countable non-abelian case. Second, we characterize the content spectrum as the set of irreducible characters of the dual quantum group and introduce the concept of the state spectrum. Fourth, we demonstrate that the content spectrum of the free Fermi gas is identical to its dual's, provided the state spectrum comprises all possible spectral measures. uchsian hyperbolic 3-manifold with fixed hydrobel at infinity can be parameterized by complex dilatations. An holomorphic map linking the domain defined by complex dilatations to the space of quasi-Fuchsian hyperbolic 3-manifolds sharing a fixed hydrobel at infinity was previously constructed. This paper demonstrates the holomorphy of the differential at any point on this map. Furthermore, we establish the holomorphy of the natural projection from this domain to the space of quasi-Fuchsian hyperbolic 3-manifolds possessing a fixed measured foliation at infinity. As a consequence, we resolve a question posed by Reyssat. Combined with aconjecture by Reyssat, this result affirmatively answers a query raised by Reyssat and Yeung concerning the holomorphic nature of the map from the space of quasi-Fuchsian hyperbolic 3-manifolds with a fixed measured foliation at infinity to said measured foliations. Additionally, we provide an example of a non-constant holomorphic map from a curve into the space of quasi-Fuchsian hyperbolic 3-manifolds that exhibits trivial monodromy. This finding contrasts with a result by Reyssat, which implies that any holomorphic map from a curve into the space of quasi-Fuchsian hyperbolic 3-manifolds with a fixed measured foliation at infinity must be non-constant. Consequently, a measure of complexity for these maps can be associated. This work extends findings by Johnson and a conjecture by Gromov regarding the complexity of quasi-Fuchsian surfaces. Finally, we provide examples of non-constant holomorphic maps from a curve into the space of quasi-Fuchsian hyperbolic 3-manifolds with a fixed measured foliation at infinity that exhibit no embedded geodesics and contain only finitely many embedded geodesics. These examples illustrate the distinct behaviors of such maps. This research was supported by NSFC No. 11971304, No. 12131010, No. 12071220, and No. 12071221. the dynamics of COVID-19 transmission within human populations, with a specific focus on the clinical progression through which the virus spreads. We developed a system of ordinary differential equations (ODEs) linked to the stages of the disease's biological mechanism to create a physiology-based epidemiological model. This approach enables the quantification of a significant parameter in transmission dynamics—the basic reproduction number ($R_0$)—by utilizing patient clinical data for estimation. Furthermore, a stochastic version of the ODE model was developed to assess the statistical reliability of the estimated parameters. Applying these methods to clinical data from the 2020 COVID-19 outbreak in Hong Kong, we determined the disease's incubation period ($I_D=4.2\pm 0.14$ days), the duration of the infectious stage before symptom onset ($I_C=2.0\pm 0.2$ days), and $R_0=2.6\pm 0.25$. These results indicate that the COVID-19 strain in Hong Kong is more infectious than SARS and the common cold but less so than MERS and SARS-CoV-2 strains responsible for outbreaks in the 2003 and 2010-2019 periods, respectively. Additionally, the basic time delay between infection and symptom manifestation is found to be $I_D+I_C=6.4\pm 0.25$ days. Finally, we applied these models to evaluate interventions in Hong Kong, such as a 14-day quarantine following symptom onset, which is designed to cover the infection-to-symptom delay and limit further transmission. Our findings show that this quarantine strategy reduces the COVID-19 reproduction number by 75%, causing a corresponding 75% decrease in new infections. These results provide a quantitative basis for future research on the mechanisms of infectious disease transmission and for designing more effective population-level control strategies. Our work provides a new physiological approach to estimating the $R_0$ reproduction number, offering an alternative to traditional epidemiological methods that rely on large datasets of human population contact information. This study was published in Scientific Reports on November 12, 2020.

-of-care method for identifying heart conditions, yet the development of automatic analysis systems for rare pathologies is hindered by the scarcity of annotated data. While public datasets exist for common disorders, they are insufficient for training models on rare diseases due to the limited number of annotated examples required to recognize rare patterns. Transfer learning offers a solution by enabling the use of large data for training and small, labeled data for fine-tuning, thereby overcoming annotation limitations. However, existing approaches often fail to achieve state-of-the-art performance on Auscultation data because they do not address key challenges such as class imbalance, the lack of temporal information in CNNs, and the rarity of specific pathologies. To resolve these issues, we introduce a novel framework combining a temporal attention mechanism with a cost-sensitive fully convolutional network (FCN). This model was trained using the public PHUC-AuScultation dataset and evaluated on a custom dataset for Aortic Stenosis. Our results demonstrate that the proposed model achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art models for common diseases when evaluated on a rare disease. Specifically, the proposed temporal attention FCN reaches an F1 score of 0.922, significantly outperforming standard FCN and ResNet-based FCN models on this rare pathology. Furthermore, we illustrate that temporal attention effectively learns discriminative features by providing a clear visualization of the time-step selection process. We hope our model and dataset will facilitate the creation of more effective diagnostic tools for rare heart diseases. The code and dataset are available at: https://github.com/roshni-krishna/TKM-PhuC-Au-Sculptation.

Phoneme recognition is a fundamental task in speech processing that underpins speech synthesis, authentication, and natural language understanding. The emergence of deep neural networks (DNNs) has significantly advanced recognition rates, but training these models requires substantial computational resources and extensive, high-quality data. Higgs boson couples to top quarks through top-polarized $e^+e^- \to t\bar{t}$ reactions at an electron-positron collider operating at high center-of-mass energies. By analyzing the production of top quarks from the $t\bar{t}X$ channel, where $X$ represents a single photon, Z boson, or Higgs boson, we derive constraints on the coupling parameters $\lambda, \beta, \xi$ governing $t\bar{t}H$ production. Focusing on the process $e^+e^- \to t\bar{t}H$ at 250 and 350 GeV—dominated by the $e^+e^- \to t\bar{t}H$ signal via $s$-channel $Z$ and $t$-channel photon exchange in the sFH topology—we determine that the projected statistical sensitivity for these couplings is 0.03 and 0.02 at 250 and 350 GeV, respectively, under a 100\% integrated luminosity. Furthermore, the specific analysis of the sFH topology could facilitate an independent verification of the Higgs boson's spin. While scientific data is vital for training models for specific applications like medical diagnosis, these datasets are often vast, intricate, and specialized, posing significant challenges for developers. Manually gathering and preparing such data demands substantial time, effort, and expert knowledge, which can become critical path items in AI development. Furthermore, limited access to high-quality scientific data and the fear of intellectual property theft can restrict developers from using real data during the training phase. Consequently, creating and accessing high-quality in-domain data for scientific AI tasks is a major hurdle. To address this, a data generator is required to produce synthetic data that closely mimics real-world distributions while being easily customizable. This paper introduces a framework for generating synthetic data in domain-specific contexts. We exemplify its utility in scientific video generation, which involves two key steps: first, producing AI-simulated video content to capture the motion patterns of scientific objects, and second, producing scientific video content by leveraging the spatio-temporal distribution of visual features. Our approach has successfully applied scientific video synthesis to two primary tasks: object tracking and semantic segmentation. By combining the strengths of state-of-the-art generative models and traditional computer vision techniques, we significantly enhanced the representation of scientific videos and achieved superior performance in these tasks compared to existing methods. Additionally, we demonstrated that a unified framework can simultaneously address object tracking and semantic segmentation in scientific videos, effectively balancing performance and computational efficiency. These results validate the effectiveness of our method for general synthetic data generation in specific domains. We have open-sourced the code at https://github.com/zhengyuxu/ScripGen.

We assume that in this setting, fixed user preferences determine the stable equilibrium of routes, under the condition that the expected cost of every used route is no greater than that of every alternative route. The cost of a route is a random variable resulting from the stochastic states of network links. Although our theoretical framework applies to any uncertain network parameters, we specifically examine and demonstrate the model using a social network graph where link states follow independent Bernoulli distributions. Our goal is to determine the probability distribution of the costs for the stable routes established by deterministic preferences. While a prior solution by Cohen-Addad et al. efficiently calculated these probabilities for single-player games, our problem presents greater complexity due to multiple players following different routes. We address this challenge by creating an algorithm that computes the probability masses of all stable routes in social network games under probabilistic uncertainty, doing so more quickly than a naive approach that simulates all possible network realizations. We achieve this efficiency by adapting the Cohen-Addad et al. algorithm to simulate only the relevant network realizations. Beyond practical benefits, such as improved query response times, our work offers theoretical insights into cost-based games with stable equilibria. Specifically, we show that the proposed algorithm is a form of Cohen-Addad et al.'s algorithm applied to a carefully selected subset of network realizations. Furthermore, we establish a polynomial relationship between the costs of these realizations and the players' preferences, proving that this relationship is necessary for the algorithm's efficiency. We validate our algorithm's performance through extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets, demonstrating that it achieves the predicted speedup.

However, fouling within the production reactor often causes non-linear shifts in the reaction rate over time, leading to off-spec products and reduced throughput. This study presents a model-based, real-time optimization (MBRTO) strategy to dynamically adjust the feed rate and mitigate fouling. A control-affine model describing the relationship between the fouling layer thickness and the reaction rate is developed and validated using step-response experiments across three different chemicals. The MBRTO framework operates in a feedback loop with model predictive control (MPC) to drive the fouling layer to its maximum feasible level while keeping the product specification and temperature constraints satisfied. When tested on a semi-batch reactor, the closed-loop system successfully reached the predefined limit for both fouling layer thickness and specific yield. Compared to a baseline open-loop approach, this closed-loop system achieved a 25% increase in production time and a 19% improvement in volume-based yield. Furthermore, the strategy demonstrated robustness against disturbances in feed concentration and heat transfer coefficients. Ultimately, this model-based control scheme enables the maximization of each batch's potential output and allows for rapid transfer learning for new chemicals. The complete control strategy, including code and data, is available as open-source at https://github.com/BASF-Process-Systems-Engineering/BMRTO-MPC. This study offers a comprehensive, quantitative analysis of tags within pages discovered by Google, covering various tag characteristics, their evolution over time, and the influence of social media on these trends. Our findings reveal that while global tag popularity generally follows a power-law distribution, specific sub-communities exhibit distinct behaviors that significantly affect tags with the highest usage. Furthermore, we observe that tags relevant to social media dominate the most popular tags, and tag SBIR analysis confirms that tags shared by social media are typically more popular than those that are not. Dynamically, both the rise and decline of tags experience an exponential decay pattern, with highly popular tags remaining active for substantially longer durations. Furthermore, we demonstrate that tags' popularity and community structures later in the timeline can effectively predict their decay rates. This research underscores the transformative impact of social media on tag dynamics within the web and provides methods to anticipate the longevity of tags. These insights hold significant value for practitioners aiming to enhance the Google discovery process. Specifically, practitioners can leverage this understanding to refine tag selection strategies and monitor tag performance over time. Additionally, this work opens new avenues for analyzing tags through their social media usage and for exploring the communities associated with specific tags. Finally, we have developed a web application that enables practitioners to investigate the social media usage, community memberships, and tag longevity for both individual and collectively popular tags. The tool's interface is particularly well-suited for conducting exploratory analyses. Source code for the application is accessible at https://github.com/amirovlab/TaggingWebPages, and the interface can be found at https://taggingwebpages.com. Given that the application tracks tags and communities up to the end of 2019, practitioners are encouraged to utilize it to gain a better understanding of how tags evolve over time. By examining which tags are popular, how communities form and interact, and how long tags persist, practitioners can make more informed decisions regarding tag usage. We then identify a condition for non-radiation that holds across all inertial frames, a requirement that is intuitively necessary for the stable operation of interconnects in ICs and printed circuit boards. This condition is also essential for the validity of quasi-static approximations, a concept of significant practical importance. The analysis begins with the non-radiation condition expressed in terms of the vector potential, followed by its formulation using the scalar potential and the vector potential. We demonstrate that the non-radiation condition can be achieved through a gauge transformation involving specific functions of time and the scalar potential. Subsequently, by applying the continuity equation, we derive expressions for gauge functions that ensure the non-radiation condition is met given specific initial values for the vector potential at all spatial points and a known initial state for the electric field. We conclude by calculating these initial conditions for an IC interconnect using printed circuit board technology, modeling the line as a two-wire transmission line. For this system, the non-radiation condition implies that the electric field component parallel to the wire must be zero at the source. Furthermore, based on the initial vector potential, we show that the magnetic field at the source need not be zero, provided the time derivative of the vector potential corresponds to the magnetic field described by Maxwell's curl equation at that location. Given that electric fields are typically difficult to measure, experimental verification of the non-radiation condition in this context appears unfeasible. Additionally, we examine the non-radiation condition within the context of a single particle's motion. Specifically, we illustrate that for a particle executing simple harmonic motion, the non-radiation condition is satisfied if its initial velocity is zero. Finally, we provide references to other articles by the authors that expand upon the discussions presented here. Practical implications of the non-radiation condition are evident, as its violation leads to significant issues, particularly because ensuring this condition is gauge invariant is generally impossible. While this gauge dependency is not a concern in most practical scenarios, the initial conditions required to establish a solution that satisfies the non-radiation condition are critical. If these conditions are not met, gauge functions must be selected to enforce the non-radiation condition, resulting in gauge-dependent solutions. Such scenarios are likely to cause problems in high-speed ICs and printed circuit boards. Although this paper offers an gauge-invariant perspective, our previous work provided gauge-dependent formulations of Jefimenko's equations

The sample efficiency of model-free algorithms is generally attributed to their superior sample complexity and lack of need for environment modeling. However, we contend that the true distinction lies in the sample efficiency of model-free versus model-based methods when a feasible environment model exists. We provide theoretical and empirical evidence supporting this claim using Gridworld and simulated robotics tasks. Our findings indicate that model-based methods can achieve comparable performance to model-free approaches while requiring at least an order of magnitude fewer samples, provided that samples collected during the model construction phase are excluded from the evaluation. This is because model-based methods remain ineffective during the modeling phase, rendering them inefficient for learning effective policies under that perspective. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the sample inefficiency of model-free approaches stems from their failure to leverage the environment model, which acts as a guide for data collection. By integrating the model into the decision process within a model-based framework, samples are utilized more effectively, thereby accelerating sample usage. Our empirical results confirm the sample efficiency of sample-driven models by applying them to deep reinforcement learning and path planning under high-dimensional states. We implemented these models using Point Clouds and Sphere encoding under dense observations. Additionally, we established a new state-of-the-art for sample-efficient model-based reinforcement learning in continuous control and applied our method to real-world robotics tasks. We released the code at https://github.com/haotongliu/Sample-Efficient-RL. This work was partially funded by the Hong Kong Research Grants Council (GRF 16205020).

Health Organization (WHO) established the International Joint Working Group on Arsenic and Infection to unify research efforts and accelerate scientific insights into the infectious disease risks associated with arsenic exposure. The group's strategy involved categorizing infections into three infection-related outcomes (IROs) and consolidating data from epidemiological studies to generate new evidence. This study focuses on the first IRO, which encompasses acute watery diarrhea and cholera. A systematic literature search was conducted to identify relevant studies, the data was compiled, and a meta-analysis was performed on acute watery diarrhea. Results indicated a positive association between arsenic exposure and acute watery diarrhea in children (p<0.05, Odds Ratio=1.37, 95% CI=1.09–1.71) and adults (p<0.05, Odds Ratio=1.52, 95% CI=1.09–2.11). No such positive association was found for cholera. Given the limited number of studies on cholera, future research should prioritize establishing exposure thresholds and investigating the underlying biological mechanisms. These findings contribute valuable data to the WHO's mission and assist in formulating scientific policies and measures to mitigate health risks linked to arsenic exposure. This process is critical for intent recognition because encountering unknown intents can severely degrade recognition accuracy and cause system failures if the dialogue system lacks the necessary intent definitions. Current approaches to new intent discovery are limited to specific tasks, such as question answering, and are often invalid for general dialogue applications. To address this, we introduce a generalized framework for identifying new intent categories by leveraging user browsing history and system responses as a proxy for intent data. We then extract latent intent features from this history using both user and system perspectives to detect novel intent categories through user-involvement and user-ir-involvement metrics, alongside an unsupervised method based on clustering analysis of system responses relative to user history. We evaluate our framework across two task-specific scenarios and two general-purpose tasks using real-world data from Stack Overflow and Reddit, alongside synthetic data tailored for intent discovery. Our findings indicate that user-user-involvement and user-system-involvement perform best in task-specific contexts, while user-system-involvement is superior in general dialogue settings. Although all methods show improved results with increased data volume, user-system-involvement continues to yield the highest accuracy even with minimal data. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that user-system-involvement is more effective at identifying new intent categories than clustering analysis when intent definitions are known, whereas clustering analysis outperforms user-system-involvement when intent definitions are unknown. These results highlight the potential of user and system perspectives as viable solutions for new intent discovery, offering practical value for improving existing dialogue systems and enabling the unsupervised identification of new intents without requiring intent definitions. This research expands the current state of the art by proposing a comprehensive framework for new intent discovery and a novel property-based approach that surpasses existing methods. By integrating user and system perspectives, our work establishes a new benchmark for this line of research. We have made our code and data publicly available at https://github.com/ashutoshkumar9999/IntentDiscovery2021.

While Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have achieved great success, their reliance on local filters and max pooling for downsampling restrict their ability to effectively model long-range relationships. In contrast, Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) and Transformers have emerged as leading architectures for long-range dependency modeling in natural language processing. To address this limitation, we introduce the Attention Guided Convolutional Network (AGCN), a hierarchical, bidirectional, bidirectional RNN (Bi-LSTM) that leverages spatial attention to predict scene objects from scene layout. AGCN processes scene depiction information in a sequence-based manner using a multi-scale mechanism, guided by scene layout through region attention. This region attention is derived from hierarchical global maximum pooling of feature maps extracted by a multi-level convolutional feature pyramid, offering global structural context. To our knowledge, AGCN is the first to integrate multi-scale Bi-LSTMs with spatial and region attention to efficiently capture multi-level dependencies in a sequence-based framework. Extensive experiments on the 3DShapeNet and 6DGP benchmarks demonstrate that AGCN significantly outperforms existing methods. The source code will be made available at https://github.com/zhengyuz/AGCN.

# Abstract

This study investigates the scaling behavior of measurements and gradients when the circuit depth increases in quantum deep learning. Focusing on photonic quantum computing, we present a task where the circuit is structured to be classically unlearnable at the output level but learnable when a mid-circuit measurement is included. We analyze the distribution of gradients and measurement values relative to circuit depth and identify that the error landscape becomes increasingly challenging for optimization as the circuit deepens. We also explore the connections between these findings and the classical literature on fair data representation. These insights suggest that careful task selection is essential for developing methods in quantum deep learning.

This paper presents a definition and analysis of a plausibly efficient algorithm model that subsumes the RAM. This model is based on a single primitive: the search tree, whose nodes represent choices. The primitive operation searches this tree for a path that is not rejected by a rejection function; the resulting point on the path is the operation's output. The model's strength lies in its ability to bound algebrizable (and thus Isola) problems using a single parameter, $s$, which represents the tree's size. We demonstrate that if algebrization is replaced by "implausibly efficient" algebrization, the IS0L = MATH result remains valid, and the parameter $s$ can be shifted from bounding the problem to bounding the rejection function's depth. Furthermore, we show that a variant of the MIP* = PSPACE result holds under these conditions. These findings suggest a potential route to achieving progress in relativized complexity classes that are as strong as, or stronger than, the IS0L = MATH parameter. Additionally, we provide robust upper and lower bounds for the parameters required for specific problems, including SAT, the unique games hierarchy, and the unique colorability hierarchy. Notably, for SAT, the upper and lower bounds align in the plausibly efficient model, contrasting with the discrepancy observed in the implausibly efficient model. This parameter is stronger than the one used in the IS0L = MATH result because it yields stronger lower bounds and applies to a broader range of problems, such as the unique colorability hierarchy. Consequently, we can now establish a result for a stronger hierarchy, and we have also derived a stronger lower bound for the unique games hierarchy. These findings suggest a pathway to a stronger version of the UG = QC result, which we will address in a subsequent paper. Finally, we offer a clearer perspective on the significance of plausibly efficient models.

The MDSI domain offers several advantages: spectral data is compactly represented; spectral variations across the scene are uniform; and the domain features uniform dimensionality and spatial extent. Ultimately, the change detector output is mapped onto the original image space through the inverse of the spectral transformation model applied to create the MDSI domain. This results in a precise change detection map that retains full spectral information. Utilizing the inverse model to report changes in the original image space ensures accurate spectral reporting and complete image coverage. This effect is fundamental to the operation of the human nose, as electrons tunneling from olfactory receptor molecules to measuring electrodes generate the sense of smell. Beyond biology, tunneling is essential in various fields including nuclear physics, chemistry, electronics, optoelectronics, and photovoltaics. The investigation into the magnetic properties of Mn-doped ZnO nanoribbons (ZnO-NRs) was conducted using the density functional theory (DFT) framework, specifically the generalized gradient approximation (GGA) with the Perdew-Burke-Bernardi (PBE) method, to clarify the mechanism behind their room-temperature magnetism. Our findings reveal that single-atom Mn substitution within the NR structure yields a maximum magnetic moment of 3 μB per atom, aligning with the 3d5 configuration of Mn. Conversely, replacing Zn atoms with Mn results in a non-magnetic ground state. When two Mn atoms substitute two adjacent Zn sites, the system exhibits a half-metalllic character. Furthermore, the application of a uniaxial magnetic field induces a spin-polarized band gap in the monodoped NR, whereas applying an electric field eliminates the band gap in the bir-doped NR. Finally, our results demonstrate that the magnetic moment of the ZnO-NR can be effectively controlled by co-doping with Mg. These outcomes suggest that Mg co-doping presents a promising strategy for designing spintronic devices based on transition metal oxides. Keywords: first-principles, Mg co-doping, nanoribbons, transition metal oxides, magnetic moment.

validity within quantum gravity because gravitational energy generates a non-varying, logarithmic potential at large scales, which causes particle wavefunctions to tunnel into one another. This phenomenon is accurately modeled by a Coulombic wavefunction, which remains a valid eigenfunction in quantum general relativity (QGR) due to its asymptotic behavior matching that of a Bessel function. By applying the superposition principle to these Coulombic wavefunctions, we derive the Schrödinger equation and the associated quantum conditions, which hold true for all values of the GR parameter. These conditions explain how an infinite set of distinct quantum states arises from a single Coulombic wavefunction, with their sequence governed by the GR parameter. We demonstrate that these states are equally spaced and vary in energy based on the particles' masses, proving that the original premise of identical, degenerate particles is false. Furthermore, we show that the quantum numbers labeling these states are constrained by quantum conditions that depend on the GR parameter, signifying that quantum gravity introduces new degrees of freedom to the system. Consequently, quantum gravity renders the number of particles ill-defined, as the transformation of a particle's state can increase the total count. Finally, we illustrate that applying a quantum gravity operation to a system yields results that are entirely distinct from those of the original system, even when utilizing the most basic quantum gravity operation: a non-singular black hole with a radius on the order of the cosmological horizon. Under these conditions, the quantum conditions are violated, confirming that quantum gravity creates new degrees of freedom and alters the system's nature. This work serves as a proof-of-concept, demonstrating that the quantum gravity parameter is capable of changing a system's identity. Therefore, it is inappropriate to apply quantum gravity separately to distinct systems, as the additive nature of quantum gravity would be compromised. Instead, it is necessary to construct a quantum gravity framework for all particle species, which will result in infinitely many new quantum states. These infinitely many states emerge from the breakdown of the original quantum conditions and are characterized by degrees of freedom associated with the quantum gravity theory. This implies that the degrees of freedom in a many-particle system are not simply the sum of individual particle degrees of freedom but are significantly greater, a point we illustrate using harmonic oscillators. Thus, the harmonic oscillator serves as a crucial non-trivial example of how quantum gravity alters a system's identity. In conclusion, quantum gravity generates new degrees of freedom that are fundamentally distinct from those present before its application, thereby changing the system's identity. Therefore,

Multimodal learning has proven effective for detecting hate speech, yet it remains underexplored when dealing with social media posts containing hate speech images. This paper presents a novel multi-modal contrastive learning framework designed for multimodal hate speech detection. We propose a multi-modal contrastive loss function that leverages the interdependence between text and image features. Experiments on two multimodal hate speech detection benchmarks show that our model outperforms existing methods. The source code is available at https://github.com/ehabshadkar/MHMHD.

In multimodal learning, the primary challenge is effectively fusing data from multiple sources. Current methods often rely on early fusion techniques, which concatenate inputs from different modalities before processing. In contrast, we propose a novel architecture called Multi-Head Modeling Network (MHMHD), which utilizes late fusion to handle heterogeneous inputs. Our approach contrasts text and image embeddings within a shared embedding space using contrastive learning. We assess the model's robustness by randomly flipping text characters and image pixels to simulate uncertainty and evaluate performance using AUC-PR and Accuracy metrics

Notably, the delayed coefficient can be transformed into a standard coefficient using a time-changing technique, a method applicable to a broad class of BSDEs with Lipschitz generators. Consequently, this paper also contributes to the development of BSDEs with a Lipschitz generator, a category to which our studied BSDEs with a Lipschitz delayed generator belong. Our results are relevant to both weak and strong well-posedness issues. Given the ongoing development of the field of BSDEs with delayed generators and the continuous creation of new challenges, this work aims to address a gap in current research. By combining techniques from Ma and Ma (2010) with those used by Guan and Zhang (2013), we achieve a resolution to this problem type. This study examines the sample complexity of policy learning through model prediction errors within a sample planning framework, where the agent trains a local model from experience and uses it to compute planning trajectories. Our primary contribution is establishing a theoretical connection between the sample complexity of learning the optimal policy and that of learning the optimal local model in an MBRL setting. While caching and compressed sensing prioritize sparsity, coded caching and distributed compression sensing exploit the sparsity of user demands. This work examines the tradeoff between sum transmission rate and outage probability in distributed compressed sensing (DCS) networks that employ cooperation among sensors. We derive closed-form expressions for outage probability and analyze rate-outage performance for both scalar and vector valued compressible sources. Focusing on the vector case, we model each sensor as a independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) Gaussian process. Our derived expressions are exact and fully aligned with those presented in the information theory community. We also evaluate the performance of the proposed DCS network against independent sensing, demonstrating that the outage probability of both scalar and vector sources is reduced when sensors are non-caught in correlation. Finally, we compare the results of our DCS network with existing literature, confirming that our approach yields a lower outage probability than methods proposed in prior work.

This paper investigates various graph-based algorithms designed to address text summarization via an extractive method. To evaluate sentence similarity, we utilize two metrics: sentence overlap and edit distance. Our findings indicate that combining a similarity metric with an information measure, specifically entropy, produces high-quality summaries. By applying different graph algorithms to construct the summary, we observe that summaries generated via the shortest path approach yield the most compelling results. Furthermore, we demonstrate that summaries produced by the k-shortest path method are statistically as effective as those generated by the shortest path, but they include twice as many distinct words. In contrast, summaries produced by the minimum spanning tree algorithm use 50% fewer words than those generated by the k-shortest path method. To address this limitation, we propose using a parameterized algorithm based on the weight of edges rather than graph topology, allowing for the control of summary length while maintaining high quality. Our experiments reveal that this parameterized approach can reduce summary length by up to 50% without significantly compromising performance. Finally, we examine the use of semantic vectors to enhance edit distance calculations, noting that while this method increases summary length, it results in lower-quality outputs compared to summaries generated without it. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to analyze entropy-based information measures for summary evaluation using graph algorithms. Our results indicate that entropy outperforms other semantic measures by up to 30% when evaluating summaries by count, and outperforms other semantic measures by up to 150% when evaluating them by length. These findings support the use of entropy as a more reliable metric for evaluating extractive summarization systems. The source code is available at https://github.com/ds-mlai/K-shot-summary. This study introduces the verification of lower bounds for polynomials using non-negative relaxation methods, which are currently the most effective computational tools for estimating the global minimum. These techniques are essential for confirming the optimality of candidate solutions and the (im)optimality of lower bounds. The primary contributions of this paper include: (i) a survey of verification methods based on Sum of Squares (SOS) and other non-negative forms; (ii) an analysis of the computational complexity involved in these procedures; (iii) a comparison of the performance of different verification approaches; (iv) the evaluation of the impact of verification efforts on the optimization process; and (v) the investigation of the interplay between verification and optimization. The authors tested these methods across numerous polynomial test cases, demonstrating that the selection of a specific technique should consider both the problem's characteristics and its scale. This paper re-examines the odd version of Tur\'an's problem, which aims to find the minimal number of triangles a graph must contain given a constraint on its edge total minus the number of its bipartite subgraphs. We establish the solution to this problem, known as the \threecolourproblem, for all cases where one vertex degree exceeds the total edge count by at least seven. Furthermore, we identify the unique extremal graphs for the edge bounds in the three-colour problem when $n\equiv 0,1 \pmod 3$ for $n\ge 23$, and for $n\equiv 2\pmod 3$ for $n\ge 19$. These findings significantly extend the previously documented results by Ahswede and Chv\'atal (1976) and Radziszowski (2002). Additionally, we refine the \threecolourproblem by replacing the number of triangles with the number of odd cycles of length at least three, a parameter we term the \oddexcess. We demonstrate that the \oddexcesslowerboundtheorem holds for all $n\le 11$ and prove a tight lower bound for $n\ge 12$. Our results confirm that the minimum number of odd cycles of length at least three in a graph with $e-\bi(e)$ edges is achieved by either a complete tripartite graph or a specific modification of one such graph involving two extra edges and two fewer triangles. To our knowledge, this resolves the \oddexcesslowerboundproblem for all $n$. Finally, we provide a sufficient condition for the tightness of this lower bound and conjecture its universal applicability. Our analysis is grounded in the theory of the odd defect, a novel extension of the defect concept introduced in a prior publication. Current state-of-the-art vehicle routing methods for delivery services typically depend on historical demand data to forecast future orders. However, in the initial phases of launching new routes, historical data is often unavailable. This paper presents a method to generate routes without relying on past order history by utilizing real-time social media data to predict customer locations. We developed a machine learning model that takes a user's social media post and geolocation into account to forecast their likely location for order pickup. We trained this model using public Foursquare check-in data from Los Angeles, Chicago, and Boston. Additionally, we adapted the DeepRoute algorithm to integrate with our location predictions. A simulation was then conducted to evaluate the performance of our approach against traditional routing methods. Using synthetic data that mirrors the distribution of real customer locations, we compared the total travel distances of our method against deep learning and linear programming baselines. Furthermore, we conducted an ablation study to assess the system's robustness under conditions of high demand and short lead times. Finally, we validated the accuracy of our location predictions by comparing them with real customer locations in the Washington D.C. area. The findings from both our simulation and empirical analysis demonstrate that our proposed system effectively reduces travel distances compared to baseline approaches.

We propose training a Generative Discriminator (GD) alongside the standard Generative Network (G) to classify patches as either showing a lane departure or belonging to normal driving scenarios. Experiments were performed on two publicly available datasets: nuScence and Waymo Open Dataset

We introduce a Bayesian quantile regression model featuring random effects, designed to account for correlations within observed survival data. This model serves as a simplified representation of a chemically active biopolymer consisting of two heads driven by self-phosphorylation, where the inter-head distance is fixed when the bond is intact. The mean-squared displacement (MSD) for both states is calculated analytively for low active Péclet numbers. The findings indicate that the effective diffusion coefficient in the hydrodynamic regime aligns with the passive regime prediction. However, the MSD analysis reveals that the anomalous diffusion characteristics of the dimer are significantly influenced by the average duration of the monomer state. Furthermore, the crossover Péclet number separating the hydrodynamic and non-hydrodynamic regimes is directly related to the average lifetimes of the monomer and dimer states. These theoretical results are fully validated through extensive active Brownian dynamics simulations. Additionally, the implications of this model for the exploration kinetics of DNA hairpins are briefly discussed. Our findings suggest that effectively controlling the monomer state's average lifetime can drastically alter the dynamical behavior of head dimers. Consequently, head dimers that are more active than the monomer above a specific Péclet number may be biologically significant. This could provide a simple mechanism for biological systems to produce molecules with tailored dynamics by utilizing a limited set of active components. Ultimately, our study offers insights into the design of active matter made of biopolymers.

We establish the existence of a value function that satisfies the Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation with integral terms, achieving this through a weak approach that incorporates a smoothing step. In applications, this result yields the existence of a stable equilibrium point for the mean-field Cournot game featuring production costs with Allee effects. This confirms equilibrium existence without requiring a high number of firms, a strong assumption in existing literature. Furthermore, the derived equilibrium is proven to be both robust and coherent. This represents the first mathematical equilibrium analysis of a mean-field Cournot game where production costs exhibit the Allee effect. The significance of Allee effects in population dynamics is well-documented; specifically, the Allee threshold acts as a critical population size below which a population cannot survive. An Allee effect is present when the per capita growth rate declines as the population size increases. Our analysis demonstrates that firms can sustain the population despite a delay-induced Allee effect, even when delays are non-negligible. This finding aligns with the assumption of limited migration between markets. This research extends the work of \cite{BHM21}, which analyzed a similar mean-field Cournot game but lacked a delay and the corresponding Allee effect. Additionally, our methodology builds upon the contributions of \cite{GP21}, which addressed the existence of a viscosity solution to a Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation with integral terms under control constraints and neither sub- nor super-differentiable costs. Our approach accommodates both uncontrolled and controlled delays, as well as Allee and Allee-free effects. The techniques employed are applicable to a broad class of mean-field games featuring Allee effects and delayed interactions. This methodology holds significant potential for advancing mean-field game theory and stochastic control theory. Our methodology offers novel contributions to the analysis of equilibria in various fields, including biology and economics. Specifically, in economics, Allee effects have gained increasing attention in population-dependent games, a phenomenon previously unaddressed in existing research. Our findings indicate that Allee effects can be overcame, thereby extending the scope of applicable equilibrium existence results. This paper also builds upon the contributions of \cite{GP21}, which did not consider Allee effects. Our findings demonstrate that Allee effects can be overcome, thus expanding the range of scenarios in which an equilibrium exists. This work offers a fresh perspective on mean-field games by presenting a rigorous existence result that does not rely on the high-number assumption.

In white dwarps and neutron stars, interactions between stellar matter and dark matter significantly alter both dark matter particles and emitted photons. These effects are incorporated via the opacity of thermal radiation and the cross sections of charged and neutral particles. Our findings for emissivity include photon suppression, which may influence constraints derived from stellar cooling. The problem requires determining if a set of binary operators, which do not necessarily be commutative, are assigned by a quantum circuit such that their final outputs can be measured simultaneously in the computational basis. The proposed algorithm reduces the asymptotic complexity of solving the commutativity problem. Furthermore, it demonstrates that the probability distribution required to verify commutativity can be generated in the same runtime as finding the classical proof, without altering the asymptotic complexity. This paper proposes a model for SRAM PUF leakage, suggesting that leakage-based TRNGs function as truncated TRNGs that sample a subset of a larger entropy pool. We demonstrate that a single memory read is insufficient to generate high-quality random numbers and introduce a novel algorithm that creates multiple leakage samples from a single power measurement to enhance randomness. This approach requires no hardware modifications beyond a standard Multiplexer, making it well-suited for SRAMs with limited pin count. Simulation results indicate that this model produces high-quality random numbers even with a single sample per activation, reducing the number of measurements needed to achieve a specific bit entropy. Each sample can be modeled as a Bernoulli trial, allowing us to calculate the total number of measurements required to achieve a target entropy as the sum of independent Bernoulli trials with varying probabilities. Using this methodology, we show that SRAM leakage can be effectively modeled as a sequence of independent Bernoulli trials with a small number of samples to generate high-quality random numbers. We validated this model on large SRAM arrays using Xilinx XC7A100T and Intel Stratix 10 FPGA devices, confirming our findings. Furthermore, we developed a SRAM leakage-based TRNG using this model, achieving an entropy estimation of 7.99 bits per number with just a single leakage sample per generation. Additionally, this model can be applied to evaluate the randomness contributions of other leakage samples from diverse locations. In conclusion, our work demonstrates that SRAM leakage can be effectively modeled as a sequence of independent Bernoulli trials, enabling the design of efficient TRNGs from a minimal number of samples. This model also holds applicability for countermeasures against Random Number Generator (RNG) attacks. This work examines the interaction between a mechanical resonator exhibiting $q$-deformation and an optical cavity Resonance. The analysis is conducted within the framework of the Caldirola-Kanai model, assuming the optomechanical system begins in the equilibrium state of the Fock $|0\rangle _M$ state. Employing the standard Born-Markov approximation, we derive the Master equation for the optomechanical system and the corresponding Lindblad operators under the rotating wave approximation. Additionally, these findings may assist experimentalists in selecting the most suitable scheme for observing $q$-deformation within the field of quantum optics. Finally, we note that the methods employed in this study are applicable to other quantum systems interacting with $q$-deformed thermal reservoirs.

This efficiency manifests in three primary forms: massive speedups for unbiased estimation of translation invariant observables, rapid convergence of quantum state generation under low-depth circuits, and the rapid thermalization of such systems following excitation. These processes are governed by constraints known as the "lightcone" and the "Mendelsohn formation," which dictate the spatial spread of support and spatial correlations, respectively, over time. This study extends the concepts of lightcone and Mendelsohn formations to broader classes of Hamiltonians by leveraging the entanglement structure of thermal states. Specifically, we demonstrate that for a subsystem of size $k$, the thermal state of an isolated quantum system evolves from the thermal state of the complementary subsystem of size $N-k$ via local deformations, where $N$ denotes the total system size. Consequently, we derive general "lightcone" and "Mendelsohn" conditions applicable to these scenarios. We illustrate the utility of these derivations through two applications: first, obtaining a general circuit lower bound for preparing thermal states of subsystems; and second, establishing general circuit lower bounds for tasks involving subsystem measurement. Furthermore, we characterize these structures using matrix product states and provide experimental validation of our findings using NMR technology. Our theoretical framework makes a significant contribution to the investigation of general quantum subsystem evolution. Furthermore, our findings directly impact the quantum advantage of variational quantum algorithms, as circuit lower bounds established in this paper cover not only standard lightcone and Mendelsohn formations but also a more comprehensive class of "generalized" lightcone and "generalized" Mendelsohn formations. This encompasses not only lightcone entanglement but also long-range correlations, offering a more rigorous foundation for analyzing the behavior of these quantum algorithms. Furthermore, our findings directly address the quantum advantage of machine learning via quantum neural networks. As a concrete example, we establish a connection between our circuit lower bounds and the expressibility of quantum neural networks. We analyze the temporal evolution of a cryptocurrency's price relative to others, quantifying its significance through in-degree metrics derived from pair-wise Granger causality. The resulting data is processed using a sliding window approach to generate time-series records of the in-degree distribution for each asset. Our primary objective is to determine the primary's status by examining the stability of these timeseries. To achieve this, we compute two key indicators: the average deviation of the primary's in-degree mean from the entire dataset, and the variance ratio comparing the primary's in-degree variance to that of the dataset. By evaluating these two measures across individual cryptocurrencies, we identify and select the most consistent primary candidate. Finally, we investigate the impact of market volatility on price dynamics by comparing the characteristics of the primary and other cryptocurrencies. Across all analyses, the Bitcoin (BTC) consistently exhibits the most stable and distinctive attributes. Additionally, we observe that the attributes of the primary are significantly affected by market volatility, whereas the properties of other cryptocurrencies remain largely unchanged. These findings align with our initial hypothesis. These results hold consistent across the entire dataset and individual analyses, with Bitcoin emerging as the primary cryptocurrency in all cases. Furthermore, our analysis of timeseries stability before and after the Trump investigation illustrates the impact of such events on price dynamics. Specifically, our findings indicate that following the investigation, both the identification of the primary and its attributes underwent significant changes. This work contributes to the field by providing insights into the role of key assets in price dynamics, demonstrating a data-driven method for identifying the primary cryptocurrency and its characteristics across various time scales, and offering initial insights into how investigations influence price dynamics. We introduce a method grounded in the bias-variance tradeoff to make this selection. Our approach is learned entirely from data by comparing a simple linear model against a "linearized" version of a non-linear tree-based classifier like XGBoost. Both models are trained alongside a control group that receives no treatment; their performance within this group is used to estimate the difference in predictive performance under a given treatment. This proof-of-concept demonstration utilizes learned biases and variances to guide model selection between a linear X-boost and a linearized X-boost. On a large-scale real-world dataset featuring a non-linear treatment effect, our selection criterion correctly identifies the superior model in 92% of test samples. By concluding with an analysis of existing challenges and proposed future research avenues in graph-based neural learning, we aim to highlight the field's current limitations and potential growth trajectories. This work synthesizes insights from recent studies to present a unified perspective on the field.

We also evaluate the performance of leading algorithms across prominent benchmarks and highlight the current limitations of self-supervised learning within the graph domain.

We introduce a straightforward method to strengthen QKD protocols against certain quantum attacks that currently lack effective countermeasures. Specifically, our technique is applicable when the sender transmits multiple copies of the same quantum state across successive time slots, provided these slots are indistinguishable to an eavesdropper. While the existence of this warm component is well-documented through X-ray observations, its physical nature remains debated. An alternative hypothesis suggests that the apparent warm phase is merely an optical illusion caused by ICM being heated by accretion shocks at the cluster outskirts and viewed through translucent filaments with lower electron densities. To test this hypothesis, we conducted MUSE (Multi Unit Spectroscopic Explorer) observations of 10 galaxy clusters within the COSMOS field. Our analysis focused on the [OIII] emission line to map the distribution of star-forming galaxies in the clusters' outskirts. We compared these observations against various hydrodynamical simulations, which showed that the [OIII]-bearing galaxies are not uniformly distributed throughout the ICM but are instead concentrated in warm filaments. These filaments possess lower electron densities that obscure the warm gas behind them, creating the observed X-ray signature of a separate warm phase. Consequently, our findings indicate that accretion shocks do heat the ICM, and the evidence for two distinct temperature phases does not necessarily imply a two-phase medium. This study marks the first application of the MUSE instrument to cluster outskirts and demonstrates the effectiveness of near-infrared integral field unit spectroscopy for investigating cluster accretion processes. The remaining COSMOS-Galaxy Cluster MUSE Observations can be accessed at the MUSE Legacy Archive (MLA) at https://www.astro.ohio-state.edu/~galclus/mla/. These data complement the existing MUSE data on cool cores presented in Mulroy et al. (2021).

Serving such a diverse array of users within limited resources creates a complex challenge. This paper introduces a general framework for optimizing resource allocation to maximize network throughput under 5G and Beyond 5G (B5G) conditions, ensuring compliance with user Quality of Service requirements. The proposed solution employs a multi-stage architecture where each stage addresses specific challenges using distinct methods. The initial stage handles user admission and scheduling, while subsequent stages tackle the non-convex optimization problem through machine learning and game theory. Specifically, a Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM) is utilized to estimate path loss and interference for user equipment (UE), followed by the use of Nash Equilibrium to distribute remaining resources. A key advantage of this approach is its ability to ensure resource allocation and EE optimization in high-density scenarios where standard protocols fail. Performance is evaluated through extensive simulations based on three real-world datasets covering various locations and conditions. Results demonstrate a 15% increase in EE compared to a Long Term Evolution (LTE) LTE-A baseline, and 20% and 18% improvements over both LTE and LTE-A equilibrium solutions, respectively. Furthermore, the study analyzes the impact of non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) and advanced beamforming techniques. Beamforming significantly enhances EE by up to 100% in the Nash Equilibrium solution, whereas NOMA offers only a marginal gain. However, in high-density areas with intense interference, NOMAM can degrade performance by up to 15% relative to orthogonal schemes. Consequently, for scenarios involving large numbers of users, non-geometric geometric (NGG) beamforming is recommended. The study also explores beam management within the proposed framework, showing that it can improve throughput by up to 30% without compromising EE. Finally, the protocol's robustness is verified under extreme conditions, including the sudden addition of new users and the loss of beam synchronization. These solutions are implemented as protocol layers within the OpenLabs platform, an extensible environment designed for the development and evaluation of future 5G and B5G networks.

Performance evaluations were conducted using the OpenLabs platform.

The proposed solution significantly enhances energy efficiency through lower latency and higher reliability, making it suitable for emerging applications in future 5G and B5G networks.

We analyze a series of runs where initial turbulence is generated either through boundary movements or internal forces within the periodic box, with some cases seeded with a uniform random velocity field. The influence of rotation was assessed by applying Coriolis forces directly to the gas. Our results indicate that at the resolutions achievable with current algorithms, initial or boundary magnetic fields alone do not significantly restrict the formation of dense regions where gravity can operate, nor do they substantially alter the overall statistics of these regions in either rotating or non-rotating setups. However, the interaction between turbulence and magnetic fields does modify the scale at which condensation occurs, an effect that becomes more pronounced as the magnetic field strength increases. When rotation is present, the orientation of the magnetic field relative to the rotation axis markedly changes how the field regulates the distribution of dense gas in non-rotating simulations but has a minimal impact in rotating ones. Specifically, when the rotation axis aligns with the magnetic field, rotating simulations exhibit far fewer small-scale dense condensations compared to non-rotating cases, whereas misaligned configurations yield results that are largely identical to those without rotation. We conclude that at the current resolution, the primary function of rotation in a magnetized turbulent medium is to impede the cascade of energy to smaller scales rather than to directly influence density fluctuations. Finally, we observe that in both rotating and non-rotating simulations, the suppression of small-scale density fluctuations by strong magnetic fields is more effective in turbulent driving via boundary movements than in internal driving mechanisms. This suggests that in forming systems driven by internal turbulence, such as galactic disks, magnetic fields may play a crucial role in shaping the characteristics of dense gas and molecular clouds. Conversely, in forming systems where turbulence originates from boundary sources, magnetic fields may be less significant. Its primary objective is to determine the optimal control that maximizes the mean-speed exponent for small perturbations while ensuring the system remains subcritical across all scales. The speed at which equilibrium approaches is analyzed using large deviation theory, which yields mean-field, self-averaging outcomes. The findings offer new insights into the design of nonlinear multi-agent systems that are both optimal and stable, a challenge that has long persisted in control theory. In the wild, animals navigate their environments using a variety of locomotion strategies, making understanding these movements crucial for creating realistic virtual creatures and next-generation AI systems. However, compiling a comprehensive inventory of species-wide locomotion strategies is a challenging task. To overcome this, we developed a data-driven approach to uncover new visual dynamics and interactions from a new class of data: large-scale, high-resolution, real-world animal videos. This work presents two primary contributions. First, we defined a new representation for visual dynamics discovery based on local volume element features, which are robust to rotation and scale. Second, we demonstrated that this representation is highly effective for unsupervised discovery, revealing new visual dynamics and interactions across an enormous dataset of over 1,000 animal videos. These discovered dynamics are compact, interpretable, and span over 100 visual categories. The resulting bucket framework not only offers a simple and effective solution for new joint discovery but also serves as a powerful tool for novel scene understanding and predicting future states. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/zqiu2018/SD.

While this distribution involves two parameters—a location parameter $\mu \in \mathbb{R}$ and a scale parameter $\sigma > 0$—we will estimate them simultaneously by treating them as a unified complex parameter defined as $\gamma := \mu + i\sigma$. The resulting region will be a domain within the complex plane, and we will provide a simple, explicit formula to represent it as either a disc or a square. The derivation of this region relies on applying the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality to an appropriately chosen vector space. Furthermore, we will demonstrate the region's uniqueness by examining the kernel of the inner product. Finally, we will select an optimal form for the region by minimizing its Lebesgue measure (either the area or the side length). As an application, we will approximate the distribution of the total sum $S = \sum_{k=1}^N X_k$ for a sequence of $N$ independent and identically distributed random variables, where $X_k$ denotes the $k$-th variable. This approach allows us to bound the probabilities of events related to $S$. The mathematical foundation for this work draws upon concepts from both statistics and complex analysis. Our findings will be illustrated through various numerical simulations and visualizations. The primary advantage of this method is that the region remains unique and retains its original form, even when $N$ is not a multiple of 4. Additionally, it is uniquely characterized as the domain that minimizes the Lebesgue measure (or side length in the case of a square). The development of this work was significantly influenced by a simulation tool we created and distributed as a Python module; a user-friendly web interface for this module is also available. A key benefit of the application is the ability to bound the probabilities of events defined by the distance between $S$ and a given disc or square in the complex plane. We envision this method as a valuable instrument for statisticians or data analysts working with Cauchy-distributed data. The statistics and analysis of such data present significant challenges, notably the lack of a well-defined "mean," and our method offers a solution to this difficulty. This work is a counterpart to our previous study on the Student distribution, for which a dedicated user interface and web interface are also available. A previous version of this paper was previously published.

across multiple patient subgroups under a single protocol, producing a multi-armed structure with several concurrent study arms. Outcomes in these trials are often continuous or categorical. When sample sizes are insufficient to ensure a sufficient number of expected events for standard analysis methods, researchers may opt to utilize time-to-event data based on study duration. In scenarios where events occur before the study concludes, the resulting censoring can be informative; however, this approach is frequently unfeasible for baskets trials due to variations in arm sample sizes that make predicting events per arm difficult. Furthermore, informative censoring often arises from informative dropout, which occurs when patients discontinue the trial due to reasons other than the primary outcome. This situation is common in basket trials because arms are closed individually based on performance; dropout here is informative as it is linked to the decision-making process regarding whether to continue or terminate an arm, rather than solely depending on the patient's health status. Consequently, the decision to terminate an arm is influenced by the outcome, rendering the process informative. This note provides an overview of methods for analyzing baskets trials under such conditions and suggests improvements to existing approaches. A key proposal involves analyzing the baskets trial as a singular multi-state process by constructing a unified life table for all arms. To leverage information from terminated arms, a terminating arm can be incorporated as an additional state within the single multi-state framework. The paper applies this methodology to a recent oncology basket trial and concludes by discussing the approach's limitations and potential extensions. Keywords: Basket trials; Informative censoring; Informative dropout; Informative termination; Multi-state analysis; Oncology; Time-to-event; Unified life table.

Our findings demonstrate a significant improvement in both visual quality and quantitative metrics. On the QISD dataset, we achieved a mean DSC of 0.614 and a mean PER of 0.186. These results surpass a strong baseline consisting of the state-of-the-art monosegmentation models MoE and HyPerNet, which recorded a mean DSC of 0.558 and a mean PER of 0.126. The proposed method is particularly valuable for improving segmentation in low-dose fluoroscopy, a currently popular clinical application where current deep learning models struggle. By utilizing radiographs, this approach not only enhances segmentation accuracy in fluoroscopy but also advances cross-modality medical image analysis. The source code and dataset are accessible at https://github.com/SebastianKluth/QISD. Our implementation will be presented at the Medical Image Computing and Computer-Assisted Intervention conference (MICCAI) and integrated into the MedMND open-source library.

These flares exhibit a broad range of energies and occur with such high frequency that they serve as ideal test subjects for theories regarding stellar magnetic field generation and the processes of magnetic energy accumulation and release. This study employs a novel analysis technique to measure the variability in flare energy release by calculating the frequency of flares as a function of energy. Furthermore, we observed that within each population, flare energy distributions vary over time. This implies that stellar flares do not adhere to a universal energy distribution and that the statistical properties of flares are influenced by the stellar evolution path. Consequently, the statistical nature of stellar flares cannot be fully explained by magnetic dynamo theories that predict magnetic field generation based solely on stellar rotation. Our findings indicate that stellar activity evolution must be a critical factor in dynamo models aiming to explain stellar magnetic fields. Finally, we suggest that future statistical studies of stellar flares should focus on categorizing different population characteristics. We investigate the deformation theory of abelian gauge theories of gravity by linearizing their field equations around arbitrary solutions. These theories are defined by a metric $g_{ab}$ and a $SU(2)$ connection $A_i^j$ governed by the condition that the curvature $F_{ij}$ lies within the standard abelian subalgebra of $su(2) \cong so(3)$. The analysis reveals that the number of degrees of freedom in these abelian models matches that of General Relativity. This conclusion is supported by deriving the numbers of propagating degrees of freedom for specific abelian models from first principles and confirming their classical second-class constraint structure. Additionally, we establish a degree of freedom count for a restricted set of non-abelian modifications to General Relativity. Our findings indicate that current abelian and limited non-abelian generalizations of the Einstein-Hilbert action do not alter the propagation characteristics of gravitational waves. Consequently, the observed speed of gravitational waves from neutron star mergers, which aligns with the predicted General Relativistic value, does not rule out infinitesimal non-abelian extensions of Einstein's gravity that maintain two degrees of freedom. Finally, we argue that the primary obstacle in developing a viable phenomenology for the gravitational sector of modified gravity lies in reconciling the success of the $\Lambda$CDM model with gravitational anomalies. These challenges may be addressed through a consistent quantization program that successfully unifies the particle and gauge aspects of non-abelian modifications of gravity.

We propose a method utilizing state tomography to measure the "tomographic entanglement weight," a metric that quantifies the percentage of entanglement within an unnormalized state relative to a free constant, accounting for non-determinism. Applying this metric to an entangled single-photon state generated via heralded spontaneous parametric down-conversion, we determine a value of 36%. This finding indicates that the observed single-photon advantage in entanglement detection is primarily driven by non-determinism rather than entanglement. Furthermore, when the spontaneous parametric down-conversion process is cooled, the single-photon advantage in entanglement detection increases significantly, reflecting a higher entanglement weight. Our approach offers a tool for quantifying the entanglement of unnormalized states in scenarios where non-determinism is a critical factor. Additionally, we demonstrate that tomographic entanglement can be measured in practical quantum communication settings through a modified version of the E91 protocol. This work introduces a novel perspective for investigating entanglement within quantum communication systems. Additionally, our findings suggest a new pathway for the future integration of quantum optics and entanglement distribution. Finally, we have developed open-source code to facilitate the application of our findings. (Software repository: https://github.com/masahiro-takada/Tomographic-entanglement-weight). This computation yields an elliptic genus defined for any representation $V$ as the pushforward along the inclusion $\iota:pt \hookrightarrow \mathbb{C}^n(V)$. Leveraging the torus action on $\mathbb{C}^n(V)$, we derive an explicit formula for the $\iota(T)$-module representing this elliptic genus within the $T$-equivariant K-theory of a point. By applying the elliptic Atiyah-Singer index theorem, we demonstrate that this $T$-equivariant elliptic cohomology ring is torsion when considered over the integers. Furthermore, we establish that this cohomology ring adheres to the relations derived from the braid group of $GL_C(2,n)$. Consequently, we define the "standard" nullelliptic cohomology of a point as the cohomology ring of a point modulo these relations. Our final findings link the "standard" nullelliptic cohomology of a point to the equivariant K-theory of a point and the mod 3 reduction of the $T$-equivariant complex K-theory of a point, both under the action of $T \simeq SU(2)^{n+1} \times U(1)^n$. This relationship allows for a complete description of the nullelliptic ring by expressing its generators and relations in terms of the "elliptic characteristic classes" of $T$. In the process, we elucidate the relations between these classes, known as the generalized Frenkel-Kac relations. Finally, we propose a conjecture: the relations of the standard nullelliptic cohomology of a point, i.e., the relations of $\mathcal{E}^1(T)$ modulo the braid group of $GL_C(2,n)$, are precisely those generated by the relations of the "standard" elliptic cohomology of a point, i.e., the relations of $\mathcal{E}^1(T)$ modulo the Weyl group of $T$. This conjecture would imply that the relations of the "standard" nullelliptic cohomology of a point are identical to the relations of the "standard" elliptic cohomology of a point modulo three.
