sound. This paper investigates an idealized ground-sound model, grounded in the theory of elastically coupled oscillators. We develop an analytical sub-model that is integrated into a broader ground-sound framework, which is then applied to a simplified robotic robot model to predict and measure the spectra of recorded impact sounds. Finally, an impulse response model is presented that allows ground-sound effects to be added to existing impact synthesis methods that previously ignored this phenomenon. Our findings offer ground-sound predictions that align closely with experimental data, matching over 90% of the spectral content. We conclude that the proposed model can enhance ground-sound realism for synthesis methods that formerly omitted it and stands alone as a viable solution for applications where ground-sound sampling is difficult. This work advances our understanding of the physics behind ground-sound generation and provides a practical tool for synthesizing it. Key contributions include introducing a ground-sound model grounded in established oscillator-coupling theory, analyzing spectral predictions against recorded data, and proposing a general impulse response approach to facilitate ground-sound synthesis. Overall, these results deepen our comprehension of ground-sound physics and provide a practical solution for generating ground-sound synthetically.

The Standard Split Method (SSM) is renowned for its robustness and efficiency in solving the Adjoint State Method within optimization tasks featuring homogeneous constraints. However, SSM is ill-suited for handling heterogeneity. To address this limitation, the authors introduce the Heterogeneous Split Method (HSM), a novel and efficient approach designed specifically for optimization problems with heterogeneous constraints. HSM leverages the mathematical properties of interfaces between different types of communities to minimize the impact of heterogeneity on the algorithm's performance. Numerical experiments demonstrate that HSM significantly reduces computational time and enhances the accuracy of the computed solution when detecting small communities. These findings confirm that HSM is a promising and viable method for community detection. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/CMAM2022/HSM.

\section{Introduction}

The high-resolution mapping of the universe's large-scale structure (LSS) has emerged as a pivotal area in modern cosmology, with significant implications for fundamental cosmology and inflation theory. The universe's matter distribution is not uniform; beyond a certain scale, galaxies and clusters form a complex network known as the "cosmic web," characterized by dense nodes, elongated filaments, planar sheets, and vast, sparse voids (Kochanov \& P\'erez, 2021). This structure imparts a distinct pattern to the light deflection caused by gravity acting on the cosmic matter, resulting in a scale-dependent tilt in the sky plane when observing the convergence field.

However, direct LSS measurements are limited by finite volume and instrumental noise, restricting access to the highest scales where this tilt is most pronounced. Consequently, there is a critical need for theoretical frameworks capable of extrapolating from the lowest measurable scales to the largest ones. While the cosmological non-linear evolution of matter can be modeled using $N$-body simulations, these are inaccurate at low redshifts due to gravitational clustering and inaccurate at high redshifts because of primordial non-Gaussianity. To overcome these limitations, we employ the Effective Field Theory of Sub-Horizon Non-Linearities (EFTofSHT), which adds effective operators to the perturbative description of cosmological non-linear evolution to accurately describe the matter distribution at observable scales.

In this work, we focus on calculating the leading-order convergence tilt of the cosmic web using EFTofSHT, a topic that has not previously been addressed in the literature. Our approach involves determining the tilt of the convergence field's angular power spectrum ($\Delta_2^2$), a quantity derived from multipole moments of the density field's power spectrum. The $k$-core of a graph $G$ is defined as the largest induced subgraph that remains connected even after the removal of any single vertex. Similarly, the $k$-sec is the largest induced subgraph where the removal of any $k$ vertices results in a disconnected graph. For graphs containing no isolated vertices, the ratio of the $k$-sec to the $k$-core does not exceed $2k$; this bound is tight for every $k \geq 2$. Furthermore, we introduce and examine several parameters that quantify the disparity between a graph and a complete one, including clique imperfection, nonreleasability, and noncontraction. We demonstrate that determining the maximum ratio between the $k$-sec and the $k$-core is NP-hard for any $k \geq 2$ across all these graph classes. However, for very sparse graphs, we prove that the problem is solvable in polynomial time and provide a formula for this ratio. Additional findings include the identification of the eight smallest nonreleasable graphs, the characterization of the smallest noncontraction graph, and the determination of the minimum edge count for a connected $k$-sec. Finally, we characterize the minimum $k$-sec of heterogeneous graphs and characterize both the $k$-sec and $k$-core within the context of star graphs. These results are complemented by related findings concerning cliques, H-free graphs, and independent sets.

the gravitational field is highly non-linear and intricate, characterized by multiple scales and components. The source terms driving this geometry evolve dynamically, often fluctuating rapidly. Consequently, the gravitational field can become dominated by high-frequency, high-wavenumber fluctuations that obscure its underlying large-scale behavior. This difficulty is analogous to observing a distant galaxy through stormy weather, where the turbulence masks the galaxy's true appearance. To resolve this, one must wait for the storm to subside, leaving the large-scale features visible. Similarly, in gravitational systems, the influence of small-scale matter inhomogeneities can be mitigated by averaging the sources and the gravitational field over a scalebar larger than that of these inhomogeneities. This process yields a "smooth" gravitational field and an effective, scale-dependent source term. This work investigates the dynamics of such a scalebar and the statistical properties of the resulting smooth field. Specifically, it examines the statistical behavior of scalebars as they collapse, the statistics of the smooth gravitational field, and how the choice of scalebar width impacts the system's dynamics. These investigations are motivated by a related study on the statistical properties of structure formation within a Weyl-curved vacuum. The paper begins with an introduction to the statistical approach to sources and the gravitational field, followed by an analysis of scalebar evolution and their statistical distribution. Subsequently, it details the statistics of the smooth gravitational field, including their time evolution, and concludes with remarks on how the chosen scalebar width influences the system's dynamics. Our findings indicate that the statistical distribution of scalebars is Rayleigh-distributed, whereas the statistics of the smooth gravitational field approach a Gaussian distribution as the system evolves. Furthermore, we observe that the choice of scalebar width can significantly alter the statistical properties of the gravitational field, a fact that must be carefully considered when interpreting simulations of complex structure formation. Finally, we explore the connection between these statistics and the power spectrum of the smooth sources. These results provide valuable insights for numerical relativey simulations of complex structure formation, such as binary black hole mergers, where scalebars are not explicitly modeled. Such understanding is crucial for interpreting the gravitational waves generated by these processes. Our results may also prove relevant to the statistical approach in cosmological relativey. In cosmology, the choice of the scalebar width represents a significant open problem, as it is not dictated by small-scale matter fluctuations as it is in numerical relativey simulations of complex sources. The proposed approach to selecting the scalebar width may offer a viable solution to this challenge.

While this effect is commonly compensated using a single rotating prism, our analysis indicates that for high-resolution systems, this approach can still result in a residual FWHM angular spread of approximately 2.5 milli-arcseconds. To address this, we introduce a novel technique based on the "double mirror + double rotating prism" configuration, which effectively compensates for atmospheric dispersion across the 0.5 to 2.0 $\mu m$ wavelength range. This design maintains a total optical path difference (TOPD) of zero throughout the compensation process and allows for reduced TOPD during observation. Additionally, the assembly can rotate and lock in either direction, offering significant space benefits for large, high-resolution instruments. A prototype has been constructed and tested, with experimental results confirming the design's feasibility. Furthermore, we have provided the corresponding design software and documentation, which are available as an open-source project on GitHub. This design software enables rapid and efficient optimization of the assembly's size and shape for specific applications. The combined advantages of no residual atmospheric dispersion, wide bandwidth, low optical path difference, and compact footprint make this design particularly suitable for future extreme and sparse interferometers. Specifically, we estimate the FWHG angular spread to be approximately 0.1 nano-radian for the Keck EELT, representing a 25,000-fold improvement over the current limit. Furthermore, we have identified that the design can be simplified to a single mirror and single rotating prism configuration for even greater compactness, a version that has already been experimentally verified. Extensive experimental data and a video are available on GitHub, a publication is currently in preparation, and the underlying software code is also shared via GitHub. These resources are expected to assist other researchers in verifying the effect and understanding the associated design principles. Less-known extensions for bit manipulation and remote control, however, are frequently misimplemented. This study identifies these issues through a systematic analysis of P4's remote control and bit manipulation specifications, P4 programs utilizing remote control features, a leading P4 compiler, and switch documentation. Our findings reveal that P4's remote control mechanisms are widely misimplemented, with errors including incomplete state, inaccessible features, and data corruption. These misconfigurations can lead to DoS attacks, security vulnerabilities, incorrect results, and wasted resources. We report that 40% of remote control features and 30% of bit manipulation operations are incorrectly implemented. Additionally, we developed diagnostic tools to identify conflicts in P4's remote control and found that 60% of P4 programs contain multiple conflicts. To address these issues, we propose design improvements and implementation fixes for both the interpreter and diagnostic tools. We have made the tools publicly available for integration into the compiler interpreter. Our work has been validated through experimentation on a real 100Gb Ethernet link using SmartPc emulators. Given the critical importance of reliable P4 programs for high-speed networks, this research provides a foundational understanding of remote control misconfigurations and the methods to detect and fix them. The implementation details for our tools can assist other researchers in integrating these features into the compiler interpreter. Furthermore, the tools presented in this research will be included in the BDNE P4 environment for future development. Furthermore, both the issues addressed and the solutions proposed can serve as a reference for other researchers working on remote control and configuration issues in configurable networks.

This study evaluates the impact of these selection functions on key flow properties within the Shallow Water Equations framework. By testing various element types, we found that high-order Lagrange elements paired with Discontinuous Galerkin formulation yield the most accurate results for specific flow metrics, including final water depth, surface elevation, and velocity divergence. Although these high-order elements increase computational costs, they are essential for achieving the necessary precision in critical climate variables. These findings are particularly relevant for designing cost-effective methods to compute water fluxes in geophysical flow models. Finally, we apply this analysis to determine surface fresh water flux in the Southern Ocean, a region characterized by complex dynamics and a significant barrier to southward transport. Our results indicate that a 4th-order continuous polynomial space provides the best compromise between result accuracy and the time and resources required for computation. This conclusion is supported by the high precision of final water depth, surface elevation, and velocity divergence, alongside a reduction in the number of degrees of freedom by a factor of 4 compared to high-order discontinuous elements. Given the substantial computational cost of shap functions in large-scale geophysical simulations, these insights hold significant value for balancing accuracy with processing time and resources. The chosen spatial approximation was utilized in a case study of the surface fresh water barrier in the Southern Ocean. Key metrics, such as the peak of this barrier in the Drake Passage and its decay south of the Confluence Meridians, were calculated with high accuracy. Furthermore, we quantified the contribution of each Shallow Water Equation term to water transport in these regions. This work offers a cost-effective approach for calculating water fluxes in Southern Ocean models and similar environments. The simulations were conducted using the open-source Spectral-Differential-Via-Differences spectral method model, Spectral2Dv2, developed by the Laboratoire de Météorologie Dynamique. The surface fresh water barrier was computed using evaporation and precipitation data from the ERA-Interim reanalysis. Key findings include a peak water thickness of 0.42 meters in the Drake Passage and a total integrated thickness of 10.62 million km³ within the Confluence Meridians (45°S to 60°S). Additionally, the transport across the Drake Passage was calculated at 1.04 Sverdrips. These outcomes were compared against established literature values.

Deep neural networks have achieved state-of-the-art results across numerous computer vision benchmarks but often struggle with distribution shifts caused by changes in input attributes like style or color. While style and attribute manipulation techniques exist for natural images, they have not yet been applied to probe model robustness during training. This work presents a unified framework for generating synthetic data that supports attribute-controlled generation, which is then used to train robust adversarially stable classifiers. The proposed method adapts existing manifold learning approaches to produce controllable transformations and offers a new criterion for selecting these adapted methods. Experiments show that training with this criterion and attribute-controlled transformations yields adaptive models that achieve strong accuracy and maintain robustness across distribution shifts in style and color.

Attribute-controlled image generation is crucial for both scientific research and practical applications. Although deep learning has advanced the field of style transfer, current approaches typically focus on simple natural images under a single paradigm. In contrast, our proposed framework supports multiple generation paradigms, offering a versatile solution for diverse tasks. By estimating the order of attributes and utilizing learning-based search to identify optimal directions within the latent space, we can perform controlled manipulation of target images according to specific preferences. This approach delivers state-of-the-art results across several tasks, including image editing, image completion, and day-night style conversion.

Controlling the style of synthesized images is a key capability of generative models. Current state-of-the-art methods offer style generation only as an adversarial attack vector through black-box analysis of network internals, lacking support for multi-paradigm generation or controlled synthesis. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a new generative network architecture that projects real images into a canonical space optimized for multi-paradigm attribute manipulation. We also propose a novel adversarial training criterion designed to robustly train deep networks using this proposed network. Our approach achieves state-of-the-art accuracy and robustness against distribution shifts in style and color, even when trained exclusively on color-transformed images, all while maintaining a high degree of synthesis control.

The goal is to train large-scale classifiers by addressing two primary obstacles: (1) the high memory usage and computational expense associated with estimating parameters for models like Linear-Chain CRF and Bi-LSTM-CRF, and (2) the limitation of existing distributed training methods, which are often confined to single-GPU memory capacity, the impracticality of feature fragmentation for context-dependent systems, and the unsuitability of standard parameter fragmentation for sparse features. To overcome these hurdles, we propose a feature-parallel distributed training method based on layer-wise parameters. This approach estimates the weights of specific features in parallel while keeping other features unchanged between iterations. We provide a theoretical analysis of the framework and present a distributed learning algorithm using coupled variational bounds for Linear-Chain CRF. Experimental results indicate that our method can train models previously too large to fit into memory and scale to arbitrarily large datasets. Furthermore, our theoretical bounds ensure a performance upper bound comparable to state-of-the-art models. Empirical evaluations on part-of-speech tagging and named entity recognition demonstrate significant gains in both convergence rate and communication efficiency. On the Loeb2005 Named Entity Recognition task, our model achieved F- Scores of 78.74, 77.93, and 77.53 for 1, 3, and 5 GPU configurations, respectively, representing substantial improvements over the previous best score of 75.11. The proposed algorithm efficiently generates three-dimensional scattering trajectories for any energy and frequency pairing, thereby enabling a detailed analysis of the resulting motion. This paper introduces a new method for understanding human actions through a hierarchical approach that leverages a state-of-the-art generative model, which is both robust and adaptable to novel methods and domains. In this study, we address motion comprehension as a two-stage process: (1) understanding dynamics using a Robust Rasterization-based Generative Model (RRGM) and (2) performing an adaptive action matching procedure. The RRGM, built upon a Generative Divergence Minimization (GDMin) framework, simulates action instances by mapping a latent code to an image sequence, thereby capturing dynamics within a robust rasterization-based representation. This model is trained on a moderate collection of sequences covering diverse actions. We demonstrate that the RRGM can simulate various actions from both the training dataset and the KITTI-360 dataset. The adaptive action matching step involves finding the optimal latent code for a test sequence by aligning it with the features extracted from the learned robust representation. We validate our approach through experiments on the Human3.6M and KITTI-360 datasets. Our results indicate that the proposed method surpasses previous state-of-the-art techniques, achieving a mean 3D human joint angular error of 10.0 degrees on the Human3.6M dataset and a mean of 4.8 degrees on the KITTI-360 dataset. Additionally, we present qualitative analyses of the generated simulations. These simulations reveal that the model captures action semantics, maintains temporal consistency, and understands movement dynamics. We also highlight the model's learnability from a limited number of training classes and its adaptability to new movements and actors without requiring additional fine-tuning. These findings suggest that the model holds substantial promise for advancing movement simulation, synthesis, and transfer in both academic and industrial contexts. Questions regarding the cosmic origin of life have been a central focus of astrobiology for over a century, yet they have not always been explicitly addressed in the context of star formation. This paper explores how astrophysicists have historically perceived SF and the pathways leading to life, spanning from the early 20th century to the present. We conclude that astrobiologists should continue to engage deeply with SF theory and observation to construct a robust framework for understanding life's origins. Furthermore, it is crucial to maintain an open dialogue about life within the broader astrophysics community, one that acknowledges both the persistent uncertainties and the exciting prospects in this field.

Observations of star-forming regions (SFRs) are essential for advancing our understanding of how stars are born and how galaxies evolve, as they serve as the building blocks of stellar evolution that shape the cosmic star formation rate density. This density, in turn, is vital for constraining cosmological models and the evolution of galaxies. However, accurately determining the star formation history of galaxies remains a significant challenge. This issue is particularly pressing in the context of the "baryon acoustic oscillation" (BAO) project, which utilizes a sample of galaxies hosting starbursts as tracers for BAO. To meet the demands of this project, we must determine the star formation history of galaxies with sufficient precision to ensure that BAO can constrain the cosmological model to the required accuracy. Consequently, we need a robust method to derive the star formation history of galaxies from observed data. However, these concepts face significant challenges when applied to finite datasets, as standard estimators often yield biased results that fail to converge to the true values even with larger samples. To address this, we introduce a correction mechanism that enhances the accuracy of estimated mutual information and directed mutual information. This mechanism is integrated into a novel iterative algorithm designed to compute equilibrium directed mutual information—the average of the standard mutual information values observed when variables are shifted from one to another over time. Our findings demonstrate that this algorithm converges for all tested variables and that the estimated values closely align with theoretical expectations when sufficient data is available. Furthermore, we apply this approach to neuroscience, specifically to infer directed connectivity between neural populations from experimental recordings. This classical approach decomposes the complex, non-linear Debye-coupled non-equilibrium plasma into simpler regions by applying Debye shielding exclusively within the double layer, while treating the regions before and after it as Poisson governed. Our analysis demonstrates that such Poisson regions cannot exist in a steady-state, collisionless plasma. Consequently, the single double layer is replaced by a comprehensive new solution that accurately models the complete structure of a re-entrant plasma double layer, incorporating all relevant plasma and electrostatic effects. This new formulation integrates the full Vlasov-Poisson-Fokker-Planck (VPF) system and represents the first comprehensive solution of its kind. It provides critical insights into plasma-surface interactions and enhances our understanding of various space and nuclear fusion phenomena. Furthermore, our findings address fundamental questions in plasma physics, offering significant advancements in mathematical plasma theory. This work is dedicated to Dr. Oleg Frazer on the occasion of his 80th birthday. The companion paper, "A New Solution of the Vlasov-Poisson-Fokker-Planck System: A Comprehensive Model of Re-entrant Double Layers," details the mathematical formulation of this solution. This study addresses the problem of detecting and localizing faults within Computer Network Security Systems (CNSSs), with a specific focus on identifying the source of Threat Generating Systems (TGSs). To achieve this, we construct a computer-assisted dynamical model of a CNSS that includes a TGS with thorny dynamics. The model is designed to detect faults by analyzing the dynamics of the resulting dynamical system. We introduce a novel algorithm capable of detecting and localizing faults, even when measurements are noisy. Simulation results demonstrate that this method effectively identifies and localizes faults across various scenarios, including those affected by noise. These findings suggest that the proposed model, together with the associated detection and localization techniques, offers valuable insights for enhancing cybersecurity protocols. The computational code for these results is available at: https://github.com/NoahFeng/DLS_TGS_CNSS.

The paper constructs a computer model for Computer Network Security Systems (CNSSs) containing Threat Generating Systems (TGSs) with complex dynamics, such as Logics, Grushin's operator, and 3D Ricker's operator. It presents a computer-assisted method for detecting and localizing faults in these systems, supported by findings from across-disciplinary research. Fault detection and localization are achieved by comparing system outputs with specific thresholds and utilizing specialized algorithms of unknown inputs and unknown parameters. The approach is effective for nonlinear models where traditional methods fail and remains functional despite measurement noise. Computational results indicate that fault detection and localization are completely accurate for small to medium levels of measurement noise. Furthermore, the methods can identify and localize TGSs with thorny dynamics, such as those found in computer viruses and malware. These results offer significant value for enhancing cybersecurity measures.

, escaping threats, and locating mates. The study of animal locomotion, both experimentally and through simulation, has yielded numerous insights into movement mechanisms and strategies. A key insight is that many animals, spanning from insects to large marine species, employ a undulatory gait by propagating a wave along a serpentine body. This undulatory locomotion is a prerequisite for the complex three-dimensional movements observed in cephalopods, which are notorious for their advanced capabilities as active camouflagers. This paper presents a simulation of active cephalopod body camouflage, focusing on motion patterns and the energetic costs required to achieve them. Our findings indicate that active cephalopods can execute a wide variety of movements at minimal energy cost, provided they do not undergo rapid shape transformations. This study presents the first measurements of inclusive jet production in pp collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV, analyzed across three rapidity regions: |η| < 0.9, 1.2 < |η| < 2.0, and 2.5 < |η| < 4.0. Using a sample of 36 fb⁻¹ of data from the CMS detector at the LHC, inclusive jet cross-sections were measured as a function of the leading (highest p_T) jet's transverse momentum and rapidity. These results were compared with predictions from various Monte Carlo event generators, showing generally good agreement. Furthermore, p_{\rm T}-scaled ratios of cross-sections across the rapidity bins were examined to reduce uncertainties related to the proton structure and to test perturbative QCD predictions based on perturbative QCD. These ratios align well with both experimental predictions and NLO pQCD predictions. Finally, a double-differential cross-section was measured as a function of the leading jet's p_{\rm T} and the inclusive dijet mass (M_{jj}), covering p_{\rm T} from 100 to 1000 GeV and M_{jj} from 150 to 1000 GeV.

Genetic programming (GP) is a form of evolutionary algorithm utilized to automatically synthesize programs, circuits, or models that perform desired tasks. Because GP produces a vast number of potential solutions for a given problem, it is often necessary to evolve multiple candidates to increase the likelihood of obtaining a high-quality result. While this is typically accomplished by running GP multiple times with random initial parameters, such an approach treats all solutions as equally likely a priori. However, domain knowledge may suggest that certain solutions are more probable than others. To leverage this, GP can be guided toward preferred solution characteristics by modifying the genetic operators to bias the search. For instance, when the target program is expected to be small, a common strategy involves attaching a penalty to larger trees within a tree-based GP framework. In another scenario, a GP system might need to identify distinct solutions to a problem, where a GP system that discovers distinct solutions is more valuable. We focused on extrinsic doping in monolayer graphene, analyzing how varied DFT-based coupling mechanisms interact with phonon dispersion and electron density. Our findings reveal that coupling strength varies significantly depending on the specific phonon mode. Relative to undoped acoustic phonons, the electron-acoustic coupling magnitude is approximately ten times stronger for in-plane phonons and roughly five times stronger for out-of-plane phonons. Under fixed electron and phonon energies, the contribution of the spinor Pomeranchuk coefficient to interaction strength is negligible compared to other terms. Additionally, the coupling is significantly weaker for acoustic phonons following size quantization in strip-like graphene. These results hold substantial value for understanding and controlling electron-phonon interactions in 2D acoustic waves through chemical or electrostatic gating. Finally, we observe that long-wavelength deformation-potential interactions are sufficiently strong to notably alter the lifetime of acoustic phonons in graphene. During room temperature electron-phonon equilibrium, deformation-potential interactions cause acoustic phonons to lose energy at a rate of about 10 fW per atom, representing their primary channel for energy dissipation. This identifies long-wavelength acoustic phonons as ideal carriers for thermal management and temperature sensing in graphene-based electronic and thermoelectric systems. Furthermore, long-wavelength strain waves can be harnessed to generate measurable currents via the deformation-potential mechanism, a phenomenon with potential applications in phononics and thermal electronics. The reported findings are supported by specific examples and hold broad applicability across 2D materials. Furthermore, the established methodology can serve as a benchmark for assessing the validity of various many-body approaches when calculating coupling strength and phonon lifetime. These outcomes offer new insights into the fundamental mechanisms governing electron-phonon interactions in graphene and other 2D materials. Finally, the developed methodology offers a fresh perspective on modeling long-wavelength acoustic phonons in graphene and similar 2D systems for use as thermal transport sensors and heat switches at the nanoscale. This work elucidates the mechanisms behind acoustic-phonon-based thermoelectrics and provides a new avenue for exploring spinor physics in graphene and similar 2D materials. Overall, long-wavelength acoustic phonons in monolayer graphene emerge as ideal candidates for a wide range of applications, including thermal management, thermoelectrics, and strain sensing in nano-electronics. Our results indicate that the new finite-field design reduces latency in a single-round fault-yield scenario by 30% while increasing throughput by 130%, with an average operation delay per syndrome of just 200ns. The relaxed version achieves an latency of 10ns per round and a fault-yield lifetime up to 100 times longer than the 2021 method, maintaining a latency of 2ns per round. Our implementation exhibits an 80% smaller area-footprint than a comparable CPU. These results confirm that the proposed approaches offer superior speed and adaptability compared to both earlier methods and state-of-the-art solutions. This paper introduces the Tuning the Training Loss Curve (T3LC) method, which utilizes error-based evaluations of the training loss curve to automate the selection of an optimal model-accuracy tradeoff. By adjusting the tolerance for the error between the predicted and actual loss using hyperparameter-based cross-validation, T3LC enables a neural network training process that operates independently of human intervention. Multiple scattering of light in disordered media hinders the creation of compact optical devices for imaging and light trapping. Deep learning has recently enabled the reconstruction of objects from partially measured or wavefront-scattered data by accounting for the transmission matrix of a random medium. However, this matrix is system-specific and can only be measured once. We introduce a feedback-based optimization technique to accelerate object formation and improve image quality at the surface of a disordered medium. This is achieved by generating high-contrast 3D objects in free space through coherent superposition of local hot spots created simultaneously throughout a disordered medium. Our approach enables the simultaneous imaging of multiple objects in reflection mode without needing a transmission matrix. We demonstrate that this method reliably creates complex, high-contrast, large-scale structures (up to 10 cm) both in and on disordered media. Keywords: optical imaging, random media, feedback optimization, optical trap arrays, optical trapping.

Optical imaging of deep-tissue biological samples is restricted by light scattering in heterogeneous media. Developing new imaging modalities for these scattering environments often requires time-consuming and complex numerical simulations or measurements of the optical properties of the specific sample or tissue. We introduce a data-driven framework that utilizes experimental data to accelerate the design of optical phase masks for scattering media. Our method involves training a convolutional neural network (CNN) on a dataset comprising input images, output images after passing through a static scattering sample, and corresponding phase masks. This approach allows for the simultaneous generation of multiple images within the sample. Furthermore, our method can be applied recursively to create a sequence of images that cannot be achieved with a single phase mask. Finally, our data-driven technique for a priori designing optical masks for scattering media and multifocus imaging opens new possibilities for optimizing optical setups for specific samples or tissue types a priori. We present a novel active neutrino search that simultaneously tests two active-sterile mixing matrices by measuring the single-particle energy spectrum from a pulsed beam of neutrinos generated from the decay of high-intensity, monochromatic muons. This experiment, known as the 1962 Rossi-Hall test, could detect active-sterile mixing because a pure two-body decay produces a sharp neutrino energy spectrum that remains unaffected by oscillations before detection. This capability allows for the simultaneous measurement of active-sterile mixing and the detailed characterization of the energy loss mechanism responsible for the energy degradation of neutrinos in the 1962 experiment. The 2021 FermilB test restores the search for active-sterile mixing at the existing Fermilab Beam Dump Experiment, while the 1962 Rossi-Hall test once again offers a means to probe active-sterile mixing.

In 1962, the famous Rossi and Hall experiment detected a significant number of electron neutrinos with energies near the muon mass, despite the neutrino production mechanism in the beam suggesting that such high energies should be impossible. This puzzle was resolved in 1983, over 20 years later, when Nu and Mu were identified as distinct particles because of the "kink" in the energy spectrum caused by the decay of the heavier muon. While multivariate meta-regression and multivariate mixed models of restricted maximum likelihood (RML) are frequently used, both approaches fail to validate their underlying assumptions when analyzing interrupted parallel trials. This study examines the performance of these techniques through simulated and real-world data. Results indicate that when pre- and post-intervention outcomes from two trials are analyzed as multivariate meta-regression, there is a heightened risk of spurious significance between the trials and erroneous conclusions regarding which trial demonstrates a greater treatment benefit. Conversely, if multiple estimates per trial are treated as independent in a multivariate RML meta-analysis, the error rates increase, though the impact is less severe compared to the multivariate meta-regression approach. Given that current simulations and analysis rely on assumptions not satisfied by practical data, both methods require simplifications that limit their applicability. Consequently, multivariate meta-analysis remains an active area of research. Until more robust analytical techniques are developed, researchers should recognize the severe limitations of existing methods and the potential for misleading inferences. Furthermore, given the substantial time investment required for trial conduct and publication, it is imperative to educate investigators about the analytical challenges associated with multivariate data to ensure the resources dedicated to trials are utilized effectively. Finally, the authors plan to release an R package in the near future to facilitate the implementation of these simulations and analyses.

Our results indicate that transverse broadening for real photons generated in photon-lead collisions is identical in magnitude but opposite in sign to that of circularly polarized photons, whereas the difference regarding linearly polarized photons is negligible. In the circular polarization case, the photon exhibits a dual behavior: it is partially absorbed by the nucleus, gaining transverse momentum, and simultaneously transfers momentum to the nucleus through its field, receiving an equal recoil. This duality provides a more intuitive understanding of the process, whereas the linearly polarized photon appears to undergo only one of these effects. Furthermore, we examine the implications of these findings for circular polarization within the PHENIX experiment. Specifically, we project the transverse broadening of circularly polarized photons colliding with a lead nucleus at RHIC to be approximately $0.14$ GeV/$c$, which is comparable to the accessible $p_T$ range for real circularly polarized photons in PHENIX. This sensitivity offers a unique opportunity to investigate the spin dependence of the photon structure function in the low-$x$ regime. Additionally, we estimate the relative contribution of background events arising from linearly polarized photons, finding it to be less than a few percent. Consequently, background corrections related to spin are minimal, and it is feasible to measure the spin dependence of the photon structure function with a precision of a few percent. These measurements would provide the first direct confirmation of photon spin dependence in the low-$x$ region, complement existing electron polarization measurements, and provide the first direct test of photon spin-duality in the low-energy domain. Such data could also provide the first evidence of spin-duality for high-energy photons. Finally, we derive an analytical expression for the transverse broadening of circularly polarized photons applicable to the RHIC, LHC, and RHIC-like energy scales.

Developing and maintaining these hierarchies is a costly and labor-intensive endeavor that often faces sustainability challenges. This study introduces a novel approach utilizing natural language processing to analyze large text collections and establish information hierarchies. We evaluated the method's performance through three distinct experiments using real-world text databases of varying sizes and formats. The creation and upkeep of extensive, structured, and controlled taxonomies—also known as classification systems or information hierarchies—are essential for effectively organizing and analyzing massive text databases. However, such systems are frequently outdated, underutilized, or incomplete. Simply imposing a taxonomy onto text data without verification fails to leverage the full power of automated text analysis. Although previous research has addressed this limitation, no current method simultaneously offers a user-friendly interface for processing diverse text sources, robust statistical validation for classification systems, and comprehensive coverage of the complete text corpus. This study addresses these gaps by integrating three R packages into a unified, stand-alone package named "comprehensive taxonomy analysis." This tool enables users to automatically test the performance of existing classification systems across entire text databases and to generate hierarchies from scratch based on the textual content. Our findings indicate that this integrated package significantly surpasses two existing R packages individually or when used together. An online demonstration is available at http://comp-tax-class.shinyapps.io/comp_tax_class_demo/. The package is openly accessible and free to modify at the URL provided in the footnote. Predicting these impacts before execution helps developers prepare for changes and mitigate side effects. While existing impact analysis techniques have achieved success, their primary focus has been on identifying components that will *not* change, leaving the prediction of specific changes to other components unexplored. This paper introduces the Shallow Semantic Dependency Graph (SSDG), a novel approach using supervised learning to predict the specific changes SSDs of a target component will undergo based on code modifications. Our method is evaluated on the Siemens benchmark, where it surpasses current state-of-the-art techniques, including static analysis methods that determine all altered components. Furthermore, an online service is deployed to demonstrate the method's accessibility. Source code and details of the SSDG method are available at: http://www.cs.ucl.ac.uk/~simonw/ssdg/.

The SSDG method is built upon a broader approach to impact prediction using machine learning, known as MLIAG. This approach treats impact prediction as a label propagation task within a graph representation of a system's components and code. By assigning semantic labels to components and code, and acknowledging that changes to code with similar semantics are more likely to trigger changes in semantically similar components, the method aims to enhance precision in predicting online system changes. To support this, we developed a methodology for generating shallow semantic dependency graphs (SSDGs) from source code and constructed a dataset by applying this labeling and SSDG generation process to existing software systems. We assessed the impact of performance and accuracy in SSDG label classification on impact prediction accuracy. Experiments on the Siemens benchmark show that our approach using MLIAG and SSDGs yields highly competitive results compared to the latest static analysis methods. Additionally, our evaluation indicates that a small volume of historical data is sufficient to train a model capable of achieving performance comparable to static analysis techniques. Source code and details of the MLIAG method can be found at: http://www.cs.ucl.ac.uk/~simonw/mliag/.

Our findings suggest that MLIAG and SSDG offer a promising new direction in impact prediction by leveraging performance and data characteristics unique to machine learning. This approach enables the application of well-established learning techniques to impact prediction and facilitates the use of historical data to enhance prediction accuracy for specific systems. The disk variant features a bulge-free central region that is photometrically and gravitationally linked to the extended disk. When a bulge-free core is absent, the nuclear disk merges with the main disk, resulting in a smooth surface brightness distribution. We examine how the magnitude of the SMBH influences the kinematics of the extended disk in baryonic models. These findings indicate that bulge-free cores in extended disks can exist independently of bars, though they may develop in their presence. Additionally, in baryonic models, such cores can exist near a critical SMBH mass threshold, whereas in barless models, they arise only when this threshold is exceeded. This approach clarifies the distinct nature and formation mechanisms of these nuclear components, distinguishing them from bulges that accompany extended disks. In AFe$_{2}$As$_{2}$ materials, a ferromagnetic (FM) sub-lattice develops on the Fe sites, which strongly opposes the antiferromagnetic (AFM) exchange interactions that are necessary to lower the system's energy below the FM state. Consequently, FM and AFM fluctuations coexist, and under certain conditions, a ferromagnetic AFM hybrid state emerges below the ferromagnetic critical temperature. This paper reviews experimental findings related to this ferromagnetic AFM hybrid state in RFe$_{2}$As$_{2}$ (R = Li, Na, K) compounds, with a specific focus on the phase diagram of KFe$_{2}$As$_{2}$. Below the FM critical temperature, superconductivity in KFe$_{2}$As$_{2}$ arises from a mixing of FM and AFM fluctuations that operate on different length scales. The FM component of the order parameter breaks time-reversal symmetry, suggesting that the superconducting pairing symmetry in KFe$_{2}$As$_{2}$ may involve an isotropic $p$-wave FM component in addition to the standard FM-broken $d$-wave AFM component. We also examine the effects of pressure and Fe substitution with Co on the phase diagram of KFe$_{2}$As$_{2}$. In doped or pressure-modified samples, the FM and AFM fluctuations continue to mix in the order parameter, but the dominant FM character prevents the appearance of the FM-broken $d$-wave AFM component. In systems where FM and AFM fluctuations are dominant and occur on comparable scales, nematicity is expected to be the leading effect, a hypothesis we test by analyzing experimental data. Finally, we explore the implications of this unique mixing of FM and AFM fluctuations on superconductivity and outline a future research agenda for this intriguing system. This paper explores the divergence between born charges and classical values by analyzing two factors: clamped-electron polarizabilities and core-electron Born charges. These two aspects are examined using a tight-binding framework and density functional theory combined with a layered jellium binary core-valence picture. Our findings indicate that clamped-electron effects are typically negligible, whereas core-electron contributions can be significant. We illustrate this with Helium dimers and oxide monomers, observing that the latter can exhibit extraordinarily large clamped-electron polarizabilities that almost completely offset large core-electron Born charges. Consequently, the total Born charge for core-electrons in oxide monomers is orders of magnitude smaller than that in hydrogen monomers. Since summing core and valence Born charges yields zero for hydrogen monomers, this implies that the total Born charge in oxide moners carries extremely high uncertainty. To resolve this, we propose a practical approach involving the calculation of clamped-electron and core-electron Born charges separately for the most prevalent anionic monomers, followed their summation. This method has been applied to ten common monomers, yielding reasonably large core-electron Born charges for oxides, azides, and sulfides that are comparable in magnitude to the valence Born charges. These revised core-electron Born charges maintain the required sum-to-zero property when combined with valence charges. Finally, we demonstrate that these updated Born charges lead to significantly improved multi-pole models of individual monomers. These findings suggest that the conventional large core-electron Born charges found in tabulations may be incorrect, and that electric multipole interactions between atoms in molecular solids are likely stronger than previously assumed. This conclusion is validated by comparing the predicted multi-pole interaction energies with experimental sublimation energies. Furthermore, the proposed approach of calculating separate clamped-electron and core-electron Born charges is readily extendable to more complex systems. This strategy could facilitate the creation of highly accurate effective Hamiltonians capable of precisely modeling electronic properties and electron-electron interactions. When a magnetic field is applied, this cone splits into two: one remains two-dimensional, while the other consists of a series of cone-like structures winding around the cone's axis. These winding structures are the magnetoplasmons we identify here as "geometric magnetoplasmons," as their existence relies on the curvature of the original cone and would not appear in a standard 3D TI under similar conditions. Their discovery expands the current understanding of plasmonic behavior and offers new avenues for advancing topological plasmonics. In a separate area, we examine functions mapping measurable spaces to the reals. While standard real-valued analysis focuses on continuity, this paper introduces and analyzes $\sigma$-continuity, a weaker property. We demonstrate that $\sigma$-continuity is equivalent to measurability when the domain is the real line or the natural numbers. However, this equivalence does not hold in general; a function is $\sigma$-continuous if and only if its sublevel sets are Borel-measurable. This distinction is crucial for probability, particularly in higher-order settings. Consequently, standard higher-order probability, which relies on continuous distributions, is replaced by $\sigma$-continuous distributions. We investigate the relationships between these two types and prove that $\sigma$-measurability implies measurability under additional assumptions, such as the Borel property of the target $\sigma$-algebra. Leveraging these insights, we address the measurement problem in higher-order probability. Specifically, we show that measurable functions exist that cannot be approximated by $\sigma$-continuous ones, even under broad conditions. This highlights the limitations of using $\sigma$-continuity—or measurability with respect to a different $\sigma$-algebra—as a substitute for full measurability in higher-order probability. Finally, we illustrate the significance of these theoretical findings through their application to higher-order Monte-Carlo integration.

Finally, the paper demonstrates that the standard higher-order probability integral can be expressed as a countable sum of integrals involving bounded, $\sigma$-continuous functions. This finding offers a novel characterization of the Lebesgue integral and enables the approximation of any probability measure by a sequence of $\sigma$-continuous functions. As a consequence, we establish the equivalence between $\sigma$-measurability and measurability for higher-order probability measures under certain conditions. This result advances the understanding of the Borel problem and provides a means to characterize Borel sets within the probability setting.

of nonsmooth optimization tasks. Obstacles to convergence often stem from Proximal Newton (PN) methods, which struggle with functions that are not locally regularizable or with infinite sequences of irregularities. This paper investigates irregularities within the context of backward stability, focusing on functional perturbations that do not significantly alter the problem. We demonstrate that regular IR methods converge globally and provide characterizations of regularity that eliminate the need for first-order continuity, thereby enabling the adaptation of PN methods for certain nonsmooth problems. Furthermore, we characterize the global convergence of PN methods and explain adaptations for other irreps. These findings facilitate a comprehensive comparison between PN and other Proximal methods, yielding applications such as the first convergence proof for the Method of Alternating Projections on general closed sets and for Projected Gradient Descent on general convex sets. Additionally, we show that in finite dimensions, PN methods exhibit superlinear convergence under significantly weaker conditions than previously thought necessary. The study also introduces smoothness concepts that generalize Hölder continuity and relates them to various PN behaviors. We define various forms of strong regularity and describe PN methods as the unique family of locally robustly quadratic parameterizations. Finally, we apply PN methods to solve the Yule-Walker Equations for Toeplitz Cholesky factors, proving that the method is globally convergent, produces solutions with superior spectral properties, and achieves superlinear convergence, outperforming existing state-of-the-art techniques. Furthermore, the first-order optimality conditions for PN methods offer a route to regularize other Proximal methods, such as Nesterov's Accelerated Gradient method. The paper concludes by outlining an research agenda on the theory of PN methods. Existing PN software is available at https://github.com/erikdahl/pn. This paper introduces a multi-objective approach to generate multi-association rules, formulating the task as three separate single-objective problems and addressing them via a unified solution algorithm. The first objective is to identify relevant items for short, concise rules; the second, in light of the APRIORI theorem, aims to discover long items that reveal hidden associations; and the third seeks to locate high-probability transactions. A key innovation of this methodology is the adaptation of the solution algorithm, which incorporates three filters: one to eliminate items appearing in fewer than a minimum number of transactions, another to prune low-correlation items, and a third to discard items with low conditional probability. Experimental results using the Shopt dataset demonstrate that our multi-objective multi-rule association method yields significantly more interesting rules than traditional single-objective approaches. Furthermore, a comparative analysis with other multi-rule multi-objective algorithms reveals that our proposed solution is both more effective and efficient. Finally, the paper emphasizes the practical value of this methodology, particularly in scenarios where data is scarce, making the minimum transaction threshold a critical decision point. Additionally, the approach is highly relevant for end-users who may lack domain expertise, as it enables them to formulate their own objectives and instantly receive multi-objective multi-rule association solutions. To the best of our knowledge, this work represents the first multi-objective multi-rule association study applied to real-world data. The source code is available at https://github.com/ahmed-ahmad1/MAmra. We formalize the task as learning a stochastic finite-state, deterministic-a-action (SFDA) MC through a sequence of fully supervised episodes, where each episode comprises a trajectory of partially observed states. The approach combines a policy gradient algorithm with a variational lower bound to derive a closed-form policy gradient, and an E-M algorithm is employed for efficient parameter estimation. A key benefit of this method is its ability to handle partially observed states without requiring any features or labels to be invariant to environmental transformations. Markov chains are widely utilized to model diverse real-world phenomena, including natural language language, human mobility, and gene regulatory networks. Consequently, there is a growing demand for methods that can identify anomalies in data representing these Markovian processes. Traditional state-of-the-art anomaly detection methods often depend on prior knowledge regarding the system's dynamics and the nature of anomalies. However, in many scenarios, prior information is unavailable, and the anomaly generation process is poorly understood. In such contexts, it is more feasible to model a new system as a potentially unknown Markov chain and use partially observed data to detect anomalies in new trajectories. Our work aims to learn an SFDA-MC from a series of supervised episodes and identify anomalies in new trajectories. The learned model serves as a representation of the system's normal behavior, enabling us to flag new trajectories as anomalous if they fail to align with this normality. This capability is particularly valuable in scenarios lacking invariant features, such as when environmental transformations occur. For instance, in a retail store, customer movement between aisles can be modeled as a Markov chain. During holidays, the store's normal behavior might be represented as an SFDA-MC learned from several weeks of customer movement data. Detecting anomalies in customer movement under environmental transformations is challenging because no features remain unchanged across these transformations. Addressing the limitations of single-modal systems in challenging conditions such as poor visibility or adverse weather, we propose a robust fusion method that effectively integrates cross-scale features from both modalities. The cross-scale mechanism selectively merges features at various levels to enhance discriminative power and account for differing characteristic scales between modalities. We evaluated the proposed method across multiple public datasets, comparing results against various baseline and state-of-the-art approaches, with particular emphasis on in-wormar and foggy fog datasets. This study introduces a novel cross-modality learning framework designed to boost the performance of person verification systems by effectively fusing different modalities. While standard methods simply concatenate features or use cross-modal attention after separate learning, our approach integrates cross-modal attention mechanisms into a dual-encoder framework during the learning process. This allows the model to adaptively select and combine useful features from multiple modalities without the need for manual modification. Extensive experiments on standard public datasets show that our method achieves superior verification performance compared to existing approaches. The code is available at https://github.com/zhengyao1998/CrossMOD.

Person verification using both appearance and infrared modalities is crucial for weakly supervised recognition tasks, especially under adverse weather conditions. Although simple fusion techniques like late feature concatenation have been explored, they often result in performance degradation due to excessive learning of high-level features that vary significantly across modalities. To overcome these issues, we introduce a novel cross-modality learning strategy that learns to fuse features from different modalities within a dual-encoder architecture. Unlike methods that rely on separate learning followed by concatenation, our model incorporates cross-modality attention layers to adaptively combine useful features from both modalities in a joint embedding space. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method outperforms other multimodal methods by effectively learning to fuse complementary features, while also offering higher efficiency and lower complexity than previous approaches. Code is available at https://github.com/zhengyao1998/CrossMOD.

While random noise augmentation has proven effective for natural image classification, its application to tabular data has been limited to noise injection in specific layers of neural networks. In this work, we introduce a fundamental framework for data augmentation in tabular tabulation. We observe that a key factor in the success of noise augmentation for natural images is aligning the augmentation with the data manifold. To our knowledge, this is the first study to address data alignment in the context of noise augmentation for tabular data. Our primary contribution is a novel technique called CAE, which effectively aligns tabular data with the data manifold. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach through a comprehensive evaluation of noise augmentation methods for tabular classification. Furthermore, we develop a general pipeline for evaluating noise augmentation in tabular data that has been adopted as a standard protocol by the community for reproducibility. Finally, our findings indicate that combining CAE with tabular neural networks yields performance that rivals top-performing tabular algorithms. Our code is accessible at [1].

By applying the Fourier transform to the Rayleigh quotient, we determine the dependencies of linear growth rates and corresponding wavelengths on various disk parameters. This study examines the spatial and temporal evolution of O and B stars in the core of the Milky Way by analyzing the radial distribution of a newly identified sub-sample of young O and B stars (OBYS). The findings also have significant implications for our understanding of the evolution of galactic centers in other spiral galaxies. Overall, these results enhance our comprehension of the evolution of the Galactic center and contribute to the study of young stars in other galaxies. Within this context, coherence is recognized as a vital resource that drives many quantum information protocols. Recently, researchers have turned their attention to free operations—those that do not consume the coherence resource—to deepen the understanding of coherence's role. These operations are fundamentally linked to the concept of invariant states, which remain invariant under the action of a specific set of operations. This study extends prior research by investigating the invariant states associated with non-unitary free operations that are strictly based on admissible states derived from incoherent states. We derive analytical forms and variational bounds that depend solely on incoherent resources to describe these invariant states. Specifically, we examine the conditions required to generate various classes of invariant states using admissible states and highlight the significance of admissible unital quantum channels in this context. Notably, the analysis reveals that admissible unitary quantum channels are entirely incapable of generating non-trivial invariant states. The insights gained from these findings are applied to identify admissible states that enable the deterministic conversion into specific classes of invariant states. Additionally, we establish the necessity conditions for marking quantum states as quantum advantage states relative to non-quantum resources. The proposed framework offers an efficient approach to characterize invariant states, potentially aiding in the detection of new quantum phases and phase transitions that are inaccessible through incoherent resources. Furthermore, these findings provide critical data regarding the reversibility of quantum resources under specific physical operations. Finally, we demonstrate that states satisfying the identified necessary conditions serve as witnesses that can detect non-quantum phases that are otherwise difficult to detect using standard quantum resources. These results are entirely derived from resource-theoretic principles and are broadly applicable to all quantum resource theories that utilize admissible states. Additionally, the variational principles established in this work facilitate the efficient determination of admissible invariant states that are non-trivial. Complementing these findings, we also examine the non-quantum nature of these states relative to a specific set of quantum resources using the necessary conditions mentioned above. These results are demonstrated across multiple quantum resource theories to illustrate their practical applicability. Additionally, we establish a general relationship between the various sets of invariant states for admissible quantum channels to demonstrate their distinct physical implications. Our theoretical analysis shows that under standard assumptions, if the number of devices is sufficiently large and they exhibit diverse computation and communication abilities, this bias becomes negligible. In this work, we present a comprehensive study of the magnetic properties of thin films composed of a p-type GaN layer integrated with a perovskite ferrimagnet, BiFeO$_3$ (BFO), across various interface conditions. By employing heteroepitaxy with heterogeneous bonding at the interface, we achieved epitaxial growth of the BFO layer on the GaN layer without any Si substrate contact, ensuring a pristine Bi/Si interface. Magnetization measurements revealed a magnetic reversal mechanism in these thin films that deviates from the predicted perpendicular and in-plane anisotropies. We investigated the magnetic behavior under different growth conditions to identify the sources of in-plane magnetic anisotropy. Our findings indicate that the observed magnetic reversal is caused by an unexpected epitaxial rotation of the BFO lattice relative to the GaN lattice, accompanied by strain at the interface. These results provide essential insights into the epitaxial orientation of the BiFeO$_3$ layer, an critical factor for achieving optimal spin-orbit torque in spintronic devices.

Our approach for detecting significant states relies on a N-gram model that tracks word frequencies within a sliding window of recent experiences. By converting graph nodes into unique identifiers, we apply this linguistic N-gram framework to reinforcement learning contexts. Specifically, we maintain a history of $m$ states and compute the occurrence probability $P(s_{t-m}:s_t)$ for any current state $s_t$ within this local context. State transitions are modeled as a Markov process, analogous to how words transition in natural language. The core mechanism involves calculating the decay margin $\delta_t$, defined as the difference between the normalized gain in occurrence probability for the current state versus a randomly selected baseline state. This margin quantifies the distinctiveness of the current state compared to others in the immediate recent history. To manage the growing history without excessive memory usage, we periodically replace the oldest experience with the most recent one, a process known as history compression. Consequently, the complete statistical model is derived from this compressed local history.

Abstract: Open-domain question answering (QA) demands extensive world knowledge. This paper fine-tunes a pre-trained causal Transformer to incorporate external entities into idiom contexts based on entity annotations. This annotation process utilizes a annotated-input causal Transformer, which is more sample-efficient than using an encoder-decoder causal Transformer for entity generation. These external entities significantly improve idiom interpretation accuracy. Furthermore, we have introduced a new Chinese QA dataset designed to test a model's capacity to leverage external knowledge. Empirical results indicate that our method effectively utilizes these external entities and outperforms baseline models in Chinese QA. This research highlights the importance of external entities and their potential in enhancing language models. Our dataset and code are available at https://github.com/AlibabaResearch/DAMO-Flare/tree/master/damo-flyai/tasks/QA/DAWOQA.

# DAWOQA: External Knowledge QA with Causal Transformers

## I Introduction

Answering open-domain questions requires comprehensive world knowledge. Current state-of-the-art models address this by enriching input contexts with external entities to boost performance. However, generating these entities is computationally expensive, particularly when using encoder-decoder causal Transformers. To overcome this limitation, we propose fine-tuning a causal Transformer on input annotated with external entities using another causal Transformer. This fine-tuning process ensures that the model can effectively leverage annotated external entities without the high costs associated with generation.

To address this, we present a compact sampling chain designed for precise detection across three distinct zones: near, mid, and far fields. The system samples these regions sequentially using three independent sensors, with each zone's signal being preamplified to maximize the effective sampling rate. Each zone is defined by specific electric field thresholds, allowing the system to switch to the most suitable sensor automatically based on the measured amplitude. The optical coupling of the sampling system ensures safety and expands the full-scale range further. Laboratory tests confirmed that the sensors function correctly within their respective zones, achieving a total full-scale range exceeding 1 MV/m. This work reports on the characterization of a prototype featuring a fully programmable trigger, demonstrating its compatibility with modern post-processing techniques. The prototype achieved a total full-scale range of 10^6 V/m, with a proven accuracy of 0.5% within its operating range. This level of precision ensures reliable data collection, enabling detailed post-processing and analysis of lightning return strokes. This work reports on the characterization of such a system. The M/LK values derived in this study also provide constraints on the metallicity and age of the stellar populations in UGC 8838. This study analytically quantifies the trade-off between infection control and economic output by examining how pandemic policies impact consumption and production. The model indicates that communication strategies and lockdowns should continue until the cumulative infection rate reaches 20% to 40%, and the intensity of restrictions must be sufficiently high to limit the daily infection rate between 0.5% and 1%. These findings rely on a novel, empirically grounded approach that integrates consumption dynamics with traditional epidemiological models. Notably, the proposed framework can be extended to other socio-economic contexts and analyzed analytically without the simplifications typically required by standard methods. Furthermore, numerical simulations reveal that locking down the entire population is ineffective for minimizing infection and death tolls, as it drives the infection rate to zero so rapidly that early transmissibility-driven outbreaks are suppressed, leaving a negligible remaining risk. Consequently, partial lockdowns are essential to maintain societal activity and balance economic impacts, while other public measures—such as testing, isolation, and the promotion of face mask usage and social distancing—should be implemented to ensure the pandemic does not exceed the critical 20% to 40% cumulative infection threshold. To address this, researchers have developed active learning (AL) methods that select the most informative samples for annotation, thereby reducing the need for large labeled datasets. However, most existing AL approaches depend on training models from scratch for every sample selection, a process that is computationally prohibitive when dealing with extensive datasets. A primary hurdle in this domain is the sparsity of such graphs; for instance, a typical Twitter graph exhibits a sparsity ratio of approximately $10^4$. This paper introduces a novel method for extracting sparsity kernels from sparsity graphs, a task critical for enhancing machine learning model performance and the human visualization of graph structures. Our approach models sparsity kernels as point cloud data and utilizes deep learning to acquire features from these sparsity graphs. We introduce the Sparsity Deep Feature Acquisition Network (SDFN) to learn sparsity graphs feature-wise and evaluate its performance using a 2-Nearest Neighbor (2NN) classification task. Experimental results on two Twitter graphs demonstrate that our method achieves a 2NN classification accuracy of 99.8%, a significant improvement over 88.5%. Furthermore, our approach reduces the number of vertices required for high-accuracy classification by a factor of 200. These findings indicate that sparsity kernel extraction from sparsity graphs using deep learning is highly effective for machine learning and related applications. To support this work, we have made our code and datasets publicly available.

Deep learning has emerged as a powerful tool for learning data representations, a process known as domain adaptation when applied across different domains. While most existing domain adaptation techniques focus on 1-D data like images or text, this work addresses the emerging challenge of domain adaptation in 2-D data, specifically coordinates. Our method is designed for scenarios where a model trained on one set of coordinates needs to be applied to a different set. To achieve this, we develop a bi-symmetric Normalizing Flow that learns the mapping between two coordinate domains by flow-based density estimation. We assess the method's effectiveness by testing its ability to handle domain shifts in point cloud registration and in learning from synthetic 2-D coordinate datasets. Our results indicate that the proposed method outperforms other state-of-the-art flow-based approaches in 2-D domain adaptation.

Oversampling is a common technique in discrete-event simulations used to reduce variance in finite-sample estimators. In this paper, we apply a coupling argument to analyze the effectiveness of this method within the Erdős-Rényi random graph model. We demonstrate that the degree of oversampling required for the method's efficacy is governed by the ratio between the average degree and the square root of the sample size. This finding complements earlier research by Baryshnikov and Diggle, which established the theoretical upper and lower bounds of oversampling needs. Our approach relies on a general inequality that quantifies the reduction in variance achieved through oversampling. This inequality is broad in application and is derived by extending a result from [11], where sample paths of a regenerative process are represented as functionals of Poisson processes.

The Hessian matrix of the log-likelihood for a categorical data model possesses a rank of at most $2g-h-1$, where $h$ denotes the codimension of the tangent space to the model within the ambient space of all possible outcomes, and $g$ represents the model's dimension. This article offers a characterization of the null space of the Hessian using Hilbert functions and free resolutions of the quotient ring by the ideal of minors of a specific rank arising from a submatrix of the Hessian. These findings have broad applications in algebraic statistics. As an illustration, we consider the latent class model for binary data in a sample of size $n$. We calculate the rank of its Hessian matrix and use this result to determine the minimal number of samples required for the Fisher information to be non-singular.

This study explores methods to extend pulse lengths beyond this constraint by utilizing a multi-bunch temporal structure. A numerical simulation was conducted using a 6 cm long FEL accelerator driven by a relativistic beam with a 3 GeV energy and a bunch density of $10^{11}$ /cm$^3$; the coherence time for this setup is approximately 60 ps. To observe pulse splitting, two bunches were positioned within a single FEL tube at separations of 100 ps, 300 ps, and 500 ps. Results indicate that increasing the inter-bunch distance allows pulses to separate more distinctly. Setting the distance between bunches to an odd multiple of the coherence time enables the removal of internal temporal structure from each pulse. Furthermore, internal reflections within the tube are identified as a viable method for generating split pulses. These findings suggest that SASE FELs equipped with precise multi-bunch generators and appropriate temporal spacing could potentially produce multi-pulsed radiation with durations exceeding the coherence time. Additionally, such multi-pulsed SASE FELs would be highly valuable for free-electron atomic and optical science. However, achieving pulse durations longer than the coherence time requires careful selection of the inter-bunch distance to eliminate internal temporal structure. To support the design of these multi-bunch generators, we have developed a computer program capable of simulating multi-pulsed SASE FELs. This research was conducted using a computer program funded by the Japanese Government.

manipulation of voting district boundaries, while the reverse process, degerrymandering, aims to reshape districting to enhance representativity and reduce bias. This study introduces a parallel tempering Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm designed for degerrymandering, utilizing a degerrymander score (GDS) based on historical voter data to evaluate a specific districting plan's bias. We demonstrate that applying this parallel tempering MCMC method to three U.S. states—where party lines align closely with district boundaries—successfully generates new districts that cross partisan lines and produce higher GDS values, indicating greater fairness. Furthermore, we confirm that our algorithm efficiently explores a wide spectrum of districting possibilities by analyzing 20 hypothetical scenarios involving one to ten states with varying population sizes and party compositions. These results are expected to assist advocates and legislators in creating equitable districts and strengthening legal arguments. However, our reliance on publicly accessible voting data presents a constraint, as this data may lack the granularity required for optimizing GDS at an individual voter level. To address this, a future direction involves integrating census-level data into a decomposition framework, potentially utilizing machine learning to enhance the algorithm's precision. Additionally, while our current approach focuses on optimizing GDS as a single metric, a subsequent endeavor will involve creating a multi-objective degerrymandering algorithm that simultaneously maximizes GDS and minimally deviates from existing district boundaries. These extensions are intended to further refine the accuracy and efficacy of district generation.
