We demonstrate that executing a random walk on a hypercube using only local knowledge of the current coordinate and a uniformly random neighbor results in optimal mixing times of $O(n \log n)$ steps for $n$-dimensional hypercubes. This contrasts with the $\Omega(n^2)$ lower bound applicable to universal local graphs. This finding resolves a conjecture by Kuhn and Suitt and validates an approach proposed by Barenboim et al. [2019]. Our methodology involves decomposing the hypercube into local groups and constructing an absorbing random walk that simulates the local group process by combining rapid exploration of individual hypercubes with the Random Choice algorithm, which randomly selects among disjoint hypercubes. We prove that this construction yields an optimal mixing time. Our approach is conceptually straightforward, offering a straightforward extension to other local graph problems.

Many reasoning tasks are modeled as search problems requiring agents to plan sequences of actions to reach specific goals. While ZS-MAR is a prominent example of such problems used to benchmark agent reasoning, its solution space is vast and characterized by numerous suboptimal paths. Current reasoning models often struggle to navigate this complexity, frequently becoming trapped in these suboptimal sequences. To mitigate this, we propose incorporating curriculum learning to guide agents from simpler to more complex tasks. Furthermore, applying curriculum learning within a fixed task necessates sampling multiple action sequences to select the optimal path for training the next agent. We introduce an online reasoning algorithm leveraging Q-learning to address this challenge, alongside a method for integrating this curriculum learning with ZS-MAR. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our curriculum learning approach significantly enhances agent performance on ZS-MAR, achieving performance gains of up to 300%. We have made our code publicly available to support reproducibility and enable future extensions of our work.

to search for supersymmetry (SUSY) decays of the charged Higgs boson, $H^\pm \to W^\pm b \bar{b}$, within a simplified model framework. The analysis focuses on a final state characterized by a single isolated lepton, missing transverse momentum, and hadronic activity consistent with two b-jets. Data from the ATLAS and CMS experiments at the LHC cover integrated luminosities of 139 fb$^{-1}$ each. For the first time, joint likelihood fits were conducted using combined ATLAS and CMS data to establish exclusion limits based on the MEM technique. The results indicate that, depending on the SUSY model, the charged Higgs boson mass is excluded up to 570 GeV for a decay width of 10 GeV and up to 610 GeV for a width of 20 GeV. Additionally, the method demonstrates sensitivity to the anomalous properties of the charged Higgs boson. The analysis employs advanced techniques for simulating the kinematics of the $H^\pm \to W^\pm b \bar{b}$ decay, including the reconstruction of the hadronic $\tau^{\pm}$ component, the application of b-tagging information, and the calculation of missing transverse momentum. These methods represent a significant advancement over previous ATLAS and CMS searches for SUSY decays of the charged Higgs boson in the two-b-jet final state. The ATLAS and CMS collaborations have conducted this search independently as well. Combined interpretations of the joint likelihoods with other searches for SUSY decays of the charged Higgs boson will be presented and discussed. * Joint work with the ATLAS and CMS collaborations.

### I. INTRODUCTION

Point clouds have become a dominant format for representing 3D data in computer vision and machine learning, finding applications in robotics, autonomous driving, and object recognition. Traditional deep learning models like Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs) and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) struggle with the high dimensionality of 3D point clouds, which often necessitates large node counts for accurate geometric and topological properties. Recently, Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) have emerged as a promising framework for learning on unstructured point cloud data [3]–[5]. These models represent point clouds as a regular node distribution within a specific domain, enabling GCN operations to achieve lower computational complexity compared to standard MLPs and CNNs.

However, existing GCN architectures typically operate on a single node distribution across the entire domain, limiting their efficiency. In contrast, our approach processes the domain as a superposition of multiple node distributions, or octaves, similar to techniques used in subband image processing [6]. By learning a node feature basis that remains invariant to rigid body transformations and applying GCN operations in parallel on each octave, we achieve a significant reduction in computational cost. This study builds upon our prior work [1], [2], which introduced harmonic functions as node features to enable the GCN pipeline to scale to much higher node counts than earlier methods.

**Related Work.** Our research focuses on developing efficient GCN architectures for point cloud processing. Our method shares a similar domain decomposition philosophy with other subband-based approaches [7], [8], though those works were originally designed for image processing in 2D pixel space. The strong chromatic index $chrom_{strong}(G)$ is the minimum number of colors needed for a strong edge-coloring of $G$. While it is established that $chrom_{strong}(ch=d) \leq 65536d^{10}$, the largest known lower bound for this parameter is $13$, derived from the Petersen graph. This paper introduces a family of graphs demonstrating that the strong chromatic index can be arbitrarily high. Specifically, for any integer $k \ge 2$, the Petersen graph with dipoles of degree d replaced by dipoles of degree kd yields a graph with a strong chromatic index of dipoles at least $(k+1)^{4}$. Consequently, as the maximum degree increases, so does the strong chromatic index. This result elevates the current known lower bound for $chrom_{strong}(P)$ to 13. Furthermore, for any integer $k \ge 2$, there exists a d-regular bipartite planar graph whose strong chromatic index is at least $k \cdot d$, where d represents the dipole degree. In terms of dipole degree, this implies that the strong chromatic index of dipoles for planar graphs is not restricted by a constant. Our findings also apply to dipoles of degree d in specific d-regular planar graphs, yielding lower bounds of dipoles at least $(k+1)^{4}$ for 4-regular graphs and $2.21k-0.05$ for 5-regular graphs. ### Introduction

Deep learning has become a dominant technology for data-driven tasks, driven by the remarkable performance of deep neural networks (NNs) on large datasets. Despite the substantial memory demands of training and running these models, the advantages of deep NNs have led to their widespread adoption. Consequently, researchers are actively exploring efficient training and approximation methods for these architectures.

A primary strategy for creating efficient NNs involves minimizing the number of trainable weights. However, the high dimensionality of these parameters creates challenges in optimization. Recent studies have shown that non-zero weights often follow a heavy-tailed distribution, meaning that after training, most weights can be accurately approximated with extreme sparsity without degrading performance. Identifying and setting these weights to zero constitutes the weight pruning process.

Pruning methods are generally categorized into three types: training-time pruning, post-training pruning, and knowledge distillation. While the first two focus on reducing weights within the original NN, the third involves training a full-sized teacher NN and a sparse student NN together, where the student learns from the teacher's outputs. During training, the student receives standard cross-entropy loss alongside additional losses from the teacher. Once trained, the student NN exhibits performance comparable to the teacher NN but with significantly fewer weights.

This study introduces the SPIG algorithm, a sparse-regularized iteration method designed as a high-performance alternative to policy iteration. Sparse-regularized policies transform the standard linear complexity of policy iteration into a near-linear profile, a principle that TM Sparse Policies (Li and Li, 2021) extended to temporal difference learning. Many inverse problems in science and engineering involve inferring the parameters of an unobserved source distribution from noisy data generated by a known operator. This paper introduces a variational Bayesian approach to parameterize the unobserved source as a probability measure, enabling the use of non-parametric methods to recover the posterior distribution over these measures. The method is demonstrated on Bayesian tomography, where it recovers posteriors over discrete attenuation coefficient profiles in 2D with results comparable to standard Bayesian reconstruction techniques but with reduced model bias. Additionally, the approach is applied to a single-cell biomechanics problem, successfully recovering a previously unreported parameter in the cell's mechanical model from experimental data. The core algorithm relies on a non-parametric Gaussian process prior over the source distribution, which yields a Bayesian method for parameterizing unobserved probability measures. By combining a Bayesian framework for inferring these measures with a recent G_Process prior for posterior computation, the study highlights the method's utility in cases where a finite number of source parameters is unlikely to capture all variability in an unobserved system. The standard single-season model estimates the probability that a species is detected during each survey, accounting for factors like imperfect senses of smell, hearing, or sight. However, individual animals may exhibit varying levels of responsiveness to surveyors, a phenomenon known as individual heterogeneity. While prior studies have addressed this by rotating surveyor positions or randomly selecting surveyors for each event to mitigate individual heterogeneity, such designs are often impractical due to high costs and logistical constraints. Consequently, surveyor responsiveness is typically assumed to be constant across events within a single survey interval. To evaluate the impact of individual heterogeneity in a more realistic single-transient survey design, we compare several single-season occupancy models using data from 300 nights of acoustic monitoring of bat calls at 12 sites. Our findings indicate that a complex model, which distinguishes between responsive and non-responsive animals, yields occupancy estimates approximately 20% higher than a simple model that assumes every animal is detected every time it occupies a site. Furthermore, the complex model produces wider confidence intervals for occupancy estimates. We observed that the simple model significantly overestimates bat occupancy, particularly when detection rates are high. These results suggest that a model incorporating individual heterogeneity is essential when occupancy is common, surveyor responsiveness is variable, and detection rates are low. Finally, we provide R code based on the 'unmarked' package to analyze single-season occupancy data that accounts for individual heterogeneity.

This study investigates transmission within contact networks featuring a stochastic, time-dependent structure. We demonstrate that the probability of disease transmission over a finite time interval $t$ can be modeled as the value of a Hamiltonian: its spatial gradient corresponds to the probability of an individual infecting another, while its time derivative represents the population's exposure risk. A first-order Hamilton-Jacobi equation of control type, incorporating state and control constraints, is derived to determine the optimal reduction of this exposure risk using a global view of the phenomenon. The paper concludes by presenting a local variant of this problem and examining two specific applications: controlling pedestrian flows in public spaces to limit virus spread and implementing speed limits on road networks to prevent major accidents. Numerical illustrations demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed methods. Furthermore, we introduce a new path planning algorithm to generate time-dependent graphs for simulating disease transmission and conduct simulations to validate the results. Key findings indicate that the derived methods effectively manage the evolution of infectious diseases, though they depend on precise data and may require adjustments to handle unforeseen events. We illustrate the technique using examples drawn from traditional telephony and modern computer networking. Descriptive names for this technique vary widely; it is frequently referred to as Dijkstra's or Forrester's method, or simply the forking method. Beginning in 1977, the author introduced it to formal methods researchers at SRI International, where it was incorporated into the Specco and Specv programs—early tools designed for communicating and distributed system verification. The method's utility is sufficiently self-evident to warrant inclusion in every formal methods course. Its significance is best underscored by a passage from Hoare's 1986 book, which notes that while formal methods are often perceived as exceedingly complex, techniques like the one described are elementary enough to be explained over lunch or dinner. The book further observes that although such a meal might be described as "lunchtime complexity," the method's simplicity makes it well-suited for verification using tools like Specco and Specv. The author extends this tribute to Jim and Bill.

This work introduces the concept of phonon gating, wherein the amplitude of a specific vibrational mode is managed via electrostatic coupling to another mode through van der Waals forces. Our results indicate that in visible-range 2D materials like MoS$_2$, the competition between these interactions is strongly influenced by Purcell enhancement. Consequently, we can identify which mechanism dominates under specific experimental conditions. This methodology is essential for developing advanced integrated photodetectors based on two-dimensional materials. Specifically, it enables the design of microcavity-enhanced phonon detectors by ensuring strong light-matter interactions and by decoupling intrinsic phonon lifetime limitations from photodetection performance.

In this work, we experimentally investigate how the position of an evanescent source relative to a waveguide affects the excitation of a quantum emitter's nonlocal collective excitation (CE). We demonstrate that nonradiative near-field energy transfer from the source to the emitter acts as a local dephasing mechanism, which suppresses the nonlocal CE and limits radiative Purcell enhancement of the emitter. This finding offers critical guidance for the precise positioning of nanosources in quantum light-matter hybrid devices and expands the scope of quantum excitation sources capable of harnessing nonlocal many-body excitations in nanophotonic structures.

We present a method to optically induce and read out a nonlocal collective excitation (CE) in a quantum emitter using non-resonant pump excitation. The pump is applied via an evanescent field near the surface of a photonic waveguide, placing both the pump and the emitter within the same Non-Hermitian Nonlocal Multiple scattering (NOMMS) region. Under these conditions, the pump rate and the nonlocal CE are excited nonlocally through the NOMMS effect. When the quantum emitter is closely positioned relative to the pump, we observe that the nonlocal CE functions as a dark excitation, which is essentially a nonradiative excitation. This near-field nonradiative energy transfer from the pump to the emitter introduces rapid local dephasing that suppresses the CE, thereby restricting the spatial positioning tolerance for the quantum emitter. A simple state model is developed to determine the reliability of turn signals, indicating that the strategy operates in a semi-passive mode by operating in contrarian or trend-following modes. State transitions occur when absolute volume shifts direction or when the separation between leading and lagging prices reaches extreme levels. Notably, the strategy can generate profits during crashes, although it may fail to exit sufficiently quickly to prevent total loss. The study also explores other state models, observing that while the strategy functions well with Drift-Diffusion models, it performs poorly with Black-Scholes models. Finally, the validity of the theory is confirmed by examining price time series through the lens of the proposed framework. Price turns are shown to be preceded by specific vix-times and average price conditions, indicating that downturns follow periods of low volatility and low average prices, whereas rallies are typically preceded by high volatility and high average prices. Additionally, the theory aligns with the observation that crashes exhibit critical slowing down. The findings suggest that the strategy's primary utility lies in identifying future turns, with secondary benefits including identifying entry and exit points for trends, filtering out false signals, and determining the optimal exit price to achieve the highest possible returns. A Python implementation of the strategy is provided. The methodology is valid because real-world price turns occur only at discrete values that allow for the movement of the maximum number of shares per unit of time. While the strategy does not predict turns, it identifies specific conditions that must exist prior to turns, such as particular vix-times and average prices. By knowing the conditions that must exist before a price turn, the strategy can accurately time entries and exits.

IPS 2021 Challenge on Socially-Aware Recommendation. This challenge aims to develop AI systems that suggest products or content for families while respecting privacy and promoting sustainability. The AI4Good competition series seeks practical machine learning applications that address current challenges and engage with real-world data. The task involves predicting what each family member will choose from a shared pool of items for a common purchase, based on the family's composition, which can include two to five individuals. To resolve this, we analyzed the data and constructed a model capable of perceiving the distinct personalities of individual family members. The results indicate that family members with divergent preferences are more likely to select different items, thereby increasing the probability of mixed selections. The final solution achieved scores of 0.4902, 0.4921, and 0.4944 for families consisting of three, four, and five members, respectively, securing first place in all three categories. Our solution balances sustainability and privacy by Slightly shifting the content of the pool to include more sustainable items and enhancing the quality of predictions for each family member to ensure their choices align with their preferences. Consequently, the system demonstrates that it is feasible to promote more sustainable purchases and maintain privacy by accurately anticipating individual family members' preferences based on minimal input data. The source code is available at https://github.com/ai4sustainability/AI4SocialRec/tree/main. The competition can be accessed at https://www.ai4good.challenge/.

ptune exoplanets have revealed a distinct population with low densities, known as "massive atmospheres" (MAs), which are thought to be primordially enriched in heavy elements. This study investigates the physical and chemical characteristics of these MAs by modeling a "hot" (Teq > 500 K) sub-Neptune around a typical F-type star. Using PETE, we explored the multi-phase physics of MAs, revealing that at the lowest density (0.02 g/cm³), a critical transition occurs from a gas-only to a gas-liquid state, which persists across all density ranges tested. We demonstrate that the accumulation of these heavy species is driven by a gravitational separation mechanism, resulting in an atmosphere with low overall density. Based on our PETE models, we propose a new framework for petroglyphs to explain the low densities and unique chemical patterns observed in MAs. Finally, we discuss how this study's findings can guide future observational efforts aimed at characterizing the physical and chemical nature of this important planetary population. To enhance computational efficiency, we introduce stochastic collocation schemes based on sparse grid collocation (SGC) for both VDTEs and mixed VTDTEs, utilizing the spectral method for spatial discretization. By employing the Gauss distribution for stochastic variables and the Gauss-Legendre scheme for deterministic ones, the stochastic collocation approach converts these stochastic problems into deterministic versions amenable to standard numerical techniques. Furthermore, spectral methods are selected for spatial discretization due to their superior convergence characteristics. Focusing on solving the resulting system of algebraic equations, spectral collocation techniques are utilized for the deterministic VDTEs and mixed VTDTEs. We subsequently develop collocation-based schemes tailored for sparse grid collocation, providing the theoretical foundations, numerical schemes, and numerical experiments necessary to validate their performance. Our findings indicate that the spectral collocation method yields high accuracy with remarkable convergence, while the sparse grid collocation method significantly reduces computational costs. These algorithms are particularly well-suited for handling problems involving high-dimensional stochastic variables. Notably, our sparse grid collocation-based schemes achieve remarkable efficiency when solving mixed VTDTEs. A key advantage of our approach lies in its flexibility; since the schemes rely on spectral collocation methods for deterministic discretization, they can be readily adapted for use in other contexts, devices, or environments. However, these methods are most effective when applied to VTDTEs with a wide range of fractional orders. To address this, we also present a transformation-based approach to convert VTDTEs into standard time fractional diffusion equations (TFDEs), which can then be solved using existing TFDE algorithms. Finally, we validate our methods through extensive numerical experiments using both 1D and 2D VTDTE models across various scenarios, utilizing regular, Gauss-Laguerre, and Gauss-Jacobi stochastic variables. These studies confirm the high accuracy and convergence of our methods while demonstrating their remarkable efficiency in terms of time and memory. Additionally, our analysis of the spectral method's stability underscores the significant influence of time step selection on stability and accuracy within our schemes. To our knowledge, this represents the first sparse grid collocation-based scheme applied to mixed VTDTEs. However, our schemes currently lack the ability to handle problems with irregular domains. True stages were originally conceived by Specker to differentiate non-isomorphic countable admissible ordinals and subsequently adapted by Spector for the analysis of recursive ordinals. This paper also presents four theorems offering a new perspective on Borel Wadge classes. These theorems utilize true stages to precisely locate the Borel hierarchy relative to $\omega$, the supremum of the recursive ordinals, demonstrating that each Borel Wadge class corresponds to a specific effective ordinal within this framework. As a direct consequence, we provide a straightforward proof confirming that every Wadge game played on Baire space possesses a winning player. Furthermore, we demonstrate that every Borel set falls into exactly one of two categories: either a $\Delta^1_1$ set with a hyperregular effective descriptive complexity, or a non-Borel set that is not uniformly reducible to any closed set. Any hyperregular $\Pi^1_1$ set serves as an example of the latter category. The efficacy of the true stage approach is evident when contrasted with the significantly greater difficulty encountered in prior descriptions of Borel sets, which relied on transfinite iterations of basic operations over the natural numbers up to the Berry ordinal—the supremum of the hyperarithmetical ordinals. True stages are particularly well-suited for this context as they extend the sequence of recursive ordinals by precisely 13 additional ordinals. We also provide an alternative characterization of hyperregular sets by establishing that every $\Pi^1_1$ set is equivalent to either a closed set or a set that is both hyperregular and non-Borel. The proof of this characterization depends on the preceding theorems regarding true stages. Finally, we outline the proof of the main result by examining the relationship between true stages and the fine structure of the ordinals up to the Berry ordinal. Specifically, we show that the order type of the set of effective limits of recursive ordinals is $ \omega \cdot \omega^{\omega^{\epsilon_0}} $. By employing a fine structure analysis of the recursive ordinals, we confirm that every Borel Wadge class has a representative at its effective supremum. This finding implies that the analysis of true stages remains applicable when investigating the sets of effective suprema of any subset of the recursive ordinals. This study investigates the merger of such unequal-mass black holes to generate gravitational waves that could be detected within a global network of three observatories in the future. To achieve this, we employed the frequency-time sensitivity curve of LALIGO and a shared sensitivity curve for the combined global network, utilizing the cumulative detection rate of massive black holes as a proxy for sensitivity. Our findings indicate that, compared to LALIGO alone, the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA (LVK) global network will achieve a 2.5 to four times greater number of cumulative detection events, with an anticipated increase of approximately 1.5 times over the next three years. When examining scenarios where the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) exceeds 8, we observed that the cumulative detection rate for massive black holes in the LVK network is at least 50% higher than in LALIGO. Furthermore, we analyzed the impact of mass ratios below 0.1 on cumulative detection rates and cumulative signal energy, revealing that lopsided binary black holes yield more cumulative signal energy within the LVK global network. These results suggest that merging lopsided black holes will be exceptionally valuable for investigating the global properties of massive black holes across the universe. Additionally, we developed an analytical model to estimate the signal energy of gravitational waves from lopsided mergers, confirming its validity across a broad range of mass ratios. This work will serve as a foundational basis for assessing the scientific potential of the LVK network in the age of gravitational-wave astronomy. This paper introduces a new exploration strategy that balances the costs of mistakes against the benefits of gaining knowledge. By utilizing Bandit algorithms, we achieve a breakthrough in streamlined methodological approaches and exponential improvements in performance. We introduce the $\epsilon$-greedy-K and UCB-K algorithms to achieve epsilon convergence and provide theoretical bounds for expected costs. Our results demonstrate that these bounds are of the same order as those in a fully observable environment, plus an additional term that decreases over time. Numerical experiments confirm our theoretical findings and highlight the trade-off between exploration and exploitation. Furthermore, our results indicate that the $\epsilon$-greedy-K algorithm is more balanced and performs more consistently compared to the UCB-K algorithm. These conclusions offer fresh insights into the field of online decision-making. Furthermore, our work establishes a bridge between reinforcement learning and the Gittins Index, suggesting that our proposed algorithms can serve as viable alternatives to the computationally demanding Gittins Index. Finally, we evaluate these methods across two distinct scenarios: a newsvendor problem with submodular utilities and a unit inventory problem.

This paper evaluates several existing navigation strategies and introduces a novel on-line path planning algorithm designed for holonomic differentiable mobile robots. We implemented this algorithm across four heterogeneous testbeds featuring various obstacle types and configurations to conduct a comprehensive comparative study. Our goal is to offer a foundation for developing new navigation algorithms and to reduce the time required to design and test new algorithims in the future. Many existing navigation algorithms lack comprehensive evaluation because they are typically tested only on simulated or simple testbeds. This paper presents a comprehensive comparison of path planning algorithms for holonomic differentiable mobile robots, which are available as open-source software and have been tested in four heterogeneous real-world testbeds. Our findings demonstrate that while navigation in simple scenarios is generally efficient and predictable using current state-of-the-art algorithms, performance in complex situations varies significantly. We contend that the path planning community needs to focus on two main areas in the future. First, researchers should investigate methods to guarantee that planned paths are both feasible and optimal given the specific robot and environment constraints. Second, there must be a concerted effort to conduct comparative studies in real-world settings using diverse robot types and complex obstacle configurations. Only through such research can the community effectively move beyond mere replications and replications-in-extend towards a new phase of genuine scientific contributions. This work is a result of the Path Planning and Holonomic Differentiable Mobile Robots special issue of the International Journal of Advanced Robotic Systems. The scientific contributions are further detailed in the corresponding article: ijars.org/articles/2019/10/18/path-planning-and-holonomic-differentiable-mobile-robots-special-issue.

This study characterizes the Witting configuration as the only configuration of 40 planes that satisfies a specific set of incidence conditions; notably, this configuration entangles the four exceptional complex projective planes with the Mutual Orthogonality of Latin Squares (MOLS) of order 4. Furthermore, we demonstrate how the geometry of the Witting configuration can generate a set of 17 squares, termed the Witting squares, and how these can, in turn, be used to construct the original Witting configuration. These squares are defined by a collection of 40 pairs of partial Latin squares, which, although not completing to full Latin squares, do complete to semi-Latin squares. The partial Latin squares are categorized based on the geometry of the Witting configuration, specifically utilizing the four exceptional planes and the Desarguesian plane. Each color in these semi-Latin squares corresponds to one of the 40 projective planes within the Witting configuration, with each plane containing exactly 22 points. These findings offer a fresh perspective on a longstanding open problem concerning the maximum number of order 4 Latin squares, for which the current record stands at 10. While a lower bound of 13 was previously established by Steinhauser in 1979 and the upper bound by Brouwer in 1989 as 16, a computer search by Kagey in 2022 revealed a set of 16 Latin squares of order 4, thereby setting a new record of 16 and closing the gap to Brouwer's upper bound.

SOD is crucial for reducing computational costs in visual tasks by allocating resources to significant areas. However, sated by progress on domain-specific datasets, the field now craves a shift toward real-world generalization. This study investigates generalization in SOD by evaluating 14 state-of-the-art DNN models across seven cross- and multi-category generalization benchmarks. Our analysis reveals that these models are often overfitted to their training data. We introduce a generalized error rate metric, offering a more rigorous assessment of a model's true generalization capability compared to performance on standard test sets. Additionally, we have made the benchmark and evaluation protocol public to encourage the development of models with enhanced generalization, a more critical attribute for practical deployment. The benchmark is available at https://github.com/ZhengNianShi/SOD-Generic-Benchmark. The results underscore the necessity of designing new, generalized SOD models. To further support this goal, we propose two novel generalized SOD tasks: cross-training evaluation and multi-category generalization. The latter addresses the most significant limitation of current SOD models. We provide the dataset and evaluation protocol at the end of this paper. We invite the community to explore this exciting new research direction and look forward to seeing innovative solutions at CVPR 2021. graduate students, this work offers a conceptual overview of quantum information theory, covering fundamental topics such as qubits, gates, measurements, and entanglement. It also serves as a collection of lecture notes from the Summer School on Quantum Information and Its Applications, 2021. Stylistically, the text mirrors the author's lecture approach: while the extensive references chapter lists relevant literature, the narrative itself avoids excessive mathematical formalism. Instead, it emphasizes intuitive understanding and conceptual clarity, illustrated throughout with examples from real experimental systems. Detailed derivations are minimized in favor of a conversational tone, and the inclusion of exercise sets aims to enhance the pedagogical value. Ultimately, the author hopes this work inspires readers to conduct their own research in the rapidly evolving field of quantum information. This edition includes twenty-one chapters and thirteen appendices, featuring ten new chapters on quantum networks, the quantum internet, quantum sensing, quantum memory, and quantum repetition codes, alongside ten revised ones. Furthermore, twenty-five exercise sets have been integrated throughout the book to strengthen its educational potential. A new chapter on quantum gravity has also been added, bringing the total to twenty-two chapters in this revised edition. The material is organized into eleven parts, beginning with the introduction of qubits and quantum measurements, followed by expositions on quantum gates and circuits, entanglement, quantum channels and decoherence, quantum algorithms, quantum cryptography, quantum teleportation and dense coding, quantum error correction, quantum memories and networks, and the quantum internet. Concluding sections include quantum thermodynamics, quantum gravity, and the future of quantum information. Additional appendices provide quantum exercises, biographical notes on key figures, quantum history, quantum philosophy, selected quantum equations, quantum jokes, practical qubit implementations, an overview of quantum information society and industry, and quantum career guidance. Throughout this revised edition, quantum information is consistently linked to actual physical qubit systems, with implementation details included in every chapter. Written as a quantum journey through time and space, the text begins with a prologue on the origins of quantum mechanics and concludes with an epilogue on the quest for a theory of everything, accompanied by quantum humor and practical insights into the implementability of quantum technologies. A website (www.qbook.in) is also featured, offering PDF copies of the book and its chapters, along with a search function by chapter and section. These operators arise from mappings with zero Jacobian, including maximal/minimal volume ellipsoids, volume preserving maps, and finite map entropy. Modern programming paradigms, such as reactive programming, now consider Concurrency-Independent Object Orientation (CIOO) as a fundamental requirement. In CIOO, the concurrency model is inherent to the language's design rather than an additional capability, and objects maintain their encapsulation principles across all execution modes, including concurrent and distributed environments. This paper presents the first formal definition of concurrency- independent object-oriented programming, built upon the framework of distributed vector addition systems with states (DVISs). We introduce and examine three DVIS-based languages: \textsc{d0}, \textsc{d1}, and \textsc{d2}, which correspond to the distributed, probabilistic, and quantum versions of the classic \textsc{d} language, respectively. These are followed by their sequential counterparts (\textsc{s0}, \textsc{s1}, and \textsc{s2}), where programs execute strictly sequentially. Our findings demonstrate that, unlike their sequential versions, these new DVIS languages possess significantly greater expressive power. Specifically, they can recognize a broader class of causal, multi-dimensional, and token-bounded languages, respectively. Furthermore, we establish that our proposed languages are strictly hierarchically structured. Finally, to better understand the source of this enhanced expressive power, we analyze the trace sets of these DVIS programs and their capacity to identify specific trace patterns. This research was partially supported by the Spanish MINECO/FEDER project no. TIN2015-65034-P and the Generalitat de Catalunya 2017-SGR 1288.

Pax Christi International (PCI) is a global network of Catholic peace organizations, with a South African presence that has been active for over fifty years. Founded in the late 1940s, the South African branch, then known as Pax Christi South Africa (PCSA), has been a consistent voice in the nation's struggle for freedom and justice. This article examines the historical, theological, and socio-political roots of PCSA, exploring its identity, development, and future direction. Drawing on an action research framework, the study utilizes various data sources, with a primary focus on archived materials from the Diocese of Pretoria, which hosted the organization's national office. The analysis centers on the legacy of these archives, which hold both personal and institutional value. The paper outlines the methodological approach used to analyze these records, detailing the life story methodology and the specific research questions addressed. Data collection was conducted between June and December 2017, followed by an analysis phase spanning January and February 2018. The section on findings begins with an overview of the archival material, describing its physical and intellectual structure. A subsequent, more detailed analysis of the content addresses the core research questions, starting with an exploration of PCSA's historical and theological foundations. The study concludes by presenting the organization's current state and its envisioned future. Finally, the work reflects on the challenges and opportunities faced by PCSA, as well as the broader PCS family in South Africa, over the coming years.

We propose a new robust value iteration algorithm to solve the associated robust dynamic programming problem, achieving performance that approaches the optimal robust cost in a computationally efficient manner. Our method relies on a specific property of convex functions known as the separable support function trick. Leveraging the associated kernel operator enables an interpretable reformulation of the problem as a convex optimization task. Through a range of numerical examples, we demonstrate that our method outperforms a state-of-the-art approach for robust value iteration, which is based on semi-infinite programming, by at least one order of magnitude in speed. In terms of geometry, the conditions for embeddability translate into necessary constraints on the parameters of flag-transitive generalised quadrangles. Galactic Center (GC) is home to a supermassive black hole (SMBH) and a dense collection of stars, stellar remnants, and star clusters. The stars within this region exhibit highly anisotropic spatial and kinematic characteristics. Over the past few decades, astronomers have proposed various theories to explain the origin of these unique stars, including the star formation history near the GC and the dynamical evolution of the stellar population. This study presents a comprehensive investigation into the age of the stars near the GC and the key factors influencing their evolution by analyzing the metallicity, luminosity, and line-of-sight velocity of 1,020 stars in the area. By applying Bayesian methods to identify chemical tagging, we categorize the GC stars into three distinct groups based on their dynamical properties. Our findings indicate that the mean ages of these groups are 1.2, 10.0, and 10.0 Gyr, respectively. We attribute the low metallicities and luminosity limits of the GC stars to the effects of tidal disruption by the SMBH and asymptotic giant branch (AGB) stars. Furthermore, the dynamical properties of the stars are interpreted as the GC area evolving from a relaxed to a core-collapsed state. Based on the distribution of the derived ages, we conclude that new stars continue to form in the GC area today, and the age distribution aligns with both the star formation history and the accretion of pre-existing stars from the galactic disk. Finally, the characteristics of the stars point to the GC area being a significant high-energy cosmic factory. The code utilized in this study is accessible at: \url{https://github.com/zhengyao1992/GalacticCenter}.

This abstract outlines our plans to implement this technique at the European XFEL. By utilizing two independent pulse pairs—a few-fs hard X-ray readout and a 100-fs FEL writing pulse—it will be possible to achieve a high repetition rate of 27,000 times per second, enabling the observation of dynamical processes on fs to ps timescales. This capability complements existing soft-X-ray methods, such as the Marangoni effect, which offer up to 10 MHz repetitions but operate at lower photon energies. We will present our plans and anticipated scientific outcomes. The proposed scheme, named XAXE (X-ray X-ray Absorption with Extreme Localization), has been selected for the first beamline of the European XFEL. Its primary objective is to initiate and monitor femtosecond-to-second timescale dynamics in both inorganic and organic systems. The scientific community's input on potential applications for this beamline is currently being sought. This proposal has been developed in collaboration with the European XFEL and PETRA III facilities, as well as the MAX IV Laboratory.

However, as entanglement manifests in various ways across different physical systems, designing efficient detection methods for general quantum states remains a significant challenge. In this study, we introduce a modified van-der Waals system comprising three atoms and two optical microcavities. Although the absence of dark matter in stellar systems is well-established, it remains uncertain whether this constraint applies universally or specifically to old, low-density stellar populations. This study investigates whether PBHs constitute the entire dark matter budget in the globular cluster 47 Tucanae. We conducted a comprehensive search for microlensing events by monitoring 1.5 million stars for 10 nights using the SuperWASP Southern Facility. The cluster's high density and age make it an ideal target for detecting long-timescale events corresponding to PBHs with masses between $10^{-2}$ and $10^3$ solar masses ($M_{\odot}$). We identified 15 clear microlensing events and analyzed them to determine if they support a PBH hypothesis. Our findings indicate that 47 Tucanae contains approximately $0.03 M_{\odot} M_{\rm{cluster}}^{-1}$ of stellar-mass PBHs, a result consistent with prior studies. However, this abundance is insufficient to explain the missing mass in the cluster, and it contradicts constraints derived from stellar dynamics in the Milky Way's Galactic Center. In recent years, deep neural networks have become the standard for classifying medical images, yet the high cost of annotated data often limits their practical application. To address this, researchers have turned to weak supervision, a method that reduces the need for manual labeling by using other data sources. A common approach within this framework involves training a classifier on labeled data and then leveraging its predictions on unlabeled data to create pseudo labels. However, the quality of these pseudo labels is highly dependent on the features the classifier has learned; if the features do not align well with the labels, the generated labels may be inaccurate. To overcome this, we propose a method that jointly trains a feature extractor and a classifier to minimize the difference between their outputs on a set of unlabeled data. This approach, an extension of Consistent Training (CT), offers a more direct optimization path than conventional classification tasks. Our evaluation on the ISIC 2019 benchmark demonstrates the effectiveness of our method. We achieved scores of 0.6466 and 0.6462 for tasks 1 and 2, placing in the top four in each category. Source code and trained models can be found at: https://github.com/alexei-ivanov/ISIC-2019-ISIC-2019-dataset-and-results.

We present a simulation encompassing eight scenarios across three domains: a structured scene understanding domain using COCO, a structured object detection domain utilizing VOCAVOC, and an object tracking domain featuring five different trackers with varying goals. Our findings indicate that self-supervised methods do not offer inherent benefits for continual learning; instead, they face the same pitfalls as supervised approaches. Specifically, most techniques struggle significantly with catastrophic forgetting in image classification, experience moderate forgetting in object detection, and face no noticeable forgetting issues in object tracking.

Consequently, choosing between self-supervised and supervised methods does not depend on the risk of catastrophic forgetting, as these risks are comparable. However, our analysis reveals that self-supervised methods are more vulnerable to performance degradation on prior tasks, particularly in scene understanding and tracking. Given these results, the primary advantage of selecting between these approaches should be evaluated based on computational efficiency regarding both time and computational resources.

To prioritize computational efficiency, we conducted experiments on COCO, VOCAVOC, and five tracking benchmarks, assessing 54 state-of-the-art methods. We also proposed a novel strategy that achieves a substantial improvement in the efficiency metric ($\Upsilon$) by adapting the batch size dynamically during training. Additionally, to enhance performance without compromising efficiency, we introduced a strategy that integrates self-supervised and supervised learning, demonstrating superior outcomes compared to using either method in isolation.

To overcome this limitation, we introduce the Recipe Prompting Method (RPM), which leverages text recipes to facilitate multi-ingredient generation. white dwarf or neutron star is tidally disrupted by a black hole. We assume the white dwarf or neutron star travels in a circular, edge-on accretion disk before its disruption. Our analysis of electromagnetic emissions indicates that as the star is stretched into a thin stream, a shocked region forms at the leading edge of the tidal tail, generating both synchrotron and blackbody radiation across radio to X-ray wavelengths. Furthermore, the star develops gravitational quadrupole asymmetry, causing it to emit gravitational waves at the orbit frequency for approximately five orbital cycles before disruption. The peak amplitude of these waves and their radiation reaction torque are most pronounced near the star's first Roche lobe. The peak gravitational wave luminosity from a white dwarf from this initial Roche lobe overflow (RLO) event can reach $10^{30}$ W, surpassing the combined luminosity of its electromagnetic and radiation reaction channels. Upon entering the accretion disk, the stellar stream becomes highly gaseous and gravitationally unstable, triggering the rapid formation of stars and the rapid growth of a mass clump that spirals toward the black hole. This clump persists for several orbits, maintaining a significant gravitational quadrupole moment that continues to emit gravitational waves. For a white dwarf with a 0.6 solar mass around a 10 solar mass black hole at an initial disk distance of 500 times the star's radius, the total gravitational wave energy released over the first year post-RLO1 (the initial RLO1 phase) and the formation of this dense clump amounts to $10^{-4} M_{\rm WD}c^2$. In this scenario, the gravitational wave signal from the first year exceeds the total gravitational wave signal emitted during the initial five orbital cycles before the first RLO1. Additionally, we demonstrate that the pre-RLO1 gravitational wave frequency can serve as a precise probe of the object's mean density, allowing for a determination of the mass ratio with an accuracy better than 1%. This precision enables the identification of an unknown object's nature based on the previously measured mean density. Consequently, the initial RLO1 frequency acts as a valuable tool for characterizing the pre-RLO1 white dwarf or neutron star. Finally, we note that the "star-eating" process, where a star is gradually consumed by a black hole within an accretion disk, produces periodic gravitational wave signals that could be detectable by the LISA observatory. A primary source of uncertainty in these measurements arises from hadronic form factors, which can be mitigated through a dispersion relation approach utilizing only experimentally accessible data. This study reports the first application of such a framework to the branching fractions of specific three-body semileptonic tau decays. To achieve this, we analyzed data from a typical dispersion relation involving experimentally measurable three-body tau decay spectra and the branching fractions for two specific decays: $\tau^- \to \pi^-\pi^0 \nu_\tau$ and $\tau^- \to \pi^-K^+ \nu_\tau$. Additionally, we calculated the form factors for these decays within the Standard Model using lattice QCD and perturbative QCD techniques. To assess potential new physics contributions, we examined simple models where the $W$ boson is replaced by a $Z'$ boson or a $Y'$ boson. To optimize the sensitivity of the selected decays to these models, we evaluated the relevant coupling constants. Finally, by comparing the formalism with experimental data, we derived the limits on $V_{td}$ and concluded that these two decays offer a novel technique for determining $V_{td}$ free from hadronic uncertainties. Furthermore, the chosen decays are sufficiently sensitive to detect non-Standard Model contributions from a $Z'$ boson. Given that lattice QCD and perturbative QCD continue to advance, this method will eventually reach a sensitivity of $10^{-4}$ for $Z'$ boson contributions. Consequently, the two decays investigated here provide a fresh approach to determining $V_{td}$. These findings will be presented in an upcoming paper to be published in Physical Review D.

To address these limitations, we propose a new framework for memory-based deblurring that utilizes a single blurry image to generate a pair of sharp frames. Experimental results demonstrate significant improvements over existing state-of-the-art methods, with the proposed solution achieving a 4.89% reduction in PSNR loss on the GTD dataset and a 5.12% reduction on the GameBlur dataset. Our analysis focuses on the evolution of eigenvalues and the emergence of oscillatory modes, with specific attention to in-plane and out-of-plane oscillations in nonsymmetric hebbian networks. Our approach combines analytical and numerical methods to investigate oscillatory dynamics in hebbian networks, analyzing both symmetric and nonsymmetric matrices. For nonsymmetric matrices, we specifically address upper Hessenberg forms. Our general findings are expected to be applicable to other linear parameter-varying (LPV) feedback systems featuring a Hessenberg structure. These structures arise in cognitive tasks within brain networks, as well as in graph theory and control theory. These results hold significant value for researchers studying dynamics in nonlinear hebbian networks. Specifically, our findings enhance the visualization of cognitive processes and offer robust conditions under which hebbian networks exhibit associated functional properties.

Light-atom scattering within the regime of coherent population trapping generates nonclassical states of motion for cold atoms, offering opportunities to create novel designs of entangled atomic "qubits" in spatial modes. We analyze the controlled generation of these entangled atoms, highlighting the conditions light-matter resonance must meet to facilitate the long-range interactions necessary for entanglement. Furthermore, we examine the constraints imposed by decoherence sources, which are essential for maintaining the atomic superpositions and entanglement necessary for quantum information processing. Finally, we present an alternative approach to producing classes of atomic entangled states through coherent scattering of entangled photons. These findings contribute to understanding the fundamental interactions governing light-matter interactions and provide new insights into the controlled generation of atomic qubits for quantum information processing and networking. The work also introduces a fresh perspective on light-atom interactions that may assist in quantum memory design and the development of quantum switches and gates within quantum information networks. This paper is part of the Special Issue: Quantum Technologies for a New Internet.

However, if the dark matter-nucleus interaction violates Lorentz invariance in a specific way, the transferred recoil energy becomes dependent on the nucleus's velocity, enabling the detection of previously invisible weakly-interacting sub-GeV dark matter. This phenomenon can be observed in direct detection experiments involving moving nuclei, such as those on Earth's rotation or orbit around the Sun. In this study, we derive an analytically exact formula for the differential recoil rate as a function of transferred energy and momentum. We apply this rate to search for dark matter interacting via Lorentz-violating operators within the non-relativistic limit, covering scenarios with and without spin. Our findings indicate that for nuclei moving at typical terrestrial velocities, the differential rate as a function of energy can reach approximately 10$^{-15}$ recoils/kg/s/GeV for a cross section of 1 pb. This represents an improvement of two to three orders of magnitude over previous estimates for similar dark matter parameters. Consequently, we have established new sensitivity limits on sub-GeV dark matter parameters based on existing experimental constraints. Looking ahead, we demonstrate that a next-generation detector with 1 kg of target mass could probe cross sections down to 1 fbpb, thereby mapping a previously unexplored parameter space. Although the differential rate lacks distinct features that would unequivocally confirm dark matter detection, the signal can be validated by reanalyzing current experimental data. We conclude by outlining future research directions, including the development of relativistic formulas and the application of these methods to direct and indirect detection scenarios. Overall, we believe our rigorous treatment of the differential recoil rate will serve as a valuable reference for upcoming experiments. Furthermore, we provide supplementary material with code for calculating the differential recoil rate and generating expected scatter plots. These tools are essential for preparing future experiments and optimizing their design. We have also released these as public repositories. While some existing literature addresses sub-GeV dark matter, our work distinguishes itself by providing an exact solution for the differential recoil rate as a function of energy and momentum, which is crucial for investigating the position-dependent effects anticipated in future halo scans. Additionally, we have extended the applicable cross section range to 1 fbpb, significantly below the 10 pb threshold established by current experimental limits. Finally, we have established new sensitivity bounds on sub-GeV dark matter parameters based on current experimental data.

Premature ventricular contractions (PVCs) are irregular heartbeats caused by electrical impulses originating from the ventricles rather than the sinoatrial node. They are associated with various cardiac conditions and can serve as early indicators of cardiovascular disease. Consequently, accurate detection and measurement of PVC-induced heart beats are vital for clinical diagnostics. However, extracting IBI values from raw pulse wave data is difficult, and existing methods often yield inconsistent results. This paper presents a hierarchical deep learning model for precise IBI measurement using data from wearable pulse wave sensors. The model is designed for robustness, requiring only small amounts of training data. It operates by sequentially combining three 1-D Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) with varying filter sizes to filter out noise and irregular heart beats during IBI estimation. We validate the model's efficacy by comparing it against benchmark IBI estimation algorithms using open-dataset IBIs and accelerometer data. Our findings show that the model's predictions align closely with ground truth IBIs across diverse datasets. Additionally, our results indicate that the model is capable of identifying PVCs and heartbeat pauses during IBI estimation using wearable sensor data.

Assumptions derived from Sanov's theorem allow the large deviations principle to be applied to finite times and forces, thereby characterizing the statistics of power fluctuations for active particles. Notably, these findings extend beyond AOUP models to systems in thermal equilibrium and can be readily generalized to other stochastic thermodynamic systems. Consequently, this work offers a model-dependent method for analyzing the large deviations of energy exchange in various stochastic systems. Conclusions drawn from this framework may serve as a foundational step toward investigating the large deviations of active particles experiencing large force fluctuations. These results are particularly pertinent for understanding small-scale active entities, such as cells moving across surfaces via extension and retraction of adhesion molecules, where analyzing large deviations in power is essential for exploring cellular energy consumption and non-equilibrium phase transitions. Additionally, this approach is applicable to the analysis of experimental data regarding energy exchange in active colloidal systems. Ultimately, these results establish a pathway for examining the large deviations of heat and work in small active systems. Such work builds upon and expands recent efforts to derive non-conventional statistical mechanics results, including those concerning the rare production of entropy and active work [1-10]. These references provide precise definitions of large deviations and demonstrate how to derive model-specific rate functions and associated families of measures. In this paper, those definitions are briefly reviewed to establish the framework for analyzing large deviations in power exchange for two common potential energies. Furthermore, by defining a reference family of measures, the text demonstrates how to apply the tangent map to derive large deviations for specific realizations of the active force and system energy, thereby connecting this approach to recent results on the large deviations of entropy production and active work. Finally, the rate functions associated with these reference families are explicitly calculated for two cases: an Active Harmonic Oscillator with a quadratic potential and an Active Pendulum with a periodic potential. These calculations rely on the fact that the large deviations of power share the same tangent map as those of heat and active work. This establishes a model-specific method for defining a reference family of measures that yields the large deviations principle for two key stochastic thermodynamic quantities: heat and work. These developments open new avenues for extending the analysis of large deviations in small active systems and can be readily adapted to other stochastic models. Indeed, the approach used here offers a general framework for establishing the large deviations principle for small active systems, providing a starting point for future research.

This paper introduces results from an experiment where two fine-tuned GPT-3 models were compared against a trilingual data augmentation strategy that pre-trained on non-English texts before further fine-tuning. We evaluated their performance on three classification tasks: sentiment analysis in German, news topic classification in Spanish, and subset classification in Russian. Our findings indicate that the translation strategy achieved performance comparable to or superior to the GPT-3 model. We attribute this partial superiority in certain tasks to the selection of non-English examples that are structurally similar to the target language samples. Given the vast diversity within each language, a more granular classification system is required to identify samples most similar to our targets, a task that is itself challenging. Finally, we show that our approach is transferable to other languages, including those with limited data and tools, such as Serbian. Higgs boson, the primary objective of the ATLAS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) has been to measure its properties, primarily through coupling, using methods applicable to any particle of the Standard Model or beyond. Given that production rates in the TeV range are substantial, these "off-diagonal" production mechanisms, which are independent of the boson's mass, offer the LHC unique potential to test the linear combination of Higgs couplings to vector bosons and top quarks predicted by the Standard Model. This paper examines the production of Higgs bosons in the mass region between 200 and 600 GeV with a focus on TeV-scale physics. Using a dataset of 35.9 fb$^{-1}$ collected by the ATLAS experiment in 2015 at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV, we present a search for TeV-scale physics in these off-diagonal production modes. The analysis employs a simplified production model featuring two independent production rates alongside two non-standard decay modes. The corresponding cross sections are determined to be 0.03 fb and 0.14 fb, respectively. These results establish the most sensitive limits to date for TeV-scale physics in off-diagonal Higgs production. Furthermore, within the context of the Standard Model, the production rate for a Higgs boson with a mass of approximately 300 GeV is constrained to be less than 1.1 fb at a 95% confidence level, representing an improvement of a factor of 10 over previous LHC limits. Additionally, a limit of 0.14 fb is set for non-Standard Model production of a 400 GeV Higgs boson decaying into $W$ or $Z$ bosons. The findings are also interpreted regarding several beyond the Standard Model theories, including supersymmetry, extra dimensions, and composite Higgs models. The data were published in 2017.

While activity-induced RV variations are typically suppressed through high-precision spectroscopy and analysis, residual effects can still mimic small planetary signals. Consequently, it is essential to quantify these residual activity signals and validate the absence of false positives by characterizing the activity state of the observed stars. This study investigates the activity levels of stellar targets used by the HARPS, HARPS-N, and ESPRESSO spectrographs to facilitate future joint analyses of these datasets. We introduce the 'Activity Flag' (AF), a straightforward and effective metric for estimating target star activity. The AF integrates six standard stellar activity indicators—$H\alpha$, $H\beta$, S' index, $R'V$, $e'$V, and $V$—into a unified 6-digit code. Each digit corresponds to an activity indicator, where values 0 and 1 denote 'quiet' and 'very active' states, respectively, derived from observed activity diagrams. Other states are interpolated between these extremes based on actual data. We applied the AF to approximately 60,000 observation nights from the HARPS archive, supplemented by new data from HARPS-N and ESPRESSO. Our results show that residual activity signals remain significant when observing very active stars, even after employing state-of-the-art data analysis techniques. Furthermore, we observed a slight increase in detection rates for both exoplanets and stellar activity signals when a target star is in a very active state. We conclude that the AF offers a robust and intuitive method for assessing target star activity, which is crucial for identifying nights where activity signals might contaminate the RV data. Additionally, the AF's simplicity suggests it could serve as a standardized metric for future joint data releases from HARPS, HARPS-N, and ESPRESSO. This paper is part of the special issue dedicated to the first decade of observations from HARPS-N.

By leveraging Berman's extension of THH to bicategories, we establish an equivalence between functors originating from the THH of a bicategory and shadows defined on that same bicategory. While extremal problems for cghs have been extensively researched, this paper investigates their associated saturation numbers. We provide an exact, asymptotically exact, or within a constant factor of the actual value of the saturation number for specific geometric and non-geometric configurations. Furthermore, we formulate a conjecture regarding the extremal saturation problem for cghs. Our analysis reveals a phase transition that occurs when the size of the vertex set $n$ relates to the subgraph size $r$. Our lower bound for $ex_{sat}(s,cr; n)$ is given by $\Omega(n^{1 + \frac{s-2}{\max\{1,s-r\}}})$. To address this limitation, we developed a four-link, non-rigid snake robot capable of efficient swimming using a single actuator. This study primarily addresses two objectives: (1) validating the ability of a centrally controlled, non-rigid snake robot to move effectively through a 3D fluid environment, and (2) investigating the relationship between the waveforms transmitted along the snake's spine and its resulting swimming performance. Our experimental findings offer insights into locomotion strategies for a wide range of non-rigid swimming robots.

While many swimming robots rely on complex and computationally demanding control methods, such as model predictive control, we propose a novel, computationally inexpensive strategy. Our results demonstrate that a simple feedback controller can achieve optimal swimming by utilizing proprioceptive data from the robot's joints. This approach significantly reduces the computational burden compared to model-based methods while maintaining the ability to swim efficiently in both viscous and inertial regimes. These findings provide valuable guidance for the future design of swimming robots that are not only morphologically efficient but also practical from an engineering perspective.

In recent years, there has been a surge in research regarding swimming robots that use models of real animals to generate efficient and robust locomotion. However, the computational demands of the control algorithms required to move these robots have received little attention. High computational requirements can be prohibitive for small or resource-limited robotic systems. This work addresses this gap by using a swimming robot to experimentally evaluate the computational cost of various control strategies. Our findings reveal that complex control methods, which often yield superior performance, are not always necessary for successful locomotion. Furthermore, we show that the complexity of a controller does not necessarily correlate with the efficiency of swimming. These results provide valuable direction for the robotic community regarding swimming robot control, particularly in balancing performance with limited computational resources.

Many robots and soft materials function effectively as undulatory swimmers by using the same traveling waves to move through diverse media. We constructed a robot that mimics the body of a swimming eel, featuring a flexible spine and a tail that can be controlled independently. By comparing the drag experienced by the spine and tail in air and water, we can identify the specific contributions to the robot's overall swimming performance.

This is because MAC success probability is highly dependent on the 2D spatial distribution of links, rendering throughput an unreliable metric for Maximally Throughput Scheduling (MTS). We propose a solution using Perceptual Computing and the Bayesian Inversion of the Monte-Carlo (BIMC) algorithm. First, robots or drones gather the coordinates of MAC users. Then, a cloud service estimates MAC success probabilities for all links and calculates a ranking for D2D nodes ready for transmission. Unlike traditional scheduling that requires a ground controller to monitor and schedule every link, BIMC only needs d2d nodes to report their locations to the perceptual service. This enables scalable scheduling that enhances security and privacy. Testing with over 10,000 simulated links in 2D shows that perceptual scheduling outperforms traditional methods, and it is efficient enough for real-time deployment. Furthermore, it offers enhanced security and privacy compared to central scheduling, as no ground controller is required to view or manage individual links. This paper details the algorithms, testing methods, and results of perceptual scheduling. Additionally, the source code is available at https://github.com/BerkeleyVisionLab/2D_D2D_scheduling. We derive an analytical formula for the time-averaged eccentricity just before the final plunge, demonstrating that it is independent of specific parameters such as the equation of state or mass ratio. In our studies, we analyzed 3000 mergers involving neutron stars with finite spins and finite tidal deformability, as well as 1000 mergers with zero spin and finite tidal deformability. In the specific cases of zero spin and finite tidal deformability, the orbital eccentricity just before the final plunge is approximately 0.97, regardless of the neutron star's equation of state or the merging stars' masses. This conclusion holds true for the vast majority of gravitational wave events, encompassing all cases where the observable tidal deformability is finite.

However, in many computer vision applications, events are identified using frame-by-frame extraction from video sequences, which is inefficient because the recorded sequences are played back continuously. To address this, event detectors should be capable of online, in-situ identification of events directly from event streams or frame-by-frame videos. Additionally, in practical applications, these detectors must perform deduplication to avoid redundant detections and ranking to prioritize event locations based on temporal and spatial information. Current state-of-the-art event detectors fail to meet these specific requirements. Consequently, we introduce the Yanyan Event Detector, which not only achieves state-of-the-art event detection performance but also implements deduplication and ranking mechanisms to identify events more efficiently and precisely in dynamic environments. Dynamic environments are characterized by the continuous occurrence of events, which can be idling, moving, or changing states. Event detection involves finding these events within images or videos, and in dynamic settings, events may happen simultaneously or sequentially. While some events are simple, others are complex, and repetitions are common. In such scenarios, deduplication and ranking are crucial to prevent redundancy and ensure timely decisions. Deduplication eliminates duplicate events, while ranking orders them according to specific criteria. Although event detection has been extensively researched, few studies have focused on deduplication and ranking. In this work, we introduce yanyan-event-detector, which not only achieves state-of-the-art event detection but also performs deduplication and ranking to enhance detection quality and practicality. Experimental results confirm that yanyan-event-detector outperforms other approaches in both F1-score and deduplication/ranking performance. We will release our code and dataset publicly to assist researchers in advancing this field.

A primary challenge in applying deep learning to real-world scenarios is the black-box nature of deep neural networks (DNNs), which hinders user trust, adoption, and regulatory compliance. Although the field of AIOps has seen rapid growth in the past decade, there is a scarcity of work addressing the explainability of such systems. This paper presents AIOpx, a framework designed to explain DNN-based AIOps systems to end-users. By leveraging a taxonomy of AI system components and insights from three case studies, AIOpx generates explanations that illustrate the role of each component during specific failure events. We assess the feasibility and efficacy of this framework by evaluating its ability to increase user understanding of and trust in AIOps systems. Our findings indicate that AIOpx effectively enhances users' comprehension of AI systems, thereby fostering greater trust, particularly among non-experts. This work paves the way for further research into explaining AI systems, advancing the broader goal of creating more transparent and trustworthy technologies.

Although remote histopathology assessment based on endoscopic images represents a significant area of research, the replacement of the pathologist's opinion with deep neural networks remains challenging. This difficulty stems from limited data, the high cost and time required for expert annotations, and the scarcity of reliable metrics to gauge annotation quality. This study presents a framework for colorectal polyp classification that addresses these annotation challenges. We propose using "annotation quality labels" generated by a pre-trained model to guide the creation of endoscopic images of polyps via adversarial training. These labels describe pathologist annotations from a histopathological perspective, enabling the verification and enhancement of annotation quality while training a deep neural network for remote histopathology-based colorectal polyp classification. The method was validated using publicly available datasets of histopathology images featuring yea/nue y stain annotations and a separate endoscopic image dataset with the same labels. Our approach outperformed remote assessment methods relying solely on expert quality data by achieving 86.2% accuracy on a test set containing 1,000 images, compared to 71.7% accuracy for the baseline. Furthermore, we demonstrated that the generated quality labels accurately reflect the diagnostic quality of annotations for individual polyps by comparing them with annotations produced under specific guidance. By ensuring adequate data for individual cases and confirming its validity through cross-validation with pathologists, our method achieves performance in remote histopathology-based polyp classification that rivals traditional endoscopic histopathology assessment. This research holds significant potential for aiding physicians in diagnosing patients with colorectal polyps.

This paper introduces a new algorithm for phase retrieval that leverages deep generative models, specifically addressing partial phase measurements while accounting for non-Gaussian priors. The proposed method is grounded in the Deep Generative Network Phase Retrieval (DGNR-PR) framework, which is defined by a specific probability distribution. We demonstrate that finding a solution corresponds to identifying a stationary point of the DGNR-PR function. Consequently, we propose an alternating minimization algorithm that treats the observation matrix as fixed and minimizes the network parameters. Numerical experiments indicate that this approach successfully recovers signals of various dimensions from measurements as low as 30% of the signal's length, even under significant noise. These results are supported by a comprehensive theoretical framework. Key findings include: (i) the proof establishing the algorithm's convergence to a stationary point; (ii) the development of a novel metric for quantifying recovery performance in phase retrieval problems; and (iii) the establishment of a metric to measure reconstruction quality when using models with poor prior knowledge. Numerical tests were performed on prior models including Gaussian, real-valued complex-valued, and real-valued periodic functions. Significant recoveries were achieved even with highly corrupted or partially lost measurements. Furthermore, we show that our method performs comparably to established techniques such as Alternating Least Squares (ALS), Phase Recovery using Artificial Neural Networks (PR-ANN), and Phase Recovery using Normalizing Flows (PR-NF). PR-ANN and PR-NF were implemented by adapting existing code from public repositories. In contrast, we demonstrate that our approach yields superior or comparable results when measurements are partial, partial and noisy, or both partial and highly corrupted. These methodologies are broadly applicable to phase retrieval problems across diverse domains, such as those utilizing single-pixel sensors. The code is available at https://github.com/sohailshah/Deep-Generative-Network-Phase-Retrieval.

Although its application to optimization is theoretically promising, the practical benefits of QAOA over heuristic methods like simulated annealing remain uncertain for small-scale instances.
